docs.title: Changelog
docs.text: Each release, newest first: what changed, then under Upgrading what to change in code, commands or installs that use the previous release.

docs.title: Version 0.22.0
docs.text:
The low-level API is SimPy, with desflow's own resources, stores and containers, so SimPy code runs there. The SimPy Compatibility page lists every modelling feature of SimPy 4.1.2 with its status in each API: 48 are native in YAML, the builder and the low-level API and checked against plain SimPy, 48 are not yet, which 0.23.0 makes native, as the Roadmap says, and 2 are differences kept by design.

  • A SimPy Compatibility page lists every SimPy 4.1.2 modelling feature with its status in each API, its forms and the tests that compare it with SimPy.
  • Patience and balking: a task's patience takes a duration such as 30 s, and orders that leave or refuse to join are counted as tasks.<task>.reneged and .balked. See Patience and Reneging and Balking.
  • A store can start with items: stores.<name>.items, add_store(..., items=[...]) and DynamicStore(..., items=[...]); a priority store takes [priority, item] pairs. initial_time takes a duration such as 8 h. See Stores and Containers and Time and Pacing.
  • A store get can take a filter, such as item.area == attr.area, and patience covers the wait for a get as well as for a resource; item_field adds the item a YAML get took to the payload. See Stores and Containers and Filtered Inventory.
  • Tasks interact as SimPy processes do: signals that tasks fire and wait for, a wait for one or all of signals, child flows, timeouts and conditions, and fail, fail_reason and on_fail for a task that fails. context.spawn returns the process it starts, and context.call starts a child flow. See Process Interaction, Tasks and Processes and Wait for One or All.
  • Interrupts and preemption: an interrupt on a task or scenario step, or context.interrupt, interrupts running task instances; on_interrupt: resume, restart or abandon says what each does; preempt: true on a priority resource lets a lower priority value take a busy unit. See Interruptions and Resources.
  • A task can hold several resources, resource: [picker, bench], acquired in that order, and hand a unit to the next task with keep; a model that acquires resources in opposite orders is refused. See Competing Resources and Resources.
  • End conditions: run.stop ends a run at a signal or a condition, and run.drain (or desflow run --drain) stops the arrivals at until and finishes the entities already in the model; start(), step(), peek() and close() step a builder or YAML run one event at a time, and finish() runs a started run on to its end. The statistics count flows.<arrival>.started and in_system, and tasks.<task>.in_progress. See End Conditions and Time and Pacing.
  • A low-level request can be cancelled with request.cancel() and given back with resource.release(request), as in SimPy. See Resources.
  • Breakdowns: resources.<name>.breakdown, add_breakdown and run_breakdowns make a resource fail at random and be repaired, interrupting the work it was doing or letting it finish; each failure and repair publishes down and repaired, and the statistics count resources.<name>.down, downtime and failures. The Preemptive Breakdowns guide becomes Breakdowns. See also Resources.
  • Schedules in every API: the builder's add_scenario and add_step, and the low-level run_scenario, take the same steps as a blueprint's scenario. See Time-varying Arrivals and Changing Demand.
  • Replay: an arrival's replay, add_arrival_replay and the low-level read_trace take arrivals from the rows of a CSV or Parquet file, or a list of dicts, at their recorded times, with the row's fields as attributes. See Local Replay and Arrivals and Services.
  • Faster runs at factor: 0: SimPy's own step processes each event, a record's timestamp is formatted once per second of the clock, and ConsoleEgress logs a batch with one call. A low-level workload runs 1.14 times faster than in 0.21.0, and printing every record costs about a seventh of what it did. See Performance Tuning, whose measurements benchmarks/throughput.py repeats.
  • simulation.lag_interval and SimulationContext(lag_interval=) set how often system.simulation.lag_seconds is published. See Time and Pacing.
  • The record contract: Records and Telemetry gives every field its type, and a docs test fails when the page and the payload models differ. simulation.timezone, SimulationContext(timezone=) and DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(timezone=) name the zone timestamps are written in, and Statistics defines which entities each count covers.
  • Replications: desflow run FILE --replications N and desflow.replicate run a model with seeds spawned from one seed, ending each replication at until, a stop or the end of a drain, and give each statistic's mean and 95% half-width; the model's sinks receive the result once, as <sim_id>.stats.<measure>.replication.<i>, .mean, .half_width and .n. See Replications and Trusting Results.
  • Experiments: desflow experiment and desflow.run_experiment compare designs with paired replications and sweeps, ending each run at until, a stop or the end of a drain, apply checks that fail the command, compare with observed values, and write CSV and JSON results and a report.md; desflow report builds the report again. See Experiments, Comparing Designs and Parameter Sweeps.
  • Input fitting: desflow fit and desflow.fit_column fit a column of measured times to every distribution family, with diagnostics and a plot, and write settings a blueprint loads with the new !include tag. See Input Fitting, Fit the Inputs and Fit a Distribution.
  • An unknown key in a blueprint or an experiment file names the closest key that place takes, such as "did you mean 'patience'?", and a misspelt name of a resource, task, signal or path names the closest one; the errors this release adds say how to fix them.
  • Easier to start: the Home page has a "Where to Start" table, the Cheat Sheet gives the common YAML keys and builder calls side by side, and every tutorial and How-To page gives its level: Basics, Intermediate or Advanced.

docs.title: Upgrading
docs.text:
• desflow needs SimPy 4.1.2 or later, where it accepted 4.0.0, and pydantic 2.6.0 or later, where it accepted 2.0.0, with which desflow 0.22.0 does not import. The conformance tests check desflow against SimPy 4.1.2, which chooses the user to preempt differently from 4.1.1 on equal keys; SimPy 4.0 also imports pkg_resources, which a new Python environment does not have.
  • A store or container built with a capacity of 0 now works, as a resource does, and holds nothing until its capacity rises; SimPy's ValueError stopped it before.
  • A priority on a store get is refused; priority orders a put into a priority store.
  • Resources grant units with the same events as SimPy's Resource, so requests at the same simulation time are granted in SimPy's order, which can change seeded output where such ties occur.
  • patience now covers a task's whole wait, its wait, its resource and its get, where it covered only the resource, so a task can renege while it waits for stock. It counts waiting time only, so a preempted task that queues again goes on with the time it has left. A task with patience needs a resource, a get or a wait.
  • A store without priority is now a SimPy FilterStore, so a get can take a filter. While no waiting get has a filter, it grants gets as simpy.Store does, one waiting get each time it is triggered, as before; while a filtered get waits, it looks at every waiting get each time, as FilterStore does, so gets at the same instant can be granted in another order.
  • A builder task whose function raises, or a YAML task whose !python payload function raises, now fails the task, publishing failed with the error as its reason and ending the entity's flow, instead of stopping the run.
  • DynamicResource.pool and DynamicResourceRequest.cancelled are gone: the resource grants units as SimPy's Resource does. Call request.cancel() to leave the queue; resource.queue.items holds (rank, request) pairs, where it held PriorityItems. A request that gives up, by cancel() or by reneging, now leaves the queue at once, so len(resource.queue.items) and the queue_length and queue_length_avg statistics no longer count it.
  • The built-in statistics publish new names: tasks.<task>.in_progress from minimal, and flows.<arrival>.started and in_system from basic. A low-level process that calls env.stats.task_queued, task_started and task_finished publishes in_progress too, and one that calls flow_started publishes the flow counts.
  • Events with the statuses balked, reneged, failed, interrupted, preempted and resumed, and a resource's down and repaired events, keyed by its name, reach the sinks, so a consumer that filters on status should expect them.
  • A scenario step now applies before every other event at its time, as SimPy applies its own until, so an arrival at the step's time draws its next gap from the new value; seeded runs whose steps fall on the time of another event can give other numbers.
  • At factor: 0, system.simulation.lag_seconds is no longer published unless lag_interval (low-level lag_monitor_interval) is set; a run that goes live publishes it from the go-live instant. At a factor above 0 it is published every simulation second, as before.
  • ConsoleEgress logs each batch with one call, one line per record, so the logging format's prefix starts each batch rather than each line. Code that reads the console log record by record splits each message into lines.
  • At factor: 0, with no go_live_at still to come, each event is processed by SimPy's own step and strict=True is not checked, as there is no wall clock to fall behind; while a go_live_at is pending, the real-time step runs as before.
  • Every timestamp now carries a time zone offset, such as 2026-10-03T12:00:00.000+10:00, so a consumer that parses it must accept +HH:MM, and a sink column without a zone, such as a PostgreSQL timestamp, now gets the UTC wall time. By default timestamps are in UTC, +00:00, where they were in the machine's local time with no offset; set timezone to an IANA name to write them in a zone. A logical_start_time or go_live_at without an offset, now and the default start are read in timezone, else in the zone of logical_start_time, else in UTC, not in local time: for a start or go-live of now, pass datetime.now(timezone.utc), not datetime.now(), whose local wall time would be read in that zone and be off by the difference. env.start_datetime always has a time zone. A start and a go-live, one with an offset and one without, no longer fail. The clock runs in UTC, so a daylight-saving change no longer adds or drops simulation time.
  • A Parquet file now has a column for every key of any row in its batch, where the first row's keys alone were written and later keys were lost; a key that first appears in a later batch adds a column to the later files, and an integer column that later gets a float becomes a double. An Iceberg table not named in schemas gains such a key as an optional column. A batch a Parquet or Iceberg sink cannot write is logged at ERROR, where it stopped the sink with no error.
  • A container's starting level keeps its type in YAML, the builder and the low-level API, so level: 1, level=1 or init=1 gives a level of 1, as SimPy does, where it gave 1.0.
  • A payload key that starts and ends with two underscores, such as __table__, is reserved: Kafka, Parquet, JSON Lines, Iceberg and the console drop it, with a warning, where they wrote it as data. Rename such a key, such as __source__ to source, to keep it. PostgreSQL and Redis still route by __table__ and __stream__. Routers, such as a Kafka topic_router or a storage path_router, no longer see the dropped keys; PostgreSQL and Redis still write any other such key as data.
  • Fitting needs the new fit extra, which installs scipy and matplotlib: pip install "desflow[fit]". The all extra includes it, so desflow[all] now installs both.
  • The glue extra needs boto3 1.26.0 and aws-glue-schema-registry 1.0.0 or later, and the glue and confluent extras need dataclasses-avroschema 0.65.7 or later; an environment with older releases upgrades them.

docs.title: Version 0.21.0
docs.text:
The simulation model grows: more distributions, stores and containers that tasks use, flows of tasks, built-in statistics and ground-truth labels. The docs gain a Learn section with a tutorial, the Shop, and a User Guide with one page per part of the library.

  • Five new distributions, uniform, triangular, gamma, weibull and empirical, and, in YAML, durations such as 5 min for every time-valued parameter. The builder's distribution parameters take numbers in seconds, and its warmup and run(until=) also take durations; the low-level API takes numbers in seconds. See Arrivals and Services and Distributions.
  • Each distribution draws from a random stream of its own, so adding an arrival leaves the other draws unchanged. A run without a seed draws one and logs it, and desflow run --seed N repeats it. See Randomness and Seeds.
  • Stores and containers that tasks take from and add to, with get and put; a container's level is a live path. See Stores and Containers.
  • A queue order per resource, fifo, lifo or priority, and a priority per task. See Resources.
  • Flows of tasks: next by name, condition or weights, entity attributes with attributes and set, and timed steps with a service and no resource. A builder arrival loop takes a task's instance id from context.next_instance(task), the counter next uses too. See Task Flow.
  • Built-in statistics at five levels, stats: none to stats: all, and a warmup that leaves the start of a run out. See Statistics.
  • Ground-truth labels: a scenario step's record publishes what it changed to when: labels sinks only. See Live Parameters.
  • Every ingress connector reads path and value, and a bad message is logged and skipped. See Ingress.

docs.title: Upgrading
docs.text:
• Python 3.11 or later is needed.
  • Ingress messages use path and value: Kafka's path_id and Redis's param_path and param_value are renamed, and a Kafka message, or a PostgreSQL ingress row, with a null value is now refused. Call send_config(topic, path=..., value=...) where it was called with path_id=.
  • For each table the PostgreSQL ingress reads, simulation_params by default, rename the columns: ALTER TABLE simulation_params RENAME COLUMN param_path TO path; and ALTER TABLE simulation_params RENAME COLUMN param_value TO value;
  • An event's key is now the entity's key, the arrival name and a counter from 1 (orders-1), not task-<task id>, and every event has two new fields after key: task and instance. PostgreSQL rows gain task and instance columns where the table has them. See Records and Telemetry.
  • telemetry entries in a blueprint no longer take publish. Use stats: minimal, which publishes the same readings as Shop.stats.resources.<name>.<reading>, and function for readings of your own.
  • Seeded runs give other numbers than before, because each distribution has its own random stream, and requests of equal priority are now served first in, first out.
  • A distribution parameter the family does not take, such as rate on a normal, is now refused at build. The builder's distribution parameters are keyword-only: write add_service("packing", "normal", mean=3).
  • Under the default fifo queue a request's priority is ignored. Add the resource with queue="priority" (YAML queue: priority; low-level DynamicResource(env, sim_id, name, queue="priority")) to rank requests; a task priority on another order is refused.
  • context.wait_for_arrival now yields the new Entity. Pass it to the task as entity=, or the task starts an entity of its own keyed by the task's name.
  • A container's current_cap is its capacity, its largest amount; a model that used it as a level moves to level. DynamicContainer(init=None) now starts at the registry's level, 0 unless the ContainerConfig gives one.

docs.title: Version 0.20.0
docs.text: The package dynamic-des is renamed desflow. The classes, the YAML format, the records and the extras are the same as in 0.19.0.

docs.title: Upgrading
docs.text:
• Install desflow instead of dynamic-des, with the same extras: pip install desflow, uv add desflow, or for example pip install "desflow[kafka]". The last dynamic-des release, 0.20.0, installs desflow with the same extras. To install desflow beside dynamic-des 0.19.0 instead, uninstall dynamic-des first: with pip, uninstalling it afterwards also removes dynamic_des and ddes, and pip install --force-reinstall --no-deps desflow puts them back.
  • Import desflow instead of dynamic_des, for example from desflow import SimulationContext.
  • Run the desflow command instead of ddes, for example desflow run shop.yaml or desflow examples.
  • import dynamic_des still works in this release. It shows a FutureWarning and gives the desflow modules, submodules such as dynamic_des.connectors.egress.kafka included. The ddes command still works too: it prints a warning and runs desflow. Both are removed in a later release, which this page will name.
  • The docs are at jaehyeon.me/desflow, and the repository is jaehyeon-kim/desflow on GitHub.

docs.title: Roadmap
docs.text: Releases come in the order shown, without dates: a release ships when it is ready. The timeline lists released work, marked with a tick, then the work planned for the coming releases, in order, marked with a clock. Each item links to its GitHub issue.

docs.title: Now and next
docs.text:
Rename to desflow

Done in 0.20.0: the package, its import name and its command are all desflow. The old dynamic-des names still work, with a warning, until a later release.

Distributions and seeds

Done in 0.21.0: more distributions, including empirical, which draws from values measured in a real system. Each distribution draws from its own random stream, so adding an arrival leaves the other draws unchanged. desflow now needs Python 3.11 or later. #42

Ingress messages

Done in 0.21.0: every ingress connector, Kafka, Redis and PostgreSQL, takes a parameter change as path and value, the names a scenario step already uses. #51

Stores, containers and priority

Done in 0.21.0: tasks take items from stores and amounts from containers, and a resource serves its queue oldest first, newest first or by task priority. #43

Flows

Done in 0.21.0: routing between tasks by a condition or by probability, entity state that an order keeps from task to task, and delays without a resource. #44

Statistics and ground truth

Done in 0.21.0: wait and service times, throughput, utilisation and queue length as telemetry, with a warm-up period; and ground-truth records of what a scenario changed, so a detector or an agent can be scored against them. #45

Native core parity

Done in 0.22.0: the operations on the SimPy Compatibility page, natively in YAML, the builder and the low-level API, each checked against SimPy: signals, interrupts, tasks needing several resources, filtered store gets, stopping and stepping a run, and customers who give up on a queue or never join it. #64

Breakdowns, changing demand and replay

Done in 0.22.0: a resource that fails and is repaired, a schedule of times at which an arrival rate or a capacity changes, and arrivals read from a local CSV or Parquet file. #65

Replications

Done in 0.22.0: run a model with many seeds and get each statistic with a confidence interval, so a result is never read from one run. #59

Experiments

Done in 0.22.0: compare designs and sweep parameters over replications, fail an experiment when a result breaks a limit, fit a distribution to measured data, and write a Markdown report, all on one machine. #66

Speed

Done in 0.22.0: faster runs that publish the same records. #24

Record contract

Done in 0.22.0: every record field documented with its type and format, payload keys such as __table__ reserved for desflow, a timezone setting for timestamps, and no lag_seconds from a run at full speed. The format is frozen before 1.0. #51

SimPy parity

In 0.23.0: every SimPy 4.1.2 feature natively in YAML, the builder and the low-level API, each checked against SimPy, such as nested conditions, event callbacks, unlimited stores and custom resource types. The SimPy Compatibility page lists each one, and the two differences kept by design. #71

Blueprint schema and AI skill

A JSON Schema for blueprints, shipped in the package, so editors complete keys and flag mistakes as you type, and a skill that teaches an AI assistant to write and check blueprints. #41

Downstream checks

With the blueprint schema: before a release, the tests of projects that use desflow, the benchtop data generators, run against the new version, and a test fails when a public class, function or argument is removed or changed. #67

desflow explain

Shows a simulation as a graph, marks each resource OK, congested or unstable (its queue grows without limit), names the bottleneck and suggests changes. desflow run --sample prints a few records from a blueprint. #47

Learn section

The shop tutorial, which extends one shop model page by page and answers a question with a number on each page, has 20 pages since 0.22.0, which added replications, comparing designs, sweeps, fitting, patience, interruptions, end conditions and more. Left: concept pages on a simulation study, checking and validating, queueing and output analysis, a final study of the whole shop and an independent problem. #60

docs.title: Later
docs.text:
The work after the Learn section, on the way to 1.0, in the order it is planned.

  • Storage and Python 3.15

    Parquet and JSONL on more cloud storage, more Iceberg catalogs, and Python 3.15 support.

    #32, #40

  • Library hooks for the server

    Changes the server will need, made before 1.0 so the server adds to the library without changing it: parameter changes that report who made them and why, and a way to load and inspect a simulation folder.

    #70

  • Reserve the gen key

    Before 1.0, a blueprint refuses a mapping with a gen key in a payload, a scenario value, a record field, a task's set or an arrival's attributes. After 1.0, gen marks a generated value, such as {gen: uniform, ...}, so no 1.0 blueprint can already use the key for something else.

    #53

  • Record contract freeze

    A final check of every record field, then the format is marked frozen: no 1.x release removes a field, renames it or changes its type.

    #51

  • 1.0

    The generated YAML key reference, a command-line page, a compatibility policy and upgrade notes.

    #54

docs.title: What 1.0 means
docs.text: From 1.0, the YAML blueprint format, the desflow command, the public Python API (SimulationContext, DynamicRealtimeEnvironment and the connectors) and the published record format stay compatible across every 1.x release. The package status moves from Beta to Production/Stable.

docs.title: Simulation model
docs.text:
• Maintenance, schedules and incidents: planned maintenance, a failure clock that runs only while a resource works, schedules that repeat by time of day, and incidents that change several parameters at once. 0.22.0 ships random breakdowns with repair and finite schedules.
  • More flow and resource features: batching, matching and splitting, setup times, and resources chosen by skill.
  • Reuse, costs and continuous flow: parts of a model defined once and used several times, costs and energy per resource state, and levels that rise and fall continuously.
  • Transport on maps: vehicles that move between locations on real roads and publish their positions.
  • Data-driven inputs: arrivals replayed from a database, or taken live from a Kafka topic.
  • Decisions from outside: a dispatcher or an agent answers for one order or session, and a run can repeat exactly from a log of those answers.

docs.title: Analysis
docs.text:
• Experiments: experiment designs, optimisation, and calibration against observed data.
  • Fitting and comparison: distribution fitting from more data sources, automatic fault-impact experiments, and fuller run comparison and fidelity scoring.

docs.title: Simulation server
docs.text:
The server ships after 1.0, as 1.x releases installed with the server extra.

  • Server API and MCP tools: desflow serve runs simulations through a REST API: upload, start, stop, change parameters during a run and follow its events. MCP tools, which let an AI agent do the same, are experimental. (#48)
  • Browser UI: the same from a browser, including each simulation's graph from desflow explain. (#49)
  • Schedules: run simulations on cron schedules. (#50)
  • Server image and odctl profile: a published image and an odctl profile run the server locally with nothing installed on the host. (#52)
  • Visualisation: animation of a running or recorded simulation, and a map view.
  • Distributed runs: workers on several machines.

docs.title: Writing simulations
docs.text:
• Generated values in blueprints: random values, IDs and timestamps in YAML, then entities, relations between records, states and ramps.
  • Preview loop: run a blueprint again each time the file changes, and check a file without running it.
  • Example gallery and visual builder.
  • Conversion: turn a YAML blueprint into builder code, and builder code into YAML with no Python, with an error that names each part that cannot be converted and how to rewrite it.

docs.title: Connectors
docs.text:
• More sinks: a webhook sink, a generic SQL sink and more.
  • Delivery faults: records delivered late, twice, damaged or not at all, to test how a pipeline handles them.
  • Lineage: each run reported to OpenLineage and OpenMetadata.

docs.title: Platform
docs.text: • More speed: cheaper record publishing, which takes about 40 percent of a run, with the same published records (#69), and a faster runtime for YAML-only blueprints if measurements show the need.

docs.title: Docs
docs.text:
• Reference: a page for each generator and connector, with examples and the records they produce, and a command-line cheat sheet.
  • How-To: generating data at scale, and testing pipelines with simulated data.

docs.title: What Is Discrete-Event Simulation?
docs.text: If you have never used simulation, start here. No maths is needed: a simulation is a way of playing out "what would happen if" on a computer, one step at a time, instead of guessing from averages.

docs.title: Simulation in Everyday Terms
docs.text:
Think of a coffee shop. Customers come in about once a minute, and the barista takes about 50 seconds per coffee. Will there be a queue at 9 in the morning? What if a second barista starts at 9:30, or a bus drops off twenty people at once?

You could answer by watching the shop with a notebook. You would not write something down every second, because most seconds nothing changes. You would write only the moments when something happens: a customer arrives, an order starts, a coffee is ready. Each of those moments is an event, and the notebook is enough to tell you who waited and for how long.

A discrete-event simulation (DES) is that notebook, written by a computer. You describe the shop: how often customers come, how long a coffee takes, how many baristas there are. The computer then plays out the events one after another, with random variation like in real life, and writes down what happens. Because it skips the quiet seconds, it can play out a day, or a year, in moments. Change the description, add a barista or double the customers, and run it again to see the difference.

desflow does this for any system with arrivals, work and limited capacity: a factory, a warehouse, a shop, a support desk, a network. What it adds is that every event is also sent out as a record, to Kafka, a database or files, so the simulation becomes a source of realistic data. Building Blocks shows the parts you describe a model with, and Queues and Capacity explains why a queue grows the way it does.

docs.title: Events and the Event List
docs.text:
This section is the same idea in the terms the rest of the docs use. A discrete-event simulation models a system as a series of events: an order arrives, a packer starts on it, the packer finishes. Each event happens at an instant, and between two events nothing changes. So the simulation keeps a list of what happens next, in time order, takes the earliest, moves its clock straight to that instant, and carries it out. Carrying out an event usually schedules more: an order that a packer starts on schedules its own finish 1.5 seconds later.

The clock jumps, so a simulated week with a few thousand events takes as long to compute as those events need, not a week. desflow runs on SimPy, which provides the event list and the clock. On top of SimPy it adds:

  • Pacing. factor makes the clock follow the wall clock (1.0), run faster or slower, or not wait at all (0.0), so the same model can drive a live dashboard or write a month of history in seconds. Time and Pacing explains it.
  • Live values. Every parameter is in a registry and can change while the simulation runs. Live Parameters explains it.
  • Records. What happens is published as events and telemetry to the sinks you attach. Records and Telemetry shows the formats.

docs.title: Entities, Resources and Queues
docs.text:
The things that flow through a model are entities: orders, visitors, support calls. An entity arrives, needs something that is limited, such as a packer or a packing bench, holds it while it is served, and leaves. That limited thing is a resource. When every unit of a resource is busy, the next entity waits in its queue. Arrivals, service times, resources and queues are what a model is built from; Building Blocks covers each one.

Queues are where the interesting behaviour comes from. Two models with the same average times can have very different waits, because a run of quick arrivals or one slow job holds everyone up. A simulation shows that directly, where an average cannot.

docs.title: From Model to Records
docs.text:
A model on its own only moves its clock. What makes it useful here is what it publishes. A task publishes queued, started and a finished event for every entity, and telemetry reports what you choose, such as how many units of a resource are busy. A sink writes each record to Kafka, a database or files, so the simulation becomes a source of realistic data for whatever reads it.

Whether that data looks real depends on the model being stable: if work arrives faster than the resources can finish it, the queue grows without limit and every later event is delayed more. Queues and Capacity explains how to tell, and how to fix it.

docs.title: SimPy and desflow
docs.text:
desflow is built on SimPy, a Python library for discrete-event simulation. SimPy provides the event list, the clock, processes and resources. desflow keeps all of them and changes four things: the clock can switch pacing, every parameter can change while the run goes on, random times are named distributions, and everything that happens is published as records. A low-level desflow model is ordinary SimPy code with these additions.

Part In SimPy In desflow Clock and pacing Environment runs without waiting; RealtimeEnvironment(factor, strict=True) follows the wall clock and raises RuntimeError when the model falls behind one class, DynamicRealtimeEnvironment, does both: factor=0 runs without waiting, go_live_at switches to real time partway through a run (SimPy's factor cannot change once set), logical_start_time gives every record a date and time, and falling behind is reported as telemetry; strict=True raises RuntimeError as SimPy's does, at a factor above 0, while YAML and the builder have no strict setting Processes generators started with env.process the same, and the builder adds @app.task, @app.arrival_loop, @app.telemetry_loop and add_process, which write the common ones for you Random times none built in: a model calls random or NumPy itself ten named distributions with checked parameters, drawn by a Sampler from the current values each time; each distribution draws from a random sequence of its own, made from the run's seed and its registry path Resources Resource, Container and Store keep the capacity they were created with: it has no setter, so assigning a new one raises AttributeError (SimPy 4.1). Resource serves requests in the order they arrive, and PriorityResource by priority DynamicResource, DynamicContainer and DynamicStore follow a capacity in the registry, and a resource that shrinks lets busy units finish. A resource serves its queue fifo, lifo or by priority, equal priorities first in, first out. run() builds the stores and containers a model declares, and tasks put to and get from them Parameters Python variables, changed only by the model's own code a registry of named paths, changed by connectors, scenarios or processes, with each change checked Output whatever the model prints or logs events and telemetry with a fixed shape, written to Kafka, Redis, PostgreSQL, files or Iceberg on background threads

User Guide pages that build on SimPy name the parts they use in their How It Works section, starting with Arrivals and Services.

docs.title: Generate Related Records
docs.text:
Related records are rows that belong together across tables. Here every customer order has 1 to 5 line items with random products, prices and quantities, and a total computed from them, written to two PostgreSQL tables, orders and order_items. Each tab shows the example written one way, and the three publish the same records. In YAML a mapping payload is a constant, so the order generator is a process in postgres_orders_logic.py, referenced with !python; Python in a Blueprint explains how references work.

YAMLBuilderLow-level

Quick Start

desflow examples get downloads the example at the release you install, into a folder of its own. Pick uv or pip:

uvpip 
# 1. Install
uv tool install "desflow[postgres]" --with-executables-from "odctl>=1.0,<2"

# 2. Download the example
desflow examples get related-records --api yaml
cd related-records/yaml

# 3. Start its service
odctl up postgres

# 4. Run it (Ctrl + C to stop)
desflow run postgres_orders.yaml

# 5. Stop its service when finished
odctl down postgres --volumes

# 1. Install
pip install "desflow[postgres]" "odctl>=1.0,<2"

# 2. Download the example
desflow examples get related-records --api yaml
cd related-records/yaml

# 3. Start its service
odctl up postgres

# 4. Run it (Ctrl + C to stop)
desflow run postgres_orders.yaml

# 5. Stop its service when finished
odctl down postgres --volumes

Full Source Code

The generator is listed under processes with kwargs, so it is called as order_generator(context, arrival="orders", max_items=5). It draws from context.sampler.rng, the generator seeded by random_seed, so a seeded run repeats the same orders.

Files live in the examples/yaml/ folder of the repository, and the label on each block below is its path there.

examples/yaml/advanced/postgres_orders.yaml
# Orders with random line items, in YAML with one Python function.
#
# Each order arrival builds an order with 1 to 5 items, random prices and
# quantities, and a total computed from them. A mapping payload is a constant, so
# the generator is Python in postgres_orders_logic.py beside this file, referenced
# with !python. Everything else is plain YAML.
#
# Two PostgresEgress instances are attached, one per table, and each keeps only the
# records whose __table__ key names its table. Each creates its table at start.
#
# Needs a database: odctl up postgres. Runs until interrupted with Ctrl + C.
# Run it from its folder with: desflow run postgres_orders.yaml

simulation:
  sim_id: Shop
  factor: 1.0
  random_seed: 42

ingress:
  - type: Postgres
    config:
      connection_dsn: postgresql://user:password@localhost:5432/odctl
      table_name: simulation_params

egress:
  - type: Postgres
    config:
      connection_dsn: postgresql://user:password@localhost:5432/odctl
      tables:
        orders:
          columns:
            order_id: INT
            customer_id: INT
            total_amount: REAL
            status: TEXT
            timestamp: TIMESTAMP
          primary_key: order_id
  - type: Postgres
    config:
      connection_dsn: postgresql://user:password@localhost:5432/odctl
      tables:
        order_items:
          columns:
            order_item_id: INT
            order_id: INT
            product_id: INT
            quantity: INT
            unit_price: REAL
          primary_key: order_item_id

arrivals:
  # No spawn: the process below waits on this arrival itself.
  orders: {dist: exponential, rate: 1.0}

processes:
  # Called as order_generator(context, arrival="orders", max_items=5).
  - function: !python postgres_orders_logic.order_generator
    kwargs: {arrival: orders, max_items: 5}
examples/yaml/advanced/postgres_orders_logic.py
"""Python for postgres_orders.yaml: an order generator with random line items."""


def order_generator(context, arrival: str, max_items: int):
    """Publishes an order and its items on every arrival.

    Draws from `context.sampler.rng`, the generator seeded by `random_seed`, so a
    seeded run repeats the same orders. The `__table__` key names the table each
    record is written to.
    """
    rng = context.sampler.rng
    order_id = 1
    item_id = 1
    while True:
        # The order's key, such as orders-1, is the record key of all its records
        entity = yield context.wait_for_arrival(arrival)

        total = 0.0
        for _ in range(int(rng.integers(1, max_items + 1))):
            price = round(float(rng.uniform(10.0, 50.0)), 2)
            quantity = int(rng.integers(1, 4))
            total += price * quantity
            context.env.publish_event(
                entity.key,
                {
                    "__table__": "order_items",
                    "order_item_id": item_id,
                    "order_id": order_id,
                    "product_id": int(rng.integers(1, 51)),
                    "quantity": quantity,
                    "unit_price": price,
                },
            )
            item_id += 1

        context.env.publish_event(
            entity.key,
            {
                "__table__": "orders",
                "order_id": order_id,
                "customer_id": int(rng.integers(1, 101)),
                "total_amount": round(total, 2),
                "status": "pending",
            },
        )
        order_id += 1

Full Source Code

The generator is added with add_process, so it is called as order_generator(context, arrival="orders", max_items=5). It draws from context.sampler.rng, the generator seeded by random_seed, so a seeded run repeats the same orders.

examples/builder/postgres_orders_example.py
"""
Orders with line items, builder API.

The builder twin of `yaml/advanced/postgres_orders.yaml`. Each order arrival
builds an order with 1 to 5 items, random prices and quantities, and a total computed
from them. Two PostgresEgress instances are attached, one per table, and each keeps
only the records whose `__table__` key names its table. Each creates its table at
start.

Needs a database: odctl up postgres. Runs until interrupted with Ctrl + C.
"""

import logging

from desflow import PostgresEgress, PostgresIngress, SimulationContext

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
)

DSN = "postgresql://user:password@localhost:5432/odctl"

ORDERS = {
    "columns": {
        "order_id": "INT",
        "customer_id": "INT",
        "total_amount": "REAL",
        "status": "TEXT",
        "timestamp": "TIMESTAMP",
    },
    "primary_key": "order_id",
}
ORDER_ITEMS = {
    "columns": {
        "order_item_id": "INT",
        "order_id": "INT",
        "product_id": "INT",
        "quantity": "INT",
        "unit_price": "REAL",
    },
    "primary_key": "order_item_id",
}


def order_generator(context: SimulationContext, arrival: str, max_items: int):
    """Publishes an order and its items on every arrival.

    Draws from `context.sampler.rng`, the generator seeded by `random_seed`, so a
    seeded run repeats the same orders. The `__table__` key names the table each
    record is written to.
    """
    rng = context.sampler.rng
    order_id = 1
    item_id = 1
    while True:
        # The order's key, such as orders-1, is the record key of all its records
        entity = yield context.wait_for_arrival(arrival)

        total = 0.0
        for _ in range(int(rng.integers(1, max_items + 1))):
            price = round(float(rng.uniform(10.0, 50.0)), 2)
            quantity = int(rng.integers(1, 4))
            total += price * quantity
            context.env.publish_event(
                entity.key,
                {
                    "__table__": "order_items",
                    "order_item_id": item_id,
                    "order_id": order_id,
                    "product_id": int(rng.integers(1, 51)),
                    "quantity": quantity,
                    "unit_price": price,
                },
            )
            item_id += 1

        context.env.publish_event(
            entity.key,
            {
                "__table__": "orders",
                "order_id": order_id,
                "customer_id": int(rng.integers(1, 101)),
                "total_amount": round(total, 2),
                "status": "pending",
            },
        )
        order_id += 1


app = (
    SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=1.0, random_seed=42)
    .add_ingress(PostgresIngress(DSN, table_name="simulation_params"))
    .add_egress(PostgresEgress(DSN, tables={"orders": ORDERS}))
    .add_egress(PostgresEgress(DSN, tables={"order_items": ORDER_ITEMS}))
    .add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=1.0)
    .add_process(order_generator, arrival="orders", max_items=5)
)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run()

Full Source Code

The generator is a SimPy process started with env.process. It draws the gaps and the order contents from one Sampler seeded with 42, in the same order as the other two, so it publishes the same orders.

examples/low-level/postgres_orders_example.py
"""
Orders with line items, low-level API.

The low-level twin of `builder/postgres_orders_example.py` and
`yaml/advanced/postgres_orders.yaml`. It wires `DynamicRealtimeEnvironment`, the
registry and the connectors by hand. With the same seed it publishes the same orders
as the other two.

Needs a database: odctl up postgres. Runs until interrupted with Ctrl + C.
"""

import logging

import numpy as np

from desflow import (
    DistributionConfig,
    DynamicRealtimeEnvironment,
    PostgresEgress,
    PostgresIngress,
    Sampler,
    SimParameter,
)

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
)

DSN = "postgresql://user:password@localhost:5432/odctl"

PARAMS = SimParameter(
    sim_id="Shop",
    arrival={"orders": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=1.0)},
)

ORDERS = {
    "columns": {
        "order_id": "INT",
        "customer_id": "INT",
        "total_amount": "REAL",
        "status": "TEXT",
        "timestamp": "TIMESTAMP",
    },
    "primary_key": "order_id",
}
ORDER_ITEMS = {
    "columns": {
        "order_item_id": "INT",
        "order_id": "INT",
        "product_id": "INT",
        "quantity": "INT",
        "unit_price": "REAL",
    },
    "primary_key": "order_item_id",
}


def order_generator(env, sampler: Sampler, max_items: int):
    """Publishes an order and its items on every arrival.

    The gaps come from the arrival's own random sequence and the order contents from
    `sampler.rng`, as in the builder version, so the two publish the same records.
    """
    rng = sampler.rng
    arrival = env.registry.get_config("Shop.arrival.orders")
    order_id = 1
    item_id = 1
    while True:
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(arrival))

        total = 0.0
        for _ in range(int(rng.integers(1, max_items + 1))):
            price = round(float(rng.uniform(10.0, 50.0)), 2)
            quantity = int(rng.integers(1, 4))
            total += price * quantity
            env.publish_event(
                f"orders-{order_id}",
                {
                    "__table__": "order_items",
                    "order_item_id": item_id,
                    "order_id": order_id,
                    "product_id": int(rng.integers(1, 51)),
                    "quantity": quantity,
                    "unit_price": price,
                },
            )
            item_id += 1

        env.publish_event(
            f"orders-{order_id}",
            {
                "__table__": "orders",
                "order_id": order_id,
                "customer_id": int(rng.integers(1, 101)),
                "total_amount": round(total, 2),
                "status": "pending",
            },
        )
        order_id += 1


def run(until=None, factor=1.0):
    env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=factor)
    env.registry.register_sim_parameter(PARAMS)
    env.setup_ingress([PostgresIngress(DSN, table_name="simulation_params")])
    env.setup_egress(
        [
            PostgresEgress(DSN, tables={"orders": ORDERS}),
            PostgresEgress(DSN, tables={"order_items": ORDER_ITEMS}),
        ]
    )
    sampler = Sampler(rng=np.random.default_rng(42))
    env.process(order_generator(env, sampler, max_items=5))
    try:
        env.run(until=until)
    finally:
        env.teardown()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    run()

docs.title: What It Does
docs.text:
When the run starts, each PostgresEgress creates its table, orders or order_items, and PostgresIngress creates simulation_params, if they do not exist. The run then writes orders and their items until you stop it. Both egresses receive every record and each keeps the records whose __table__ key names its table.

In a second terminal, raise the arrival rate while it runs:

docker exec -it postgres psql -U user -d odctl -c "INSERT INTO simulation_params (path, value) VALUES ('Shop.arrival.orders.rate', '5.0');"

docs.title: Parquet History, Kafka Live
docs.text:
One run writes ten minutes of backdated history to Parquet, then publishes to Kafka in real time. Each tab shows the example written one way, and the three publish the same records. The sections after the tabs explain why one run is better than two, how the settings fit together and what to get right.

YAMLBuilderLow-level

This example builds the simulation of the Builder tab from a YAML blueprint, with no Python. Until go_live_at the run is unpaced and writes backdated history to Parquet. From go_live_at it is paced in real time and publishes to Kafka.

Quick Start

# 1. Install
pip install "desflow[kafka,parquet]" "odctl>=1.0,<2"

# 2. Download the example

cd backfill-live/yaml

# 3. Start its service

# 4. Run it
desflow run backfill_live.yaml

# 5. Stop its service when finished
odctl down kafka-lite --volumes

What It Does

Ten minutes of history are written to data/backfill/ within the first second, then the run publishes to sim-events and sim-telemetry in real time for 60 seconds and ends. The history folder is created on the first write, and KafkaEgress creates the two topics when it starts.

Full Source Code

logical_start_time: -10m and go_live_at: now are read against one moment, when the file is loaded, so they are exactly ten minutes apart, and until: 11m adds one minute of live tail. when: history sends the records stamped before go_live_at to Parquet, and when: live sends the rest to Kafka.

Files live in the examples/yaml/ folder of the repository, and the label on each block below is its path there.

examples/yaml/backfill_live.yaml
# Backfill then go live in one run, in YAML.
#
# The YAML version of examples/builder/backfill_live_example.py. Until
# go_live_at the clock is detached from the wall clock, so ten minutes of backdated
# shop orders are written to Parquet as fast as the machine allows. From go_live_at
# the run is paced at one simulated second per real second, and the same events go
# to Kafka for one minute.
#
# Needs a broker: odctl up kafka-lite.
# Run it from its folder with: desflow run backfill_live.yaml

simulation:
  sim_id: Shop
  # Unpaced to begin with, so the history costs no real time.
  factor: 0.0
  random_seed: 42
  logical_start_time: -10m
  # From here the same run is paced at one simulated second per real second.
  go_live_at: now

egress:
  - type: Parquet
    config:
      default_path: data/backfill/events.parquet
    # Records stamped before go_live_at.
    when: history
  - type: Kafka
    config:
      event_topic: sim-events
      telemetry_topic: sim-telemetry
      bootstrap_servers: ${KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS:-localhost:9092}
    # Records stamped at or after go_live_at.
    when: live

# Only batch_size governs the history. The interval flush starts at go-live, so the
# live tail also flushes every 10 seconds.
batching:
  batch_size: 2000
  flush_interval: 10.0

resources:
  packers: {current_cap: 4, max_cap: 10}

services:
  packing: {dist: normal, mean: 2.0, std: 0.2}

arrivals:
  orders: {dist: exponential, rate: 0.5, spawn: pack_order}

tasks:
  pack_order:
    service: packing
    resource: packers
    payload: {path_id: Shop.service.packing, status: finished}

# The packers' readings every 30 simulation seconds.
stats: {level: minimal, interval: 30}

run:
  # Ten minutes of history, then one minute of live tail.
  until: 11m

Full Source Code

examples/builder/backfill_live_example.py
"""
Backfill-then-live Example.

One run produces both halves of a tiered dataset. Until `go_live_at` the clock is
detached from the wall clock, so ten minutes of backdated shop orders are written to
Parquet as fast as the machine allows. From `go_live_at` the same run is paced at one
simulated second per real second, and the same events are published to Kafka as they
happen. Doing this in two processes would mean repeating the seed and the start
instant in both, and keeping them in step by hand.
"""

import logging
import os
import time
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone

from desflow import (
    KafkaAdminConnector,
    KafkaEgress,
    ParquetStorageEgress,
    SimulationContext,
)

# Logging is configured here rather than in a wrapper, because this script is run
# directly. Without it the run produces no output at all.
logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO,
    format="%(asctime)s [%(levelname)s] %(name)s: %(message)s",
    datefmt="%H:%M:%S",
)

logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS = os.getenv("KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS", "localhost:9092")
EVENT_TOPIC = "sim-events"
TELEMETRY_TOPIC = "sim-telemetry"

# How much history to generate, and how long to keep tailing once live. The live half
# costs real time, second for second, so it is short by default.
HISTORY = timedelta(minutes=float(os.getenv("HISTORY_MINUTES", "10")))
LIVE_SECONDS = float(os.getenv("LIVE_SECONDS", "60"))

base_path = os.getenv("DEST_PATH", "data/backfill")

# The go-live instant is now, so everything before it is history and everything after
# it is the live tail. These sit at module scope because the builder below needs them,
# and the builder has to stay at module scope for the decorators to attach to it.
GO_LIVE_AT = datetime.now(timezone.utc)
# Cut to milliseconds, as timestamps are, so a record stamped in the go-live
# millisecond is live
GO_LIVE_AT = GO_LIVE_AT.replace(microsecond=GO_LIVE_AT.microsecond // 1000 * 1000)
LOGICAL_START_TIME = GO_LIVE_AT - HISTORY

# Records carry their logical time as an ISO string with its zone offset, so the
# predicates that split the two sinks read it as a time and compare instants.


def is_history(record: dict) -> bool:
    """True for records stamped before the go-live instant."""
    return datetime.fromisoformat(record["timestamp"]) < GO_LIVE_AT


def is_live(record: dict) -> bool:
    """True for records stamped at or after the go-live instant."""
    return datetime.fromisoformat(record["timestamp"]) >= GO_LIVE_AT


def history_router(data: dict) -> str | None:
    """Drops telemetry and flattens the event payload, as Parquet needs flat rows."""
    if data.get("stream_type") != "event":
        return None

    if isinstance(data.get("value"), dict):
        data.update(data.pop("value"))

    return f"{base_path}/events.parquet"


# ==========================================
# 1. Infrastructure Builder
# ==========================================
app = (
    SimulationContext(
        sim_id="Shop",
        # Unpaced to begin with, so the history costs no real time.
        factor=0.0,
        random_seed=42,
        logical_start_time=LOGICAL_START_TIME,
        # From here the same run is paced at one simulated second per real second.
        go_live_at=GO_LIVE_AT,
    )
    .add_egress(ParquetStorageEgress(path_router=history_router), when=is_history)
    .add_egress(
        KafkaEgress(
            event_topic=EVENT_TOPIC,
            telemetry_topic=TELEMETRY_TOPIC,
            bootstrap_servers=BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS,
        ),
        when=is_live,
    )
    # Only batch_size governs the history. The interval flush is a simulation process,
    # started only when factor is non-zero as the egress is set up, and this run starts
    # at 0.0. It starts at go-live, so the live tail also flushes every 10 seconds.
    .with_batching(batch_size=2000, flush_interval=10.0)
    .add_resource("packers", current_cap=4, max_cap=10)
    .add_service("packing", dist="normal", mean=2.0, std=0.2)
    .add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=0.5)
    # The packers' readings every 30 simulation seconds
    .with_stats("minimal", interval=30.0)
)


# ==========================================
# 2. Simulation Logic
# ==========================================
@app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="packers")
def pack_order(task_id: int, context):
    """Returns the flat payload that both sinks receive for a finished task."""
    return {"path_id": "Shop.service.packing", "status": "finished"}


@app.arrival_loop("orders")
def arrival_generator(context):
    task_id = 0
    while True:
        entity = yield context.wait_for_arrival("orders")
        context.spawn(pack_order(task_id, context, entity=entity))
        task_id += 1


# ==========================================
# 3. Execution
# ==========================================
def run():
    """Generates the history instantly, then tails live for LIVE_SECONDS."""
    os.makedirs(base_path, exist_ok=True)

    try:
        admin = KafkaAdminConnector(bootstrap_servers=BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS, max_tasks=100)
        admin.create_topics(
            topics_config=[
                {"name": EVENT_TOPIC, "partitions": 1},
                {"name": TELEMETRY_TOPIC, "partitions": 1},
            ]
        )
        time.sleep(2)
    except Exception as e:
        logger.warning(f"Could not explicitly create topics: {e}")

    logger.info(
        "Backfilling from %s to %s into '%s/', then tailing live to Kafka for %.0fs.",
        LOGICAL_START_TIME.strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"),
        GO_LIVE_AT.strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"),
        base_path,
        LIVE_SECONDS,
    )

    app.run(until=HISTORY.total_seconds() + LIVE_SECONDS)

    logger.info("Run complete. History is in '%s/', the tail is in Kafka.", base_path)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    run()

Full Source Code

Scripts live in the examples/ folder of the repository, and the label on the block below is this one's path there.

examples/low-level/backfill_live_example.py
"""
Backfill-then-live Example, low-level API.

The low-level twin of `builder/backfill_live_example.py`. One run produces both
halves of a tiered dataset. Until `go_live_at` the clock is detached from the wall
clock, so ten minutes of backdated shop orders are written to Parquet as fast as the
machine allows. From `go_live_at` the same run is paced at one simulated second per
real second, and the same events are published to Kafka as they happen.
"""

import logging
import os
import time
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone

import numpy as np

from desflow import (
    CapacityConfig,
    DistributionConfig,
    DynamicRealtimeEnvironment,
    DynamicResource,
    KafkaAdminConnector,
    KafkaEgress,
    ParquetStorageEgress,
    Sampler,
    SimParameter,
)

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO,
    format="%(asctime)s [%(levelname)s] %(name)s: %(message)s",
    datefmt="%H:%M:%S",
)
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS = os.getenv("KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS", "localhost:9092")
EVENT_TOPIC = "sim-events"
TELEMETRY_TOPIC = "sim-telemetry"

HISTORY = timedelta(minutes=float(os.getenv("HISTORY_MINUTES", "10")))
LIVE_SECONDS = float(os.getenv("LIVE_SECONDS", "60"))
base_path = os.getenv("DEST_PATH", "data/backfill")

GO_LIVE_AT = datetime.now(timezone.utc)
# Cut to milliseconds, as timestamps are, so a record stamped in the go-live
# millisecond is live
GO_LIVE_AT = GO_LIVE_AT.replace(microsecond=GO_LIVE_AT.microsecond // 1000 * 1000)
LOGICAL_START_TIME = GO_LIVE_AT - HISTORY

PARAMS = SimParameter(
    sim_id="Shop",
    arrival={"orders": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=0.5)},
    service={"packing": DistributionConfig(dist="normal", mean=2.0, std=0.2)},
    resources={"packers": CapacityConfig(current_cap=4, max_cap=10)},
)


def is_history(record: dict) -> bool:
    """True for records stamped before the go-live instant."""
    return datetime.fromisoformat(record["timestamp"]) < GO_LIVE_AT


def is_live(record: dict) -> bool:
    """True for records stamped at or after the go-live instant."""
    return datetime.fromisoformat(record["timestamp"]) >= GO_LIVE_AT


def history_router(data: dict) -> str | None:
    """Drops telemetry and flattens the event payload, as Parquet needs flat rows."""
    if data.get("stream_type") != "event":
        return None
    if isinstance(data.get("value"), dict):
        data.update(data.pop("value"))
    return f"{base_path}/events.parquet"


def pack_order(env, sampler, packers, key, task_id):
    """What @app.task does: queued, started, the service time, then finished."""
    path_id = "Shop.service.packing"
    env.publish_event(
        key,
        {"path_id": path_id, "status": "queued"},
        task="pack_order",
        instance=task_id,
    )
    env.stats.task_queued("pack_order", task_id)  # counted as in progress
    with packers.request() as request:
        yield request
        env.publish_event(
            key,
            {"path_id": path_id, "status": "started"},
            task="pack_order",
            instance=task_id,
        )
        env.stats.task_started("pack_order", task_id)
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(env.registry.get_config(path_id)))
        env.publish_event(
            key,
            {"path_id": path_id, "status": "finished"},
            task="pack_order",
            instance=task_id,
        )
        env.stats.task_finished("pack_order", task_id)


def arrival_generator(env, sampler, packers):
    gap = env.registry.get_config("Shop.arrival.orders")
    task_id = 0
    while True:
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(gap))
        env.process(pack_order(env, sampler, packers, f"orders-{task_id + 1}", task_id))
        task_id += 1


def run():
    """Generates the history instantly, then tails live for LIVE_SECONDS."""
    os.makedirs(base_path, exist_ok=True)
    try:
        admin = KafkaAdminConnector(bootstrap_servers=BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS, max_tasks=100)
        admin.create_topics(
            topics_config=[
                {"name": EVENT_TOPIC, "partitions": 1},
                {"name": TELEMETRY_TOPIC, "partitions": 1},
            ]
        )
        time.sleep(2)
    except Exception as e:
        logger.warning(f"Could not explicitly create topics: {e}")

    env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(
        factor=0.0,  # unpaced, so the history costs no real time
        logical_start_time=LOGICAL_START_TIME,
        go_live_at=GO_LIVE_AT,  # from here, one simulated second per real second
    )
    env.registry.register_sim_parameter(PARAMS)
    env.setup_egress(
        [
            ParquetStorageEgress(path_router=history_router),
            KafkaEgress(
                event_topic=EVENT_TOPIC,
                telemetry_topic=TELEMETRY_TOPIC,
                bootstrap_servers=BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS,
            ),
        ],
        batch_size=2000,
        flush_interval=10.0,
        predicates=[is_history, is_live],  # matched to the providers by position
    )
    # The packers' readings every 30 simulation seconds
    env.setup_stats("Shop", "minimal", interval=30.0)
    packers = DynamicResource(env, "Shop", "packers")
    sampler = Sampler(rng=np.random.default_rng(42))
    env.process(arrival_generator(env, sampler, packers))

    logger.info(
        "Backfilling from %s to %s into '%s/', then tailing live to Kafka for %.0fs.",
        LOGICAL_START_TIME.strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"),
        GO_LIVE_AT.strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"),
        base_path,
        LIVE_SECONDS,
    )
    try:
        env.run(until=HISTORY.total_seconds() + LIVE_SECONDS)
    finally:
        env.teardown()
    logger.info("Run complete. History is in '%s/', the tail is in Kafka.", base_path)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    run()

docs.title: Why One Run Rather Than Two
docs.text:
A tiered demo usually needs two datasets: a backdated history sitting in a lake, and a live stream arriving now. They have to be the same shop, with the same packers, the same distributions and the same task ids, or the join between them is meaningless.

Producing them takes two settings that contradict each other. History wants factor=0.0, so a week of events is generated as fast as the machine allows. A live tail wants factor=1.0, so events arrive one simulated second per real second.

Without go_live_at, the only way to get both is to start two processes with the same random_seed and the same logical_start_time, one fast-forwarding into Parquet and one pacing into Kafka. That costs:

  • A second full execution of the same simulation, so the history is generated twice.
  • Seed and start instant duplicated in two places, which have to be edited together. Change one and the two halves silently stop being the same shop.
  • No guarantee about the seam. Each process decides on its own where its half ends, so the join can overlap or leave a gap.

go_live_at replaces both processes with one. The run generates history unpaced up to that logical instant, then switches to real-time pacing and keeps going. There is one seed, one start instant and one seam.

docs.title: How the Three Settings Fit Together
docs.text:
Three separate settings make up the feature, and each answers a different question.

Setting Question it answers logical_start_time Where does the logical clock start? Set it in the past to backdate the history. go_live_at At which logical instant does pacing stop being factor and become real time? when on add_egress Which sink receives each record?

They are independent. go_live_at changes pacing only; it never routes a record. when routes records only; it never changes pacing. Using them together is what produces a tiered dataset, and the two instants have to agree: pass the same instant to go_live_at and to the predicates, or the seam in the data will not match the seam in the pacing.

In the Builder version, the three settings make the run:

examples/builder/backfill_live_example.py:builder
app = (
    SimulationContext(
        sim_id="Shop",
        # Unpaced to begin with, so the history costs no real time.
        factor=0.0,
        random_seed=42,
        logical_start_time=LOGICAL_START_TIME,
        # From here the same run is paced at one simulated second per real second.
        go_live_at=GO_LIVE_AT,
    )
    .add_egress(ParquetStorageEgress(path_router=history_router), when=is_history)
    .add_egress(
        KafkaEgress(
            event_topic=EVENT_TOPIC,
            telemetry_topic=TELEMETRY_TOPIC,
            bootstrap_servers=BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS,
        ),
        when=is_live,
    )
    # Only batch_size governs the history. The interval flush is a simulation process,
    # started only when factor is non-zero as the egress is set up, and this run starts
    # at 0.0. It starts at go-live, so the live tail also flushes every 10 seconds.
    .with_batching(batch_size=2000, flush_interval=10.0)
    .add_resource("packers", current_cap=4, max_cap=10)
    .add_service("packing", dist="normal", mean=2.0, std=0.2)
    .add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=0.5)
    # The packers' readings every 30 simulation seconds
    .with_stats("minimal", interval=30.0)
)

Time and Pacing describes how the switch is applied, and the cases where go_live_at is before the start or after the end of the run.

docs.title: Two Details to Get Right
docs.text:
Predicates compare times read from the timestamp. A record carries its logical time as an ISO string with its zone offset, such as +00:00, so record["timestamp"] >= GO_LIVE_AT raises a TypeError. Read it with datetime.fromisoformat and compare instants, which holds whatever zone each side is written in. Cut the go-live instant to milliseconds, as timestamps are, so a record stamped in the go-live millisecond counts as live. Take the instant with datetime.now(timezone.utc): a datetime without an offset is read in the run's timezone, else in the zone of logical_start_time, else in UTC, not in the machine's local time.

examples/builder/backfill_live_example.py:clock
GO_LIVE_AT = datetime.now(timezone.utc)
# Cut to milliseconds, as timestamps are, so a record stamped in the go-live
# millisecond is live
GO_LIVE_AT = GO_LIVE_AT.replace(microsecond=GO_LIVE_AT.microsecond // 1000 * 1000)
LOGICAL_START_TIME = GO_LIVE_AT - HISTORY

# Records carry their logical time as an ISO string with its zone offset, so the
# predicates that split the two sinks read it as a time and compare instants.

flush_interval has no effect before go_live_at, so batch_size decides the history. The interval flush is a simulation process, and it is only started if factor is non-zero when the egress is set up. This run starts at factor=0.0, so until go-live records leave the buffer only when it fills to batch_size. That sets the number of Parquet part files. From go-live the interval flush starts, so the live tail also flushes every flush_interval, and that decides how often Kafka sees anything. Give each sink its own batch_size and flush_interval to separate those two jobs:

docs/snippets/pages/backfill_live.py:per-sink
app.add_egress(parquet, when=is_history, batch_size=200_000)
app.add_egress(kafka, when=is_live, batch_size=500, flush_interval=1.0)

docs.title: What the Run Logs
docs.text: The two halves look different enough that the second can be mistaken for a hang. History finishes within the same second the run starts, then nothing is logged at all until teardown, because from go_live_at the run waits on the wall clock exactly as a live twin does. Logical clock reached go-live is the line that confirms the switch.

docs.title: Low-level API
docs.text:
go_live_at behaves identically on DynamicRealtimeEnvironment, alongside logical_start_time:

docs/snippets/pages/backfill_live.py:low-level
go_live_at = datetime.now(timezone.utc)

env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(
    factor=0.0,
    logical_start_time=go_live_at - timedelta(days=7),
    go_live_at=go_live_at,
)

env.factor reports 0.0 until the logical clock reaches go_live_at, and 1.0 afterwards.

docs.title: Fast-Forward to Iceberg
docs.text:
A day of a shop's orders, generated at factor=0.0 and appended to an Apache Iceberg table through an Iceberg REST catalog. Each tab shows the example written one way: as a YAML blueprint, with the builder API, or with the low-level API. Ways to write a simulation compares the three.

ParquetStorageEgress writes files and leaves registering them as a table to you. IcebergStorageEgress appends into an Iceberg table instead, so one run ends with a table another engine can query.

Each flush of the buffer is one Iceberg commit. Every commit writes a manifest, a manifest list and a new metadata.json, so query planning slows down as snapshots accumulate. That is why this example gives the provider a large batch_size of its own: a day of events lands in four snapshots.

YAMLBuilderLow-level

This example builds the simulation of the builder example in the Builder tab from a YAML blueprint, with no Python. A day of shop orders is generated at factor: 0.0, and each flush of the buffer becomes one Iceberg commit.

Quick Start

desflow examples get downloads the example at the release you install, into a folder of its own. Pick uv or pip:

uvpip 
# 1. Install
uv tool install "desflow[iceberg]" --with-executables-from "odctl>=1.0,<2"

# 2. Download the example
desflow examples get iceberg --api yaml
cd iceberg/yaml

# 3. Start its service
odctl up catalog

# 4. Run it
desflow run iceberg.yaml

# 5. Stop its service when finished
odctl down catalog --volumes

# 1. Install
pip install "desflow[iceberg]" "odctl>=1.0,<2"

# 2. Download the example
desflow examples get iceberg --api yaml
cd iceberg/yaml

# 3. Start its service
odctl up catalog

# 4. Run it
desflow run iceberg.yaml

# 5. Stop its service when finished
odctl down catalog --volumes

What It Does

The run appends a day of lifecycle events to the simulation.events table and ends on its own. batch_size: 200000 on the egress makes each flush one commit, so the day lands in a few snapshots. Without a router, each event is written to default_table as one flat row, and telemetry is left out.

The catalog is contacted on the first write, not when the blueprint is loaded, so a blueprint with a wrong catalog address still loads and fails when the first batch is written.

ICEBERG_URI, ICEBERG_WAREHOUSE, S3_ENDPOINT, S3_ACCESS_KEY, S3_SECRET_KEY and S3_REGION override the catalog and credentials.

Full Source Code

catalog is a mapping of PyIceberg catalog properties, passed to PyIceberg's load_catalog. schemas names a type for each column, so timestamp is created as a timestamp rather than inferred as a string, and the ISO time each record carries is converted before the write.

Files live in the examples/yaml/ folder of the repository, and the label on each block below is its path there.

examples/yaml/iceberg.yaml
# Lakehouse data generation in YAML.
#
# The YAML version of examples/builder/iceberg_example.py. A day of shop
# orders is generated at factor 0, and each flush of the buffer becomes one Iceberg
# commit. Without a router, each event is written to default_table as one flat row
# and telemetry is left out. The catalog is contacted on the first write.
#
# Needs the odctl catalog profile: odctl up catalog. ICEBERG_URI, ICEBERG_WAREHOUSE,
# S3_ENDPOINT, S3_ACCESS_KEY and S3_SECRET_KEY override the catalog and credentials.
# Run it from its folder with: desflow run iceberg.yaml

simulation:
  sim_id: Shop
  factor: 0.0
  random_seed: 42
  # A day before now, so the records are stamped as history.
  logical_start_time: -1d

egress:
  - type: Iceberg
    config:
      # PyIceberg catalog properties, passed to load_catalog.
      catalog:
        name: odctl
        type: rest
        uri: ${ICEBERG_URI:-http://localhost:8181}
        warehouse: ${ICEBERG_WAREHOUSE:-s3://warehouse/}
        s3.endpoint: ${S3_ENDPOINT:-http://localhost:8333}
        s3.access-key-id: ${S3_ACCESS_KEY:-user}
        s3.secret-access-key: ${S3_SECRET_KEY:-password}
        s3.region: ${S3_REGION:-us-east-1}
      default_table: simulation.events
      # Pinned rather than inferred, so timestamp is a timestamp, not a string.
      schemas:
        simulation.events:
          sim_ts: double
          timestamp: timestamp
          key: string
          path_id: string
          status: string
    # One commit per flush, sized so a day of events lands in a few snapshots.
    batch_size: 200000

resources:
  packers: {current_cap: 4, max_cap: 10}

services:
  packing: {dist: normal, mean: 2.0, std: 0.2}

arrivals:
  orders: {dist: exponential, rate: 2.0, spawn: pack_order}

tasks:
  pack_order:
    service: packing
    resource: packers
    payload: {path_id: Shop.service.packing, status: finished}

run:
  until: 1 day

Quick Start

desflow examples get downloads the example at the release you install, into a folder of its own. Pick uv or pip:

uvpip 
# 1. Install
uv tool install "desflow[iceberg]" --with-executables-from "odctl>=1.0,<2"

# 1. Install

# 2. Download the example
desflow examples get iceberg --api builder
cd iceberg/builder

ICEBERG_URI, ICEBERG_WAREHOUSE, ICEBERG_NAMESPACE, S3_ENDPOINT, S3_ACCESS_KEY, S3_SECRET_KEY and S3_REGION override the catalog and credentials.

Running it twice appends to the same table rather than replacing it, which is what an Iceberg table is for. Use odctl down catalog --volumes to start from nothing.

Full Source Code

This script simulates the shop over a 1-day period. It routes lifecycle events into one Iceberg table and pins the schema so the event time is a real timestamp rather than the string inference would give.

Scripts live in the examples/ folder of the repository, and the label on the block below is this one's path there.

examples/builder/iceberg_example.py
"""
Lakehouse Data Generation Example.

The Iceberg twin of `builder/parquet_example.py`. The same fast-forward engine,
but each flush of the buffer becomes one Iceberg commit rather than one Parquet file,
so the run ends with a table another engine can query instead of a folder someone
still has to register.

Every commit writes a manifest, a manifest list and a new `metadata.json`, so the
buffer is sized to produce a handful of snapshots rather than hundreds. That is what
`batch_size` on `add_egress` is for.

Requires the odctl `catalog` profile: `odctl up catalog`.
"""

import logging
import os
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone

import pyarrow as pa

from desflow import IcebergStorageEgress, SimulationContext

# Logging is configured here rather than in a wrapper, because this script is run
# directly. Without it the run produces no output at all.
logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO,
    format="%(asctime)s [%(levelname)s] %(name)s: %(message)s",
    datefmt="%H:%M:%S",
)

logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

NAMESPACE = os.getenv("ICEBERG_NAMESPACE", "simulation")
EVENTS_TABLE = f"{NAMESPACE}.events"

# Pinned rather than inferred. Inference reads the ISO timestamp the environment
# writes as a string, which is not what a consumer of an event table expects.
EVENTS_SCHEMA = pa.schema(
    [
        ("sim_ts", pa.float64()),
        ("timestamp", pa.timestamp("us")),
        ("key", pa.string()),
        ("path_id", pa.string()),
        ("status", pa.string()),
    ]
)


def create_table_router(events_table: str):
    """
    Router Factory: Generates a router returning `namespace.table`, and reshapes
    each event into the pinned schema.
    """

    def table_router(data: dict) -> str | None:
        if data.get("path_id") == "system.simulation.lag_seconds":
            return None

        if data.get("stream_type") != "event":
            return None

        # FLATTEN EVENT INTO THE PINNED COLUMNS
        nested_value = data.pop("value", None)
        if isinstance(nested_value, dict):
            data.update(nested_value)

        # A pinned timestamp column takes a datetime. PyArrow rejects the ISO string
        # the environment writes, so the conversion belongs here.
        data["timestamp"] = datetime.fromisoformat(data["timestamp"])

        return events_table

    return table_router


# ==========================================
# 1. CATALOG CONFIGURATION
# ==========================================
# RestCatalog fetches the catalog configuration as it is constructed, so building
# the client below contacts the catalog when this module is imported. Creating the
# namespace waits longer: the connector does that on its first batch, inside the run.
def build_catalog():
    """Connects to the Iceberg REST catalog from the odctl `catalog` profile."""
    from pyiceberg.catalog.rest import RestCatalog

    return RestCatalog(
        "odctl",
        **{
            "uri": os.getenv("ICEBERG_URI", "http://localhost:8181"),
            "warehouse": os.getenv("ICEBERG_WAREHOUSE", "s3://warehouse/"),
            "s3.endpoint": os.getenv("S3_ENDPOINT", "http://localhost:8333"),
            "s3.access-key-id": os.getenv("S3_ACCESS_KEY", "user"),
            "s3.secret-access-key": os.getenv("S3_SECRET_KEY", "password"),
            "s3.region": os.getenv("S3_REGION", "us-east-1"),
        },
    )


router = create_table_router(EVENTS_TABLE)

# The day of backdating this example exists to demonstrate. It sits at module scope
# because the builder below needs it, and the builder has to stay at module scope for
# the decorators further down to attach to it.
LOGICAL_START_TIME = datetime.now(timezone.utc) - timedelta(days=1)

# ==========================================
# 2. Infrastructure Builder
# ==========================================
app = (
    SimulationContext(
        sim_id="Shop",
        factor=0.0,
        random_seed=42,
        logical_start_time=LOGICAL_START_TIME,
    )
    .add_egress(
        IcebergStorageEgress(
            catalog=build_catalog(),
            table_router=router,
            schemas={EVENTS_TABLE: EVENTS_SCHEMA},
        ),
        # One commit per flush. Sized so a day of events lands in a few snapshots.
        batch_size=200_000,
    )
    .add_resource("packers", current_cap=4, max_cap=10)
    .add_service("packing", dist="normal", mean=2.0, std=0.2)
    .add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=2.0)
)


# ==========================================
# 3. Simulation Logic
# ==========================================
@app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="packers")
def pack_order(task_id: int, context):
    """
    Returns the exact flat dictionary expected by the table router
    to represent the 'finished' state of the lifecycle.
    """
    return {"path_id": "Shop.service.packing", "status": "finished"}


@app.arrival_loop("orders")
def arrival_generator(context):
    task_id = 0
    while True:
        entity = yield context.wait_for_arrival("orders")
        context.spawn(pack_order(task_id, context, entity=entity))
        task_id += 1


# ==========================================
# 4. Execution
# ==========================================
def run():
    """Generates 1 day of shop orders instantly, into an Iceberg table."""
    logger.info(
        "Generating historical data mimicking start from "
        f"{LOGICAL_START_TIME.strftime('%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S')}"
    )
    logger.info("Fast-forwarding (factor=0.0)...")

    # The clock detaches and executes 1 day of operations instantaneously
    app.run(until="1 day")

    table = build_catalog().load_table(EVENTS_TABLE)
    logger.info(
        f"Wrote {table.scan().to_arrow().num_rows} rows to '{EVENTS_TABLE}' "
        f"in {len(table.metadata.snapshots)} snapshots at {table.location()}"
    )


if __name__ == "__main__":
    run()
