docs.title: Complex Routing (Kafka)
docs.text:
Level: Intermediate

Records often belong in different Kafka topics: task events in one, telemetry in another, and alarms in a topic that someone watches. KafkaEgress takes a topic_router function that picks the topic for each record, instead of one event topic and one telemetry topic.

With a router, KafkaEgress does not create topics at start, because only the router knows which ones it uses, so create them first. The snippets below publish to Kafka, so start a broker first with odctl up kafka-lite. See Installation for the one-time odctl install. Tear it down with odctl down kafka-lite --volumes.

docs.title: Writing a Custom Router
docs.text:
A topic router is a Python function that receives one record, as a dictionary with its stream_type, key or path_id, task, instance and value, and returns the topic name as a string. KafkaEgress sends every record it receives, so the router must always return a topic. To drop records, give the provider a when predicate on add_egress, which filters them before they reach the router.

This router sends telemetry, alarms and other events to three topics:

docs/snippets/guides/complex_routing.py:router
def custom_kafka_router(data: Dict[str, Any]) -> str:
    """Picks a topic for each record by its kind and its value."""
    if data.get("stream_type") == "telemetry":
        return "shop-telemetry"

    value = data.get("value")
    if isinstance(value, dict) and (
        value.get("status") == "packing_failed" or value.get("level") == "ERROR"
    ):
        return "system-alarms"

    # Every other event, including a payload that is not a dict.
    return "shop-events"

docs.title: Attaching the Router
docs.text:
Pass the router as topic_router to KafkaEgress:

docs/snippets/guides/complex_routing.py:egress
app = (
    SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=1.0)
    .add_resource("packers", current_cap=1, max_cap=1)
    .add_egress(
        KafkaEgress(
            bootstrap_servers="localhost:9092",
            topic_router=custom_kafka_router,
        )
    )
)

docs.title: Run the Shop
docs.text:
The shop packs an order about every 2 seconds, and every tenth order fails, so all three topics receive records. The minimal statistics give shop-telemetry a reading every 10 seconds:

docs/snippets/guides/complex_routing.py:shop
app.add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=0.5)
app.add_service("packing", dist="constant", value=1.5)
app.with_stats("minimal", interval=10)  # readings for shop-telemetry


@app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="packers")
def pack_order(task_id: int):
    if task_id % 10 == 9:  # every tenth order fails, for system-alarms
        return {"status": "packing_failed"}
    return {"status": "packed"}


@app.arrival_loop("orders")
def orders(context: SimulationContext):
    while True:
        order = yield context.wait_for_arrival("orders")
        context.spawn(pack_order(context.next_instance("pack_order"), entity=order))

Before the run, the script creates the three topics with KafkaAdminConnector:

docs/snippets/guides/complex_routing.py:run
if __name__ == "__main__":
    logging.basicConfig(
        level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
    )
    # With a router, KafkaEgress creates no topics, so create them first
    admin = KafkaAdminConnector(bootstrap_servers="localhost:9092")
    admin.create_topics([{"name": topic} for topic in TOPICS])
    app.run(until="1 min")

Run it with python complex_routing.py while kafka-lite is up. The Kafka UI of kafka-lite, at http://127.0.0.1:8086, shows the records arriving in shop-events, shop-telemetry and system-alarms.

docs.title: Full Script
Dynamic Topology: Resources Changed Mid-run
docs.text:
Level: Intermediate

Sometimes the layout itself changes during a run: a dock opens a new bay, or a shop adds a gift wrapping station. Here a supervisor process adds gift wrappers at 12 seconds, and from then on new jobs go to the wrappers as well as the packers.

The builder (SimulationContext) creates every resource before the clock starts and has no call to add one later. A resource added during the run is written with the low-level API: register its parameters, then create the DynamicResource that reads them.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
docs/snippets/guides/dynamic_topology.py
import logging

from desflow import (
    CapacityConfig,
    ConsoleEgress,
    DynamicRealtimeEnvironment,
    DynamicResource,
    SimParameter,
)

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)

WORK = 3.0  # seconds each job takes
NEW_JOBS_EVERY = 4.0  # seconds between rounds of new jobs
ADD_WRAPPERS_AT = 12.0  # simulation time at which the gift wrappers are added

PARAMS = SimParameter(
    sim_id="Shop",
    resources={"packers": CapacityConfig(current_cap=1, max_cap=5)},
)


def worker(env, resources, name, job_id):
    resource = resources[name]
    key = f"{name}-{job_id}"
    env.publish_event(key, {"resource": name, "status": "queued"})
    with resource.request() as req:
        yield req
        env.publish_event(key, {"resource": name, "status": "started"})
        yield env.timeout(WORK)
        env.publish_event(key, {"resource": name, "status": "finished"})


def supervisor(env, resources):
    job_id = 0
    while True:
        yield env.timeout(NEW_JOBS_EVERY)

        if env.now >= ADD_WRAPPERS_AT and "wrappers" not in resources:
            # Give the gift wrappers their registry paths, then create the resource
            # that reads its capacity from them.
            env.registry.register_sim_parameter(
                SimParameter(
                    sim_id="Shop",
                    resources={"wrappers": CapacityConfig(current_cap=2, max_cap=5)},
                )
            )
            resources["wrappers"] = DynamicResource(env, "Shop", "wrappers")
            env.publish_event(
                "supervisor",
                {
                    "status": "wrappers_added",
                    "capacity": resources["wrappers"].capacity,
                },
            )

        # One new job for every resource that exists now.
        for name in list(resources):
            env.process(worker(env, resources, name, job_id))
        job_id += 1


def run(until=20.0, factor=1.0):
    env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=factor)
    env.registry.register_sim_parameter(PARAMS)
    env.setup_egress([ConsoleEgress()])

    resources = {"packers": DynamicResource(env, "Shop", "packers")}
    env.process(supervisor(env, resources))
    try:
        env.run(until=until)
    finally:
        env.teardown()  # flushes the buffers and stops the threads
    return resources


if __name__ == "__main__":
    run()

Save it as dynamic_topology.py and run python dynamic_topology.py. It runs for 20 seconds in real time (factor=1.0) and prints each event.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
• PARAMS registers only the packers when the run starts.
  • supervisor wakes every NEW_JOBS_EVERY seconds. At ADD_WRAPPERS_AT it calls env.registry.register_sim_parameter with a SimParameter that holds only the wrappers, which adds the paths Shop.resources.wrappers.current_cap and Shop.resources.wrappers.max_cap. It then creates DynamicResource(env, "Shop", "wrappers"), which reads its capacity from those paths, and publishes wrappers_added.
  • New jobs are started for every resource in resources, so the wrappers get jobs from the round in which they are added.
  • worker is one job: it publishes queued, started and finished with the resource it used.
  • run creates the environment, starts the supervisor and calls env.teardown() at the end, which writes the records still in the buffers.

The wrappers' capacity is live like any other. A scenario, a connector or a process can change Shop.resources.wrappers.current_cap once the path exists, as Live Parameters describes.

docs.title: Fit a Distribution
docs.text:
Level: Intermediate

Fit a column of your own measured times, such as the gaps between orders in an order log, and load the result into a model. It builds on Fit the Inputs, which fits the shop's packing times and checks what the choice changes, and on Input Fitting, which describes every option and outcome. Fitting needs the fit extra: pip install "desflow[fit]".

docs.title: Make the Column
docs.text:
A service is fitted to its durations. An arrival is fitted to the gaps between arrivals, not to the times they happened, so turn an order log's times into gaps first:

docs/snippets/guides/fit_a_distribution.py:gaps
with LOG.open(newline="", encoding="utf-8") as handle:
    placed = [
        datetime.fromisoformat(row["placed_at"]) for row in csv.DictReader(handle)
    ]
# An arrival is fitted to the gaps between orders, not to the times themselves
return [
    (later - earlier).total_seconds() for earlier, later in zip(placed, placed[1:])
]

order_log.csv is an illustrative log of 300 orders placed one afternoon, with the time each was placed to a tenth of a second. Write the gaps to a CSV column to fit them with desflow fit instead.

docs.title: Fit It
docs.text:
State the unit and the bounds. The gaps are in seconds and none can be below 0:

docs/snippets/guides/fit_a_distribution.py:fit
result = fit_column(gaps(), unit="s", lower=0)
print(result.text())  # every candidate, its status and diagnostics

On the command line, desflow fit gaps.csv --column gap_seconds --unit s --lower 0 --out fitted/orders.yaml does the same. The table for the 299 gaps:

299 rows: 299 used, 0 missing, 0 invalid
family            status              AIC      KS p (approx.)  parameters or reason
exponential *     fitted             1205 0.03517      0.8404  rate=0.36388
normal            fitted             1487  0.1707   4.359e-08  mean=2.74816, std=2.88857 (can draw below the lower bound 0)
lognormal         skipped                                      lognormal needs every value above 0; 5 are not
truncated_normal  did not fit                                  RuntimeError: Maximum number of function evaluations has been exceeded.
constant          skipped                                      the values are not all equal
uniform           rejected                                     its mean is 12.75, the data's is 2.748: more than 25% apart
triangular        rejected                                     its mean is 7.702, the data's is 2.748: more than 25% apart
gamma             skipped                                      gamma needs every value above 0; 5 are not
weibull           skipped                                      weibull needs every value above 0; 5 are not
empirical         fitted                                       values: 299 numbers
* best: exponential

docs.title: Read the Table
docs.text:
• Skipped families were not fitted, and the reason says why. Here the log's times are to a tenth of a second, so 5 gaps are 0, and gamma, weibull and lognormal, which need every value above 0, are skipped.
  • Did not fit means scipy's fit failed; its message is the reason. Here the truncated normal's search did not settle, because the gaps are far from a normal shape.
  • Rejected families were fitted, but their mean or standard deviation is more than 25% from the data's, or a parameter is out of range. Here uniform and triangular reach far beyond most gaps.
  • Fitted families have an AIC, lower is better, and a Kolmogorov-Smirnov p-value, which is approximate. The exponential has the lowest AIC and a p-value of 0.84, and its rate of 0.364 an order a second is one over the mean gap of 2.75 seconds. normal fits too, but it can draw below 0.

Two families within an AIC of 2 of each other fit about equally well; run the model with each and see whether the answer changes, as Fit the Inputs does. Read --plot fit.png, or result.plot("fit.png"), as well as the table.

docs.title: Load It
docs.text:
YAMLBuilderLow-level

Write the best fit with --out, or from Python:

docs/snippets/guides/fit_a_distribution.py:write
path = Path(folder) / "fitted" / "orders.yaml"
path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
path.write_text(result.yaml(source="order_log.csv, gaps between placed_at"))

and include it. An arrival also needs the task it spawns, so the include names the file and adds spawn:

docs/snippets/yaml/fit_a_distribution.yaml:include
arrivals:
  # The fitted gaps, with the task each order starts added to them
  orders: !include {file: fitted/orders.yaml, spawn: pack_order}

The file:

docs/snippets/yaml/fitted/orders.yaml
# Fitted by desflow fit from order_log.csv, gaps between placed_at: exponential, from 299 values in s, written in seconds.
dist: exponential
rate: 0.36388
docs/snippets/guides/fit_a_distribution.py:load
# The best fit's settings, such as dist="exponential", rate=0.4
.add_arrival("orders", **result.settings())

DistributionConfig(**result.settings()) makes the arrival's config for a SimParameter.

result.settings("normal") takes another fitted family instead of the best.

docs.title: When Nothing Fits
docs.text:
When every family is skipped, rejected or did not fit, the best is the empirical distribution: the data itself, which a run draws from at random. For many values, a histogram is shorter:

docs/snippets/guides/fit_a_distribution.py:empirical
result = fit_column(gaps(), unit="s", candidates=["empirical"], bins=10)

On the command line, --candidates empirical --bins 10. An empirical distribution never draws a value outside the data's range, so it cannot produce a gap longer than the longest one in the log.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
The whole script fits the gaps and runs the shop for an hour with the fitted arrivals; one packer packs 1,302 orders. Run it from docs/snippets/guides/ with python fit_a_distribution.py:

docs/snippets/guides/fit_a_distribution.py
"""Fit a Distribution: the gaps between orders in an order log, fitted and loaded.

order_log.csv is an illustrative log of 300 orders placed one afternoon, with the
time each was placed. The script turns the times into the gaps between orders,
fits them, prints the table of candidates, and runs the shop for an hour with the
fitted arrivals. `write` saves the settings for a blueprint's `!include`.
"""

import csv
import logging
from datetime import datetime
from pathlib import Path

from desflow import SimulationContext, fit_column

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.WARNING, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
)
LOG = Path(__file__).resolve().parent / "order_log.csv"


def gaps():
    """The gaps between consecutive orders, in seconds."""
    with LOG.open(newline="", encoding="utf-8") as handle:
        placed = [
            datetime.fromisoformat(row["placed_at"]) for row in csv.DictReader(handle)
        ]
    # An arrival is fitted to the gaps between orders, not to the times themselves
    return [
        (later - earlier).total_seconds() for earlier, later in zip(placed, placed[1:])
    ]


def fit():
    """Every family fitted to the gaps."""
    result = fit_column(gaps(), unit="s", lower=0)
    print(result.text())  # every candidate, its status and diagnostics
    return result


def histogram():
    """The empirical alternative: the gaps as a histogram of 10 bins."""
    result = fit_column(gaps(), unit="s", candidates=["empirical"], bins=10)
    return result


def write(result, folder):
    """Writes the best fit where a blueprint includes it."""
    path = Path(folder) / "fitted" / "orders.yaml"
    path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    path.write_text(result.yaml(source="order_log.csv, gaps between placed_at"))
    return path


def shop(result) -> SimulationContext:
    """One packer, with the fitted arrivals."""
    app = (
        SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0, random_seed=42)
        .add_resource("packers", current_cap=1, max_cap=2)
        .add_service("packing", dist="gamma", shape=4, scale=0.375)
        # The best fit's settings, such as dist="exponential", rate=0.4
        .add_arrival("orders", **result.settings())
        .with_stats("basic")
    )

    @app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="packers")
    def pack_order(task_id):
        return {"event_type": "order_packed"}

    @app.arrival_loop("orders")
    def order_loop(context):
        task_id = 0
        while True:
            order = yield context.wait_for_arrival("orders")
            context.spawn(pack_order(task_id, entity=order))
            task_id += 1

    return app


if __name__ == "__main__":
    app = shop(fit())
    app.run(until="1 h")
    finished = app.env.stats.readings()["Shop.stats.flows.orders.finished"]
    print(f"orders packed in an hour: {finished}")

docs.title: Connecting to Secure Kafka Clusters
docs.text:
Level: Advanced

The Kafka connectors pass any keyword argument they do not use themselves to the Kafka client underneath, so SASL, mTLS, OAuth and AWS IAM work without code of your own. KafkaIngress and KafkaEgress use aiokafka. KafkaAdminConnector uses kafka-python for create_topics and aiokafka for send_config and collect_data, so its arguments must suit the library each method uses.

Every example here connects to a managed or secured cluster. No odctl profile runs a secured broker, so the full script at the end needs a cluster of your own that uses SASL PLAIN, such as Confluent Cloud. To try the connectors locally without security, start a broker with odctl up kafka-lite and see Installation.

docs.title: Confluent Cloud (SASL PLAIN)
docs.text:
For Confluent Cloud, or any cluster that uses SASL PLAIN or SCRAM, pass security_protocol, sasl_mechanism and the credentials:

docs/snippets/guides/kafka_security.py:sasl
egress = KafkaEgress(
    bootstrap_servers="pkc-xxxx.us-east-1.aws.confluent.cloud:9092",
    # Passed as they are to the Kafka client
    security_protocol="SASL_SSL",
    sasl_mechanism="PLAIN",  # or SCRAM-SHA-512
    sasl_plain_username="<YOUR_API_KEY>",
    sasl_plain_password="<YOUR_API_SECRET>",
)

With no topic_router, KafkaEgress creates sim-events and sim-telemetry when it starts, and passes the security settings to the admin client that creates them.

docs.title: On-Premise Cluster (mTLS)
docs.text:
For a cluster that requires mutual TLS, build an SSL context from your certificate files. aiokafka takes only ssl_context, not the certificate paths, and kafka-python accepts the same context, so one context serves every connector.

docs/snippets/guides/kafka_security.py:mtls
from aiokafka.helpers import create_ssl_context

from desflow import KafkaIngress

ssl_context = create_ssl_context(
    cafile="/path/to/ca.pem",
    certfile="/path/to/service.cert",
    keyfile="/path/to/service.key",
)

ingress = KafkaIngress(
    topic="sim-commands",
    bootstrap_servers="secure-broker.internal.company.com:9093",
    security_protocol="SSL",
    ssl_context=ssl_context,
)

docs.title: AWS MSK (IAM)
docs.text:
Amazon MSK with IAM access control uses sasl_mechanism="OAUTHBEARER" with a token provider. The token comes from the aws-msk-iam-sasl-signer-python package, which you install yourself.

Each library checks the provider's type. aiokafka requires a subclass of aiokafka.abc.AbstractTokenProvider with an async token(). kafka-python requires a subclass of kafka.sasl.oauth.AbstractTokenProvider with a plain token(). One object cannot be both, so the connectors that use aiokafka get one provider, and create_topics gets the other.

docs/snippets/guides/kafka_security.py:msk
from aiokafka.abc import AbstractTokenProvider as AsyncTokenProvider
from aws_msk_iam_sasl_signer import MSKAuthTokenProvider
from kafka.sasl.oauth import AbstractTokenProvider as SyncTokenProvider

from desflow import KafkaAdminConnector, KafkaEgress

def msk_token() -> str:
    # Uses the AWS credentials of your environment, or the EC2 or EKS role
    token, _ = MSKAuthTokenProvider.generate_auth_token("us-east-1")
    return token

class AsyncMSKTokenProvider(AsyncTokenProvider):
    async def token(self):
        return msk_token()

class SyncMSKTokenProvider(SyncTokenProvider):
    def token(self):
        return msk_token()

msk = dict(
    bootstrap_servers="b-1.my-msk.amazonaws.com:9098",
    security_protocol="SASL_SSL",
    sasl_mechanism="OAUTHBEARER",
)

# KafkaIngress and KafkaEgress use aiokafka
egress = KafkaEgress(
    **msk, topic_router=my_router, sasl_oauth_token_provider=AsyncMSKTokenProvider()
)

# create_topics uses kafka-python
admin = KafkaAdminConnector(**msk, sasl_oauth_token_provider=SyncMSKTokenProvider())
admin.create_topics([{"name": "sim-events", "partitions": 3}])

The same OAUTHBEARER setting works with a token provider of your own for Okta, Auth0 or another single sign-on provider.

docs.title: Use It in a Simulation
docs.text:
A connector with security settings is added like any other. This simulation publishes its events through the SASL egress above:

docs/snippets/guides/kafka_security.py:shop
app = (
    SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=1.0, random_seed=42)
    .add_resource("packers", current_cap=1, max_cap=1)
    .add_service("packing", dist="constant", value=1.5)
    .add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=0.5)
    .add_egress(egress)  # the SASL egress above
)


@app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="packers")
def pack_order(task_id: int):
    return {"event_type": "order_packed"}


@app.arrival_loop("orders")
def orders(context: SimulationContext):
    while True:
        order = yield context.wait_for_arrival("orders")
        context.spawn(pack_order(context.next_instance("pack_order"), entity=order))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    logging.basicConfig(
        level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
    )
    app.run(until="1 min")

Put your broker address and credentials in egress, then run python kafka_security.py. It runs for one minute.

docs.title: Full Script
docs.text:
Full script

The complete file. It needs a Kafka cluster that uses SASL PLAIN:

docs/snippets/guides/kafka_security.py
"""The secured Kafka connections of the Secure Kafka page, and a shop that uses one.

The simulation publishes to a cluster that uses SASL PLAIN, such as Confluent Cloud: put your
broker address and credentials in the `sasl` section, then run `python
kafka_security.py`. The mTLS and MSK examples read certificate files or call AWS, so
they sit in functions this file defines and does not call.
"""

import logging

from desflow import KafkaEgress, SimulationContext


def my_router(data: dict) -> str:
    return "sim-telemetry" if data.get("stream_type") == "telemetry" else "sim-events"


egress = KafkaEgress(
    bootstrap_servers="pkc-xxxx.us-east-1.aws.confluent.cloud:9092",
    # Passed as they are to the Kafka client
    security_protocol="SASL_SSL",
    sasl_mechanism="PLAIN",  # or SCRAM-SHA-512
    sasl_plain_username="<YOUR_API_KEY>",
    sasl_plain_password="<YOUR_API_SECRET>",
)


def mtls_ingress():
    from aiokafka.helpers import create_ssl_context

    from desflow import KafkaIngress

    ssl_context = create_ssl_context(
        cafile="/path/to/ca.pem",
        certfile="/path/to/service.cert",
        keyfile="/path/to/service.key",
    )

    ingress = KafkaIngress(
        topic="sim-commands",
        bootstrap_servers="secure-broker.internal.company.com:9093",
        security_protocol="SSL",
        ssl_context=ssl_context,
    )
    return ingress


def msk_connectors():
    from aiokafka.abc import AbstractTokenProvider as AsyncTokenProvider
    from aws_msk_iam_sasl_signer import MSKAuthTokenProvider
    from kafka.sasl.oauth import AbstractTokenProvider as SyncTokenProvider

    from desflow import KafkaAdminConnector, KafkaEgress

    def msk_token() -> str:
        # Uses the AWS credentials of your environment, or the EC2 or EKS role
        token, _ = MSKAuthTokenProvider.generate_auth_token("us-east-1")
        return token

    class AsyncMSKTokenProvider(AsyncTokenProvider):
        async def token(self):
            return msk_token()

    class SyncMSKTokenProvider(SyncTokenProvider):
        def token(self):
            return msk_token()

    msk = dict(
        bootstrap_servers="b-1.my-msk.amazonaws.com:9098",
        security_protocol="SASL_SSL",
        sasl_mechanism="OAUTHBEARER",
    )

    # KafkaIngress and KafkaEgress use aiokafka
    egress = KafkaEgress(
        **msk, topic_router=my_router, sasl_oauth_token_provider=AsyncMSKTokenProvider()
    )

    # create_topics uses kafka-python
    admin = KafkaAdminConnector(**msk, sasl_oauth_token_provider=SyncMSKTokenProvider())
    admin.create_topics([{"name": "sim-events", "partitions": 3}])
    return egress, admin


app = (
    SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=1.0, random_seed=42)
    .add_resource("packers", current_cap=1, max_cap=1)
    .add_service("packing", dist="constant", value=1.5)
    .add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=0.5)
    .add_egress(egress)  # the SASL egress above
)


@app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="packers")
def pack_order(task_id: int):
    return {"event_type": "order_packed"}


@app.arrival_loop("orders")
def orders(context: SimulationContext):
    while True:
        order = yield context.wait_for_arrival("orders")
        context.spawn(pack_order(context.next_instance("pack_order"), entity=order))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    logging.basicConfig(
        level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
    )
    app.run(until="1 min")

docs.title: Multi-Resource Handoffs
docs.text:
Level: Intermediate

A handoff passes an order from one resource to the next without letting go of the first too early. Here a picker carries each order to a packing bench. The order keeps the picker until the bench is free, so for a moment it holds both, and then it releases the picker. It builds on Competing Resources, which measures what such a holding costs, and on Resources.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Give the first task the resource and keep it: pick holds the picker and, instead of releasing it when it finishes, hands it to the next task.
  2. Give the next task the second resource: pack waits for the bench while the order still holds the picker, and gives the picker back as soon as it publishes started.
  3. Acquire the two resources in the same order everywhere. A task that takes the bench first and the picker second would be refused when the model is built, because two orders could then wait for each other for ever.

In YAML the same tasks are keep: [picker] on pick and resource: bench on pack; in the low-level API the picker's request is released by the next process instead of a with block.

docs.title: Example
Performance Tuning
docs.text:
Level: Advanced

Make a run that generates data go as fast as the machine allows, and measure how many records a second it publishes. It builds on Time and Pacing, which explains factor, and on Egress, which explains batches.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Run at factor: 0, without go_live_at. The run then waits for no wall clock, each event is processed by SimPy's own step, and no lag telemetry is published; a pending go-live keeps the real-time step until it is reached.
  2. Ask only for the statistics you read: minimal reads a few values at each interval, while typical and all add work at every task step, as Statistics explains.
  3. Leave the console for looking at a run. It writes one line per record; a file or a stream sink costs less per record, and a counting sink almost nothing.
  4. Give a lake sink a large batch_size, such as 10,000, because the batch is the file; a stream sink can keep a small one.
  5. After building a large model, gc.freeze() leaves the objects built so far out of garbage collection; in the measurements below it saved about 9 percent.

This function runs a model with a counting sink in place of its own, and returns the records it published and how many a second, counted from the start of run() to the end of its teardown:

docs/snippets/guides/performance_tuning.py:measure
def throughput(app: SimulationContext, until: float) -> dict:
    """Runs a model with a counting sink: the records and records per second."""
    count = Count()
    app.add_egress(count)
    gc.collect()
    gc.freeze()  # leave the objects built so far out of garbage collection
    started = time.perf_counter()
    app.run(until=until)
    seconds = time.perf_counter() - started
    gc.unfreeze()
    return {"records": count.records, "per_second": round(count.records / seconds)}

For an hour of this shop, ten orders a second and 25 packers, it returns 108,688 records, at about 100,000 a second on the machine below:

docs/snippets/guides/performance_tuning.py:shop
def shop() -> SimulationContext:
    """Ten orders a second and 25 packers, with no sink of its own."""
    app = (
        # factor 0: no wall clock to wait for
        SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0, random_seed=42)
        .add_resource("packers", current_cap=25, max_cap=25)
        .add_service("packing", dist="normal", mean=2.0, std=0.4)
        .add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=10.0)
        # minimal: readings every 10 s, not the costlier task statistics
        .with_stats("minimal", interval=10)
    )

    @app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="packers")
    def pack_order(task_id: int):
        return {"event_type": "order_packed"}

    @app.arrival_loop("orders")
    def order_loop(context: SimulationContext):
        while True:
            order = yield context.wait_for_arrival("orders")
            context.spawn(pack_order(context.next_instance("pack_order"), entity=order))

    return app

At factor: 0 no system.simulation.lag_seconds is published, so the count holds only the shop's own records: with a lag reading every second it would be 3,600 more.

docs.title: Measurements
docs.text:
benchmarks/throughput.py in the repository runs one low-level workload, 5,000 simulation seconds of 10 orders a second, at factor: 0 with a fixed seed, and gives the median of seven runs. Each line changes one thing, so the effect of a change is the ratio of two lines. These are from an arm64 Mac (macOS 26) with Python 3.12.13; "run" is env.run() alone, and "total" adds the teardown, which waits until every sink has taken every batch:

Configuration Run, seconds Total, seconds Records core only, nothing published 0.248 0.248 0 as shipped, counting sink 0.531 1.138 157,771 with 0.21.0's real-time step at factor: 0 0.555 1.164 157,771 with 0.21.0's timestamp 0.555 1.163 157,771 with a lag reading every second, 0.21.0's default 0.535 1.144 162,771 0.21.0: the three lines above together 0.604 1.211 162,771 as shipped, with gc.freeze() after setup 0.485 1.092 157,771 ConsoleEgress, to /dev/null 0.648 1.251 157,771 0.21.0's ConsoleEgress, one log call per record 0.672 1.902 157,771
  • 0.22.0 against 0.21.0: the run takes 0.531 seconds against 0.604, 1.14 times faster, from the three changes: SimPy's own step at factor: 0, a timestamp formatted once per second of the clock (300 against 580 nanoseconds a record), and no lag readings at factor: 0.
  • Console: in the total, run and teardown, logging a batch with one call takes 0.11 seconds more than a counting sink; one call per record took 0.76 seconds more. A terminal is slower than /dev/null, so a run that prints to one costs more than this.
  • Teardown: about 0.6 seconds of every total is the teardown. Once the queues are empty, it waits half a second for a file sink to close its last file, so a short run spends most of its time there.

Where the time goes, from a sampling profile of the run "as shipped" (a thread reads the main thread's stack every 0.2 milliseconds, as py-spy does from outside, which needs root on macOS):

Part Share of the run SimPy's scheduler 28 percent publishing a record: the value made JSON-safe 18 percent publishing a record: building it, its timestamp, buffering and flushing 21 percent resource request and release 14 percent drawing samples 9 percent SimPy events and processes 8 percent the model's own generators and the rest 3 percent

A draw through Sampler.sample costs about 360 nanoseconds, against 200 for numpy's Generator.normal alone; a request granted and released costs about 1,760 nanoseconds, and a timeout about 260.

Python versions. The run "as shipped" takes 0.517 seconds on Python 3.11.15, 0.531 on 3.12.13, 0.492 on 3.13.14 and 0.556 on 3.14.6. No version is more than 13 percent faster than another.

PyPy. desflow does not install on PyPy, because orjson, which it depends on, does not support PyPy. With the other dependencies installed by hand, the run "as shipped" took 0.851 seconds on PyPy 3.11.15, 1.6 times slower than CPython 3.12. Drawing samples, which goes through numpy, took 23 percent of a short profile (96 samples), against 9 percent on CPython.

Real sinks. With the same workload, the total was 1.134 seconds with a counting sink, 1.262 with Parquet on the local disk, and 3.558 with Kafka (the odctl kafka-lite profile on the same machine, JSON values): a sink that sends over the network can take longer than the model.

Run uv run --all-extras python benchmarks/throughput.py configs to measure your machine, and micro, profile or sinks for the other parts.

docs.title: Reneging and Balking
docs.text:
Level: Intermediate

Give a task a time limit on its wait, a condition that stops it joining at all, or both, and account for every entity afterwards. It builds on Patience, which explains both ideas, and on Resources, which explains how a request is granted.

docs.title: Leave After a Wait and Refuse to Join
docs.text:
A task's patience is how long it may wait, for its wait, then its resource and then its get, before it leaves the queue and publishes reneged. It counts waiting time only: it pauses while the task is served, so a task that is preempted and queues again goes on with the time it has left; a get that gives up is cancelled, so it takes nothing later. Its balk is a condition checked before it joins the queue; when it holds, the task publishes balked and never asks for the resource. Here each order brings its own patience as an attribute, and no order joins after the courier's last collection at 100 seconds:

YAMLBuilderLow-level examples/yaml/patience.yaml:pack
tasks:
  pack:
    service: packing
    resource: packers
    # Each order's own patience: it leaves the queue when it runs out.
    patience: attr.patience
    # No new orders once the courier has made its last collection.
    balk: t >= 100
    payload: {event_type: order_packed}
examples/builder/patience_example.py:pack
@app.task(
    service_id="packing",
    resource_id="packers",
    # Each order's own patience: it leaves the queue when it runs out
    patience="attr.patience",
    # No new orders once the courier has made its last collection
    balk="t >= 100",
)
def pack(task_id, context):
    """Packs one order."""
    return {"event_type": "order_packed"}
examples/low-level/patience_example.py:pack
def pack(env, sampler, packers, key, patience, task_id):
    """Balks after 100 s; otherwise waits at most `patience` for a packer."""
    path_id = "Shop.service.packing"

    def publish(value):
        env.publish_event(key, value, task="pack", instance=task_id)

    flow = key.rsplit("-", 1)[0]
    env.stats.flow_started(flow)  # the order enters the shop
    # No new orders once the courier has made its last collection
    if env.now >= 100:
        publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "balked"})
        env.stats.task_balked("pack", task_id)
        env.stats.flow_ended(flow)
        return
    publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "queued"})
    env.stats.task_queued("pack", task_id)
    with packers.request() as req:
        # Each order's own patience: it leaves the queue when it runs out
        yield req | env.timeout(patience)
        if not req.triggered:
            publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "reneged"})
            env.stats.task_reneged("pack", task_id)
            env.stats.flow_ended(flow)
            return
        publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "started"})
        env.stats.task_started("pack", task_id)
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(env.registry.get_config(path_id)))
        publish({"event_type": "order_packed"})
    env.stats.task_finished("pack", task_id)
    env.stats.flow_finished(flow)

A low-level process writes both by hand: an if before the request, and SimPy's request | env.timeout(patience), which happens when either event does. Leaving the with block takes a waiting request out of the queue at once, so it is never granted later.

patience takes seconds, a duration such as 30 s, an expression such as attr.patience, or in the builder a function of the task id and the entity's attributes. balk takes any condition an expression can write, such as level.stock == 0.

docs.title: Ties Between a Grant and a Patience
docs.text:
A unit can come free at the same instant a waiting order's patience runs out. Plain SimPy does not settle this with a rule: the event scheduled first is processed first. desflow grants units with the same events SimPy uses, so it gives the same answer:

  • a patience timeout scheduled after the holder's service end (the order arrived at 3 with a patience of 3, the holder started at 0 with 6 seconds of service) is processed after the release, and the order is served;
  • a patience timeout scheduled before it (the order arrived at 0 with a patience of 6, just after the holder) is processed first, and the order reneges.

This function runs both:

docs/snippets/guides/reneging_and_balking.py:tie
def tie(waiter_at: float, patience: float) -> str:
    """The outcome of an order whose patience ends when the packer comes free."""
    app = SimulationContext("Shop", factor=0)
    app.add_resource("packers", current_cap=1, max_cap=1)
    app.add_service("hold", dist="constant", value=6)
    app.add_service("packing", dist="constant", value=1)
    capture = Capture()
    app.add_egress(capture)

    @app.task(service_id="hold", resource_id="packers")
    def holder(task_id):
        return {"event_type": "held"}

    @app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="packers", patience=patience)
    def pack(task_id):
        return {"event_type": "order_packed"}

    def script(context):
        context.spawn(holder(0))  # takes the packer at 0 and keeps it until 6
        if waiter_at:
            yield context.env.timeout(waiter_at)
        context.spawn(pack(0))
        yield context.env.timeout(0)

    app.add_process(script)
    app.run(until=8)
    statuses = [
        r["value"].get("status")
        for r in capture.records
        if r["stream_type"] == "event" and r["task"] == "pack"
    ]
    return "reneged" if "reneged" in statuses else "served"

tie(3, 3) returns served and tie(0, 6) returns reneged. A model that must not depend on this order can avoid exact ties, for example by drawing patience from a distribution.

docs.title: Check the Balance
docs.text:
Every order that arrives ends in one of four places: packed, reneged, balked, or still in the shop when the run ends, waiting (queued) or being packed (started). The last event of each entity key says which. With statistics at basic or above, the finished, reneged and balked counts must match those events:

docs/snippets/guides/reneging_and_balking.py:balance
def balance(path: str) -> Counter:
    """Every order that arrived, by what became of it."""
    app = SimulationContext.from_yaml(path)
    capture = Capture()
    app.add_egress(capture)
    app.run()
    last = {}
    for record in capture.records:
        if record["stream_type"] == "event":
            value = record["value"]
            last[record["key"]] = value.get("status", value.get("event_type"))
    outcome = Counter(last.values())
    # queued or started: still in the shop when the run ended
    stats = app.env.stats.readings()
    name = "Shop.stats.tasks.pack.{}".format
    assert outcome["order_packed"] == stats[name("finished")]
    assert outcome["reneged"] == stats.get(name("reneged"), 0)
    assert outcome["balked"] == stats.get(name("balked"), 0)
    return outcome

For the example below it returns 49 packed, 7 reneged, 17 balked and 1 being packed, 74 orders in all. A mean wait counts only the orders that were served, so report the reneged and balked counts beside it.

docs.title: Time-varying Arrivals
docs.text:
Level: Intermediate

Change the arrival rate and the staffing at set times, such as a rush at lunch or a second packer for an afternoon, and know exactly which events a change reaches. It builds on Changing Demand, which asks what a rush does to waits, and on Live Parameters, which explains registry paths.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Find the registry path of each parameter that changes: Shop.arrival.orders.rate for an exponential arrival, Shop.resources.packers.current_cap for the number of packers.
  2. Write one step for each change, with the simulation time it applies at, at, in seconds or as a duration such as 20 min.
  3. Return each parameter to its usual value with a later step; a schedule does not repeat on its own.

Here orders arrive twice as fast from 120 to 180 seconds, and a second packer works for that time:

YAMLBuilderLow-level examples/yaml/changing_demand.yaml:schedule
scenario:
  # The rush: twice the orders, and a second packer, from 120 to 180 seconds
  - {at: 120, path: Shop.arrival.orders.rate, value: 0.8}
  - {at: 120, path: Shop.resources.packers.current_cap, value: 2}
  - {at: 180, path: Shop.arrival.orders.rate, value: 0.4}
  - {at: 180, path: Shop.resources.packers.current_cap, value: 1}
examples/builder/changing_demand_example.py:schedule
# The rush: twice the orders, and a second packer, from 120 to 180 seconds
app.add_scenario(
    [
        {"at": 120, "path": "Shop.arrival.orders.rate", "value": 0.8},
        {"at": 120, "path": "Shop.resources.packers.current_cap", "value": 2},
        {"at": 180, "path": "Shop.arrival.orders.rate", "value": 0.4},
        {"at": 180, "path": "Shop.resources.packers.current_cap", "value": 1},
    ]
)

add_step(at, path=..., value=...) adds one step; a step can also carry a record, a ground-truth label, or an interrupt.

examples/low-level/changing_demand_example.py:schedule
# The rush: twice the orders, and a second packer, from 120 to 180 seconds
SCHEDULE = [
    {"at": 120, "path": "Shop.arrival.orders.rate", "value": 0.8},
    {"at": 120, "path": "Shop.resources.packers.current_cap", "value": 2},
    {"at": 180, "path": "Shop.arrival.orders.rate", "value": 0.4},
    {"at": 180, "path": "Shop.resources.packers.current_cap", "value": 1},
]

run_scenario(env, SCHEDULE, until=300) is the SimPy process that applies the steps; start it with env.process, beside the arrivals.

The steps change the registry, so everything that reads the path follows: the next arrival gap is drawn from the new rate, and the packers grant or owe units as on Resources.

docs.title: Boundaries
docs.text:
A step that applies at the same time as another event has to come first or second, and a run that ends at a step's time has to apply it or not. Both are settled the way SimPy settles its own end time:

  • A step at time t applies before every other event at t. It is scheduled as an urgent event, as SimPy's run(until=t) is, so an arrival at t draws its next gap from the new value.
  • Steps at the same time apply in the order written.
  • A step at or after until never applies, as an event due at exactly until does not run.

This function runs orders every 10 seconds, with a step at 30 seconds that makes the gap 5:

docs/snippets/guides/time_varying_arrivals.py:boundary
def arrivals(until: float) -> tuple:
    """Orders every 10 s, every 5 s from 30 s: the arrival times, and the gap in
    force at the end."""
    app = (
        SimulationContext("Shop", factor=0)
        .add_arrival("orders", dist="constant", value=10)
        .add_step(30, path="Shop.arrival.orders.value", value=5)
    )
    times = []

    @app.arrival_loop("orders")
    def order_loop(context):
        while True:
            yield context.wait_for_arrival("orders")
            times.append(context.env.now)

    app.run(until=until)
    return times, app.env.registry.get("Shop.arrival.orders.value").value

arrivals(50) returns arrivals at 10, 20, 30, 35, 40 and 45 seconds, and a gap of 5 at the end: the order of 30 drew its gap after the step. arrivals(30) returns arrivals at 10 and 20 seconds and a gap of 10: the step at 30 is at until, so it never applies, and neither does the arrival due at 30.

docs.title: Wait for One or All
docs.text:
Level: Intermediate

Make a task wait for the first of several things, or for all of them, and read which happened. It builds on Process Interaction, which introduces signals and a wait with a limit, and on Tasks and Processes, which lists every kind of branch.

docs.title: Wait for the First
docs.text:
wait: {any: {...}} ends when the first branch happens, as SimPy's AnyOf (a | b) does. Name each branch; after the wait, wait.<branch>.done says which happened. Here an order waits for a restock or 30 seconds, and a builder function that declares wait reads the branches:

docs/snippets/guides/wait_for_one_or_all.py:first
def first(gap: float) -> dict:
    """Which branches were done when the order's wait ended."""
    app, capture = _shop()
    app.add_signal("restocked")
    seen = {}

    @app.task(
        wait={"any": {"stock": {"signal": "restocked"}, "limit": {"timeout": 30}}}
    )
    def order(task_id, wait):
        # `wait` holds each branch's done, ok and value
        seen.update({name: branch["done"] for name, branch in wait.items()})
        return {"event_type": "resumed"}

    @app.task(signal="restocked")
    def restock(task_id):
        return {"boxes": 6}

    def script(context):
        context.spawn(order(0))
        yield context.env.timeout(gap)
        context.spawn(restock(0))

    app.add_process(script)
    app.run(until=60)
    return seen

first(10) returns {"stock": True, "limit": False}: the restock came first. first(50) returns {"stock": False, "limit": True}. In YAML the same wait is

examples/yaml/process_interaction.yaml:dispatch
dispatch:
  # The courier's departure, or 40 seconds, whichever comes first.
  wait:
    any:
      courier: {signal: courier_left}
      limit: {timeout: 40 s}
  payload: {event_type: dispatched}
  next:
    when: [{condition: wait.courier.done, task: by_courier}]
    default: by_post

and in the low-level API it is yield env.any_of([restocked.wait(), env.timeout(30)]).

When an any wait ends, its losing branches are cleaned up: a signal, timeout or condition branch is dropped, so it does nothing later. A losing child flow ({task: name}) keeps running to its end, as SimPy leaves a process running when nothing waits for it.

docs.title: Two at the Same Instant
docs.text:
Two branches can happen at the same simulation time. SimPy's AnyOf holds every event processed before the AnyOf itself, so both are in its value, and desflow reports both as done:

docs/snippets/guides/wait_for_one_or_all.py:tie
def two_at_once() -> dict:
    """Two signals fire at the same instant: both branches are done."""
    app, capture = _shop()
    app.add_signal("boxes").add_signal("labels")
    seen = {}

    @app.task(
        wait={"any": {"boxes": {"signal": "boxes"}, "labels": {"signal": "labels"}}}
    )
    def order(task_id, wait):
        seen.update({name: branch["done"] for name, branch in wait.items()})
        return {"event_type": "resumed"}

    @app.task(signal="boxes")
    def deliver_boxes(task_id):
        return {"item": "boxes"}

    @app.task(signal="labels")
    def deliver_labels(task_id):
        return {"item": "labels"}

    def script(context):
        context.spawn(order(0))
        yield context.env.timeout(5)
        context.spawn(deliver_boxes(0))
        context.spawn(deliver_labels(0))

    app.add_process(script)
    app.run(until=10)
    return seen

two_at_once() returns {"boxes": True, "labels": True}. A model that routes on one branch should therefore check the branch it cares about, not assume that only one is done.

docs.title: Wait for All
docs.text:
wait: {all: {...}} ends when every branch has happened, as SimPy's AllOf (a & b) does. If a branch fails first, the wait fails at once, with that branch's reason, and the task publishes failed; branches still pending are cleaned up as for any, so a child flow runs on. Here the restock fails at 2 while the inspection, a child flow, runs until 4:

docs/snippets/guides/wait_for_one_or_all.py:all
def all_with_a_failure() -> list:
    """(time, task, status) of the order and its inspection: the restock fails at 2,
    the order fails at once, and the inspection, still running, ends at 4."""
    app, capture = _shop()
    app.add_signal("restocked")
    app.add_service("inspecting", dist="constant", value=4)

    @app.task(
        wait={"all": {"stock": {"signal": "restocked"}, "check": {"task": "inspect"}}}
    )
    def order(task_id):
        return {"event_type": "resumed"}

    @app.task(service_id="inspecting")
    def inspect(task_id):
        return {"event_type": "inspected"}

    @app.task(
        signal="restocked", fail="attr.broken == 1", fail_reason="broken delivery"
    )
    def restock(task_id):
        return {"boxes": 6}

    def script(context):
        context.spawn(order(0))
        yield context.env.timeout(2)
        delivery = Entity("restocks-1", "restocks", {"broken": 1})
        context.spawn(restock(0, entity=delivery))

    app.add_process(script)
    app.run(until=10)
    return [
        (e["sim_ts"], e["task"], e["value"].get("status", "finished"))
        for e in capture.events
        if e["task"] in ("order", "inspect") and e["value"].get("status") != "started"
    ]

all_with_a_failure() returns [(0.0, "order", "queued"), (2.0, "order", "failed"), (4.0, "inspect", "finished")]. The order's failure goes to its on_fail task when it has one, and otherwise ends its flow.

A wait never holds a resource. Waiting for all of several things that each free up a resource does not grant the resources together: the task asks for its resource only after the wait, and another task can take the unit in between. To hold several resources at once, list them on the task, resource: [picker, bench], as Resources describes.

docs.title: Example
docs.text: The process-interaction example waits for a child flow, then for the first of a courier's signal and a time limit. Tasks and Processes shows how to download and run it.

docs.title: Python in a Blueprint: !python
docs.text:
Level: Intermediate

A blueprint holds configuration as plain YAML, and the YAML Blueprints page covers that. When a simulation needs logic that YAML cannot express, the file can reference a Python object with !python module.attribute in place of a value. This guide covers when to use it, how a reference is found, what each field receives and the security note, and ends with the OML hot rolling twin as a worked case.

The advanced Postgres example is a complete blueprint with one Python process. Every file on this page is in the repository under docs/snippets/.

docs.title: When to Use It
docs.text:
Use !python when a blueprint needs one of these:

  • Field values with logic. Random or weighted choices, fields derived from other fields and state carried from one event to the next are a payload function or a process.
  • More than a task can describe. Collecting several entities into one, such as a batch, is a process. Routing (next), priorities (priority and queue: priority), stores and containers, several resources per task (resource: [...] and keep), preemption (preempt: true) and breakdowns (breakdown:) are plain YAML.
  • Readings other than the built-in statistics. stats: minimal publishes resource, store and container readings, a container's level among them. Use a telemetry function to publish variables and derived metrics.
  • Routing over several destinations, and serializers. A router or an Avro serializer is a Python object.
  • Setup a connector does not do itself, such as topics that only a router knows about.
  • A connector from another package.

A setting that is a value needs no Python. Environment variables, relative times, when: history and when: live, filesystem and catalog mappings, Iceberg schemas and Postgres tables are all plain YAML, as YAML Format lists. A value can still come from a module when another program already defines it, as the hot rolling twin below reads its broker address from src/config.py.

docs.title: How a Reference Is Resolved
docs.text:
!python module.attribute imports module and returns its attribute. The reference can name anything: a function, a class, a dictionary or a constant.

The longest prefix that is a module is imported, and the rest is read as attributes, so pkg.module.func and module.Class.attribute both work. The folder of the YAML file is added to the front of sys.path, unless it is already on it, before anything is resolved, so a module beside the blueprint is found from any working directory. Other modules are found on the normal sys.path, which includes installed packages. ${VAR} is replaced inside a reference too, so !python ${LOGIC}.ticker picks the module from the environment.

Every reference is resolved and checked when the file is loaded, so a wrong reference fails before the run starts, with the file and line.

Field Must be Called as processes[].function a generator function function(context, **kwargs) when the run starts tasks.<name>.payload a callable, or a mapping payload(task_id, context) once per finished task telemetry[].function a callable function(context) every interval egress[].when a callable, or history or live when(record), True to send the record to that sink ingress[].type, egress[].type a class, or a short name type(**config) while the blueprint is built run.before[] a callable before() once, at the start of run() any value under config, simulation or run.until whatever that argument takes not called

docs.title: Processes, Payloads and kwargs
docs.text:
This blueprint keeps the shop in YAML and moves three pieces of logic into Python: a payload that picks each order's delivery, a breaks process with arguments, and a predicate that keeps telemetry off the terminal:

docs/snippets/yaml/hybrid.yaml
# The shop with its logic in Python. YAML keeps the blueprint and the
# experiment; shop_logic.py beside this file holds what YAML cannot express.
simulation:
  sim_id: Shop
  factor: 0
  random_seed: 1

egress:
  - type: Console
    # Only events reach the terminal; telemetry is dropped.
    when: !python shop_logic.events_only

resources:
  packers: {current_cap: 1, max_cap: 3}

services:
  packing: {dist: normal, mean: 4.0, std: 1.0}

arrivals:
  orders: {dist: exponential, rate: 0.2, spawn: pack_order}

tasks:
  pack_order:
    service: packing
    resource: packers
    # Called as choose_delivery(task_id, context) for every packed order.
    payload: !python shop_logic.choose_delivery

processes:
  # Called as breaks(context, resource="packers", every=50, duration=5).
  - function: !python shop_logic.breaks
    kwargs: {resource: packers, every: 50, duration: 5}

scenario:
  - {at: 1 min, path: Shop.arrival.orders.rate, value: 0.4}

run:
  until: 3 min
docs/snippets/yaml/shop_logic.py
"""Python for the blueprints beside it: a payload, a process with arguments, a
predicate and a custom reading."""


def choose_delivery(task_id: int, context):
    """Picks each order's delivery from the shared generator, so a seed repeats it."""
    delivery = "standard" if context.sampler.rng.random() < 0.9 else "express"
    return {"status": "finished", "order_id": task_id, "delivery": delivery}


def breaks(context, resource: str, every: float, duration: float):
    """Waits `every` seconds, then takes every packer off for a break of `duration`."""
    path = f"{context.sim_id}.resources.{resource}.current_cap"
    registry = context.env.registry
    while True:
        yield context.env.timeout(every)
        normal = registry.get(path).value
        registry.update(path, 0)
        context.env.publish_event(f"{resource}-break", {"status": "down"})
        yield context.env.timeout(duration)
        registry.update(path, normal)
        context.env.publish_event(f"{resource}-break", {"status": "up"})


def events_only(record: dict) -> bool:
    """Egress predicate: keeps events and drops telemetry."""
    return record["stream_type"] == "event"


def packers_report(context):
    """A custom reading: orders waiting per packer, and the live arrival rate."""
    packers = context.get_resource("packers")
    waiting = len(packers.queue.items)
    context.publish("waiting_per_packer", waiting / max(packers.capacity, 1))
    rate = context.env.registry.get(f"{context.sim_id}.arrival.orders.rate").value
    context.publish("arrival_rate", rate)  # as Shop.arrival_rate

What each reference receives:

  • payload is called as choose_delivery(task_id, context) for every packed order. It draws from context.sampler, the generator seeded by random_seed, so the deliveries repeat with the seed.
  • processes entries are called as function(context, **kwargs) when the run starts. kwargs is how one function serves several resources.
  • when is called with every record and returns True to send it to that sink.

The run shows both:

[EVT] {'sim_ts': 5.369, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'orders-1', 'task': 'pack_order', 'instance': 0, 'value': {'status': 'finished', 'order_id': 0, 'delivery': 'standard'}}
[EVT] {'sim_ts': 50.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'packers-break', 'task': None, 'instance': None, 'value': {'status': 'down'}}
[EVT] {'sim_ts': 55.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'packers-break', 'task': None, 'instance': None, 'value': {'status': 'up'}}

A process is written either as a bare reference, - !python module.func, which is called as func(context), or as a mapping with function and kwargs, which is called as func(context, **kwargs). kwargs is what lets a blueprint start a process whose signature is not (context). When the signature differs more, write a small adapter: a generator function that takes the context, picks out what the process needs, and hands over with yield from.

docs/snippets/hot_rolling/hot_rolling_adapter.py:arrivals
def arrivals(context, product):
    yield from arrival_process(
        context.env,
        product,
        VARIABLE_PASSES,
        MAX_PASSES,
        context.sampler,
        context.get_resource(f"mill_{product}"),
    )

A process must be a generator function, one that contains yield. The check runs when the file is loaded and looks only at the function, so an adapter that returns a generator instead of yielding from one is rejected. Write adapters with yield from.

docs.title: Routers, Serializers and Connector Classes
docs.text:
A router replaces the default destination of every record. path_router on Parquet and JSONL and table_router on Iceberg each take a function that receives a record and returns its destination, or None to drop it. topic_router on Kafka must always return a topic. To drop records before Kafka, give the sink a when predicate. With a router, records are written as the router leaves them, so flattening events and dropping telemetry become the router's job. Kafka also leaves topic creation to the caller, because only the router knows which topics it uses. The hot rolling twin below sends every record to one of four topics with topic_router: !python routing.custom_topic_router.

A serializer is an object, so it is built in a module and referenced. KafkaEgress takes default_serializer and topic_serializers, for example default_serializer: !python serializers.AVRO, where serializers.py builds a ConfluentAvroSerializer with the registry URL and the schema.

A connector from another package is referenced by class: type: !python my_package.MyEgress. Its config is passed to the constructor, as for a built-in one.

docs.title: Setup with run.before
docs.text:
run.before lists functions called with no arguments, once, at the start of run(). Connectors already create what they write to when they can: Kafka its event and telemetry topics, Postgres the tables under tables, and Parquet and JSONL their folders. run.before is for anything else, such as the five topics the hot rolling twin below creates for its router.

Put such setup in a function rather than at the top of the module. The module is imported when the file is loaded, so its top-level code runs even when the file is loaded and never run.

docs/snippets/yaml_build/connectors.yaml:before
run:
  until: 1 hour
  before:
    - !python routing_logic.make_output_folder

The module beside the blueprint holds the setup function, and the path_router its Jsonl sink uses:

docs/snippets/yaml_build/routing_logic.py
"""Python for docs/snippets/yaml_build/connectors.yaml: a router and a setup step."""

import os


def daily_path(record: dict):
    """Writes each event under its day; drops telemetry by returning None."""
    if record["stream_type"] != "event":
        return None
    return f"events/day={record['timestamp'][:10]}/events.jsonl"


def make_output_folder() -> None:
    """Called once by run.before, when the run starts, not when the file is loaded."""
    os.makedirs("events", exist_ok=True)

docs.title: Worked Case: Lift the OML Hot Rolling Twin
docs.text:
The OML hot rolling digital twin is a steel mill written with the low-level API. Its generator.py builds a SimParameter with three arrivals, three services, three resources, three containers and three variables, wires Kafka in both directions with a topic router, and starts the processes in sim_logic.py. Those processes take (env, sampler, resource, ...), not a context, and sim_logic.py runs to 262 lines of multi-stage routing, wear and physics.

The configuration moves to YAML. The processes keep their logic, and a small adapter changes only how they are called.

docs/snippets/hot_rolling/hot_rolling.yaml
# The OML hot rolling digital twin as a blueprint. The parameters and the Kafka
# wiring that generator.py builds in Python are declared here. The processes stay
# in sim_logic.py, and hot_rolling_adapter.py beside this file adapts them.
#
# Place this file and the adapter in sim_control/, then run from there:
#   desflow run hot_rolling.yaml
simulation:
  sim_id: HotRolling
  factor: 1.0
  random_seed: 42

ingress:
  # Control commands from the dashboard.
  - type: Kafka
    config:
      bootstrap_servers: !python src.config.KAFKA_BROKER
      topic: !python src.config.TOPIC_CONTROL_INGRESS

egress:
  # One producer; the router picks one of four topics for every record.
  - type: Kafka
    config:
      bootstrap_servers: !python src.config.KAFKA_BROKER
      topic_router: !python routing.custom_topic_router

arrivals:
  structural: {dist: exponential, rate: 0.2}
  microalloyed: {dist: exponential, rate: 0.15}
  high_alloy: {dist: exponential, rate: 0.1}

services:
  pass_roughing: {dist: normal, mean: 2.0, std: 0.2}
  pass_intermediate: {dist: normal, mean: 4.5, std: 0.5}
  pass_finishing: {dist: normal, mean: 8.0, std: 1.2}

resources:
  mill_structural: {current_cap: 4, max_cap: 10}
  mill_microalloyed: {current_cap: 4, max_cap: 10}
  mill_high_alloy: {current_cap: 4, max_cap: 10}

containers:
  # The wear is the level; current_cap is the most wear a roll can have
  wear_structural: {current_cap: 100.0, max_cap: 100.0, level: 0.001}
  wear_microalloyed: {current_cap: 100.0, max_cap: 100.0, level: 0.001}
  wear_high_alloy: {current_cap: 100.0, max_cap: 100.0, level: 0.001}

variables:
  velocity_structural: {type: abrupt, value: 0.0}
  velocity_microalloyed: {type: abrupt, value: 0.0}
  velocity_high_alloy: {type: abrupt, value: 0.0}

processes:
  # Started in the order generator.py starts them.
  - function: !python hot_rolling_adapter.drift
    kwargs: {product_lines: [structural, microalloyed, high_alloy]}
  - function: !python hot_rolling_adapter.monitor
    kwargs: {product_lines: [structural, microalloyed, high_alloy]}
  - function: !python hot_rolling_adapter.primer
    kwargs: {product: structural}
  - function: !python hot_rolling_adapter.arrivals
    kwargs: {product: structural}
  - function: !python hot_rolling_adapter.primer
    kwargs: {product: microalloyed}
  - function: !python hot_rolling_adapter.arrivals
    kwargs: {product: microalloyed}
  - function: !python hot_rolling_adapter.primer
    kwargs: {product: high_alloy}
  - function: !python hot_rolling_adapter.arrivals
    kwargs: {product: high_alloy}

# A reproducible drift experiment, which the dashboard otherwise drives by hand:
# gradual wear on the structural line from 10 minutes.
scenario:
  - at: 10 min
    path: HotRolling.variables.velocity_structural
    value: {type: gradual, value: 0.5, freq: 1}

run:
  before:
    - !python hot_rolling_adapter.create_topics
docs/snippets/hot_rolling/hot_rolling_adapter.py
"""Adapts the hot rolling processes to the calls a blueprint makes.

A blueprint calls every process as `function(context, **kwargs)`. The processes in
sim_logic.py take `(env, sampler, resource, ...)` instead, so each function here
takes the context, picks out what the process needs, and hands over with
`yield from`. Only the wear paths in sim_logic.py change, from `current_cap` to
`level`.
"""

import time
import uuid

from desflow import KafkaAdminConnector
from generator import telemetry_monitor
from sim_logic import arrival_process, drift_engine, roll_slab
from src.config import (
    KAFKA_BROKER,
    TOPIC_CONTROL_INGRESS,
    TOPIC_GROUND_TRUTH,
    TOPIC_LIFECYCLE,
    TOPIC_PREDICTION_REQUESTS,
    TOPIC_TELEMETRY,
)

# The command-line options of generator.py, fixed here.
VARIABLE_PASSES = False
MAX_PASSES = 5


def drift(context, product_lines):
    yield from drift_engine(context.env, product_lines)


def monitor(context, product_lines):
    yield from telemetry_monitor(context.env, product_lines)


def primer(context, product):
    """Rolls a first slab, so the mill does not start dry."""
    yield from roll_slab(
        context.env,
        uuid.uuid4().hex[:8].upper(),
        product,
        VARIABLE_PASSES,
        MAX_PASSES,
        context.sampler,
        context.get_resource(f"mill_{product}"),
    )


def arrivals(context, product):
    yield from arrival_process(
        context.env,
        product,
        VARIABLE_PASSES,
        MAX_PASSES,
        context.sampler,
        context.get_resource(f"mill_{product}"),
    )


def create_topics():
    """Creates the five topics generator.py creates before it starts."""
    KafkaAdminConnector(bootstrap_servers=KAFKA_BROKER).create_topics(
        topics_config=[
            {"name": TOPIC_CONTROL_INGRESS, "partitions": 1},
            {"name": TOPIC_TELEMETRY, "partitions": 1},
            {"name": TOPIC_LIFECYCLE, "partitions": 1},
            {"name": TOPIC_PREDICTION_REQUESTS, "partitions": 3},
            {"name": TOPIC_GROUND_TRUTH, "partitions": 3},
        ]
    )
    time.sleep(2)

What moved. The whole SimParameter, both Kafka connectors with the custom topic router, the seed, the factor and the topic creation. The broker address and the topic names stay in src/config.py, and the blueprint references them. containers and variables carry the wear levels and drift velocities the processes read and write.

What stayed. drift_engine, arrival_process, roll_slab and telemetry_monitor, with one change: they read and write the wear at HotRolling.containers.wear_<grade>.current_cap, and a container's current_cap is now its capacity, so those paths in sim_logic.py and dashboard.py become .level. The adapter is one generator function per process. Each takes the context, picks out the environment, the sampler and the mill resource, and hands over with yield from. The primer slab and the arrival loop are separate entries, so they start in the order generator.py starts them.

What is new. The scenario turns on gradual wear on the structural line at ten minutes. The twin's dashboard does this by hand over Kafka. As a scenario it repeats exactly, and it can still be combined with the dashboard, because both write to the same registry.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
A reference that cannot be resolved stops the load with its line:

Error: err.yaml:6: !python shop_logic.missing: 'shop_logic' has no attribute 'missing'

A module that exists but fails on one of its own imports is reported with that error, rather than as a missing module.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
Loading a blueprint runs the imports it names. !python imports modules, and importing a module runs its top-level code. A blueprint is therefore as trusted as a Python script: load only files you would run as code, in a local or trusted CI workflow.

Every other node is constructed by yaml.SafeLoader, and the tag is registered on a subclass of it, so yaml.safe_load elsewhere in the process is unaffected. Only !python and !include are added to YAML. Every other tag, such as !!python/object, is rejected as yaml.safe_load rejects it.
