docs.title: Distributions
docs.text:
Every distribution family desflow can draw from, generated from the registry of distributions in the code. Arrivals and Services explains how a draw works, and how each family is seeded and changed live.

Each family lists its parameters, the rules they must follow, and the registry path of each parameter that can change during a run. The mean, variance and value with no random generator are computed by the family's own functions for the example given. In a blueprint, a time-valued parameter (mean, std, low, mode, high, scale, value, values, edges) also takes a duration such as 5 min. The builder and the low-level API take these parameters in seconds only, so add_service("packing", dist="constant", value=120), not value="2 min"; a task's patience takes a duration in the builder as well.

Family Parameters Live paths exponential rate .rate normal mean, std .mean, .std lognormal mean, std .mean, .std truncated_normal mean, std, low .mean, .std, .low constant value .value uniform low, high .low, .high triangular low, mode, high .low, .mode, .high gamma shape, scale .shape, .scale weibull shape, scale .shape, .scale empirical values, weights, edges, counts none

docs.title: exponential
docs.text:
Gaps between independent arrivals; the memoryless distribution.

dist exponential Parameters rate Defaults none Rules rate > 0, in events per second Registry paths <sim_id>.service.<name>.rate (and .arrival. for an arrival) Uses a random number yes

For the example {dist: exponential, rate: 0.5}: mean 2, variance 4, and with no random generator every draw is 2.

docs.title: normal
docs.text:
Symmetric times around a mean. Draws below 0.00001 s (min_delay) are raised to it, which raises the mean; truncated_normal avoids that.

dist normal Parameters mean, std Defaults std 0 Rules std >= 0; a std of 0 gives the mean every time Registry paths <sim_id>.service.<name>.mean, <sim_id>.service.<name>.std (and .arrival. for an arrival) Uses a random number yes

For the example {dist: normal, mean: 3.0, std: 0.5}: mean 3, variance 0.25, and with no random generator every draw is 3.

docs.title: lognormal
docs.text:
Positive times with a long right tail, given by their mean and std.

dist lognormal Parameters mean, std Defaults std 0 Rules mean > 0, std >= 0 Registry paths <sim_id>.service.<name>.mean, <sim_id>.service.<name>.std (and .arrival. for an arrival) Uses a random number yes

For the example {dist: lognormal, mean: 4.0, std: 3.0}: mean 4, variance 9, and with no random generator every draw is 4.

docs.title: truncated_normal
docs.text:
A normal that draws again below low instead of clamping.

dist truncated_normal Parameters mean, std, low Defaults std 0, low 0 Rules std >= 0; low is 0 when not given; with std 0, mean >= low Registry paths <sim_id>.service.<name>.mean, <sim_id>.service.<name>.std, <sim_id>.service.<name>.low (and .arrival. for an arrival) Uses a random number yes

For the example {dist: truncated_normal, mean: 1.0, std: 1.0, low: 0.0}: mean 1.288, variance 0.6297, and with no random generator every draw is 1.

docs.title: constant
docs.text:
The same time every draw, such as a conveyor or a set-up.

dist constant Parameters value Defaults none Rules value >= 0 Registry paths <sim_id>.service.<name>.value (and .arrival. for an arrival) Uses a random number no

For the example {dist: constant, value: 1.5}: mean 1.5, variance 0, and with no random generator every draw is 1.5.

docs.title: uniform
docs.text:
Every time between low and high equally likely.

dist uniform Parameters low, high Defaults none Rules low < high Registry paths <sim_id>.service.<name>.low, <sim_id>.service.<name>.high (and .arrival. for an arrival) Uses a random number yes

For the example {dist: uniform, low: 1.0, high: 2.0}: mean 1.5, variance 0.08333, and with no random generator every draw is 1.5.

docs.title: triangular
docs.text:
An expert's estimate: the shortest, the most likely and the longest time.

dist triangular Parameters low, mode, high Defaults none Rules low <= mode <= high, low < high Registry paths <sim_id>.service.<name>.low, <sim_id>.service.<name>.mode, <sim_id>.service.<name>.high (and .arrival. for an arrival) Uses a random number yes

For the example {dist: triangular, low: 1.0, mode: 1.25, high: 2.25}: mean 1.5, variance 0.07292, and with no random generator every draw is 1.5.

docs.title: gamma
docs.text:
Times less variable than exponential. A whole-number shape is the Erlang distribution: that many exponential steps in a row.

dist gamma Parameters shape, scale Defaults none Rules shape > 0, scale > 0; mean = shape * scale Registry paths <sim_id>.service.<name>.shape, <sim_id>.service.<name>.scale (and .arrival. for an arrival) Uses a random number yes

For the example {dist: gamma, shape: 9.0, scale: 0.1667}: mean 1.5, variance 0.2501, and with no random generator every draw is 1.5.

docs.title: weibull
docs.text:
Time to failure: a shape below 1 fails early, above 1 wears out.

dist weibull Parameters shape, scale Defaults none Rules shape > 0, scale > 0 Registry paths <sim_id>.service.<name>.shape, <sim_id>.service.<name>.scale (and .arrival. for an arrival) Uses a random number yes

For the example {dist: weibull, shape: 1.5, scale: 3600.0}: mean 3250, variance 4.869e+06, and with no random generator every draw is 3250.

docs.title: empirical
docs.text:
Times taken from real data: listed values with optional weights, or a histogram of edges and counts. Taken at load; they do not change live.

dist empirical Parameters values, weights, edges, counts Defaults none Rules values, or edges and counts; one weight per value and one count per bin, each 0 or more and adding up to more than 0; edges increasing Registry paths none: the lists are taken at load Uses a random number yes

For the example {dist: empirical, values: [1.2, 1.5, 1.5, 2.1, 3.0]}: mean 1.86, variance 0.4104, and with no random generator every draw is 1.86.

docs.title: Records and Telemetry
docs.text:
Everything a simulation publishes is a record of one of three kinds: a telemetry record for a single value, an event record for something that happened to an entity, and a label record for the ground truth of a scenario step. The records have the shape of the TelemetryPayload, EventPayload and LabelPayload models, and they are the same whichever way the simulation was written.

All three share stream_type, sim_ts and timestamp. Telemetry names its value in path_id; an event names its entity in key and its task in task and instance; a label carries what a step changed:

docs.title: Record Shape
docs.text:
Every sink, router and when predicate receives records as plain dictionaries, with these keys in this order. The type is the Python type a sink receives, and the JSON type a JSON sink writes:

Field Type Telemetry Event Label stream_type string "telemetry" "event" "label" sim_ts float simulation seconds simulation seconds simulation seconds timestamp string logical time logical time logical time path_id string the name of the value key string the entity's key, such as orders-1 task string or null the task's name, or None instance any JSON value or null the task's instance id, or None path string or null the registry path the step changed, or None old any JSON value or null the value before the step, or None new any JSON value or null the value after the step, or None label object the step's record mapping value any JSON value a single value the event's value

As ConsoleEgress prints them, a statistic and the three events of one task:

[TEL] {'sim_ts': 10.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.resources.packers.in_use', 'value': 0}
[EVT] {'sim_ts': 3.672, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'orders-1', 'task': 'pack_order', 'instance': 0, 'value': {'path_id': 'Shop.service.packing', 'status': 'queued'}}
[EVT] {'sim_ts': 3.672, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'orders-1', 'task': 'pack_order', 'instance': 0, 'value': {'path_id': 'Shop.service.packing', 'status': 'started'}}
[EVT] {'sim_ts': 5.369, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'orders-1', 'task': 'pack_order', 'instance': 0, 'value': {'event_type': 'order_packed'}}

And two labels, as a JSON Lines sink writes them:

{"stream_type":"label","sim_ts":30.0,"timestamp":"...","path":"Shop.arrival.orders.rate","old":0.5,"new":1.5,"label":{"fault":"order_surge","cause":"flash sale"}}
{"stream_type":"label","sim_ts":45.0,"timestamp":"...","path":null,"old":null,"new":null,"label":{"fault":"label_printer_offline"}}

sim_ts is simulation seconds. timestamp is logical_start_time plus the simulation time, as an ISO 8601 string with milliseconds and the offset of the run's time zone, such as 2026-10-03T12:00:00.000+10:00, or +00:00 in UTC, the default; Time and Pacing describes the zone. sim_ts is rounded to the millisecond and timestamp cut to it, so their milliseconds can differ by 1.

docs.title: Field Values
docs.text:
• sim_ts is rounded to three decimal places and is always a float, so simulation time 0 is 0.0.
  • key and path_id are strings. bytes and bytearray are decoded to strings; any other type, such as an int, raises a Pydantic ValidationError at the call.
  • task is the name of a builder or YAML task; instance is its instance id, an integer from 0 for a builder or YAML task, or what a low-level process passes. publish_event and publish_label do not check task, instance or path, so a low-level process that passes another type writes that type; the types in the table are what the builder and YAML write.
  • value, old, new and label are converted to plain JSON values before any sink sees them. A Pydantic V2 model becomes a dictionary, a datetime an ISO string, and a NaN or an infinity None, in a model at any depth as in a plain dictionary.
docs/snippets/pages/records.py:values
class Reading(BaseModel):
    sensor: str
    celsius: float
    taken_at: datetime


def readings(context: SimulationContext):
    while True:
        yield context.env.timeout(30.0)
        reading = Reading(
            sensor="spindle", celsius=float("nan"), taken_at=datetime.now()
        )
        # The model becomes a dict, taken_at an ISO string, and NaN becomes None
        context.env.publish_event("sensor-spindle", reading)

docs.title: Task Events
docs.text:
@app.task and a YAML task publish three events for each run that is served, all with the entity's key, the task's name and its instance id:

Event value queued {"path_id": "<sim_id>.service.<service>", "status": "queued"} started {"path_id": "<sim_id>.service.<service>", "status": "started"} finished exactly what the task returns, or the YAML payload

A run that is not served, or fails, publishes one other event in place of its finished event:

Event When value balked its balk condition held, so it never joined the queue and publishes no queued {"path_id": ..., "status": "balked"} reneged its patience ran out before it was served; it left the queue at that moment {"path_id": ..., "status": "reneged"} failed its fail condition held, its wait failed, or its function raised {"path_id": ..., "status": "failed", "reason": ...}

An interrupted run publishes these as well, and its finished event when it ends:

Event When value interrupted an interrupt reached it; its units and waits were given up {"path_id": ..., "status": "interrupted", "cause": ...} preempted a request of a lower priority value took its unit {"path_id": ..., "status": "preempted", "resource": ...} resumed after an interrupt or a preemption, it holds its units again and is served {"path_id": ..., "status": "resumed"}

status and path_id are strings; reason is a string, cause any JSON value the interrupt was given, or None, and resource the name of the resource that was taken.

With statistics at basic or above, entities that enter and leave are counted as <sim_id>.stats.flows.<arrival>.started, .finished and .in_system, and from minimal each task's <sim_id>.stats.tasks.<task>.in_progress; each of the outcomes above is counted as <sim_id>.stats.tasks.<task>.balked, .reneged, .failed, .interrupted, .preempted and .resumed, published once the first one happens, and a flow that ends in a failure as <sim_id>.stats.flows.<arrival>.failed. Patience shows balking and reneging, and Tasks and Processes failures, and Interruptions interrupts and preemption. A failed task publishes started before its failure when it got that far, and a task with a wait publishes queued when the wait starts.

A resource with a breakdown publishes an event at each failure and each repair. Its key is the resource's name, and it has no task or instance:

Event When value down the resource failed; its capacity is 0 until the repair {"status": "down", "reason": "failure"} repaired the repair ended; its capacity is current_cap again {"status": "repaired", "reason": "failure"}

With statistics at minimal or above, such a resource publishes <sim_id>.stats.resources.<name>.down, 1 while it is down, and from basic .downtime, the seconds it has been down, and .failures; Breakdowns checks them against the events.

A task with no service has {"status": ...} without path_id. A timed step, with a service and no resource, publishes no queued. A task with no service, resource or get publishes only the finished event, as soon as it starts. The key is the arrival's name and a counter from 1, such as orders-1, on every event of every task the entity passes through; Task Flow describes it. A low-level process publishes whatever it passes to env.publish_event(key, value, task=..., instance=...).

docs.title: Telemetry Names
docs.text:
Published by path_id the built-in statistics <sim_id>.stats.<kind>.<name>.<statistic>, such as Shop.stats.resources.packers.in_use; Reference, Statistics lists every name replications, once at the end <sim_id>.stats.<measure>.replication.<i> for each replication from 1, then <sim_id>.stats.<measure>.mean, .half_width and .n, where the measure is a statistic's name without the sim id, such as tasks.pack.wait_mean context.publish(name, value) and a YAML telemetry function <sim_id>.<name> env.publish_telemetry(path_id, value) path_id, as given the lag monitor system.simulation.lag_seconds, every lag_interval: by default every simulation second at a factor above 0, and none at factor: 0 (Time and Pacing) docs/snippets/pages/records.py:telemetry
@app.telemetry_loop(interval=10.0)
def report(context: SimulationContext):
    # path_id is Shop.packers_free: the sim_id is added in front
    packers = context.get_resource("packers")
    context.publish("packers_free", packers.capacity - packers.in_use)

env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=0.0)
env.setup_egress([ConsoleEgress()])
env.publish_telemetry("plant.power_kw", 412.5)  # path_id exactly as given
# key, task, instance and value as given; task and instance are optional
env.publish_event("orders-17", {"status": "shipped"}, task="ship", instance=16)
# A ground-truth label, which only a when: labels sink receives
env.publish_label({"fault": "slow_packing"}, path="Shop.service.packing.scale")

docs.title: Reserved Payload Keys
docs.text:
A key of a record's value, an event's or a telemetry value that is a mapping, that is two underscores, a name of at least one character, then two underscores, such as __table__ or __stream__, belongs to desflow, not to the data. A sink that routes by one uses it and removes it: PostgresEgress writes the record to the table its __table__ names, and RedisEgress to the stream its __stream__ names. Every other sink, KafkaEgress, the Parquet, JSON Lines and Iceberg sinks and ConsoleEgress, drops every such key and logs one warning per key the first time it meets it:

KafkaEgress drops the payload key '__table__': keys that start and end with two underscores are reserved for desflow, and only a sink that routes by one, such as PostgreSQL's __table__ or Redis's __stream__, uses it. Rename the key to keep it as data.

The record itself is not changed, so a PostgreSQL sink on the same run still finds its __table__. A sink drops the keys before its router sees the record, so a Kafka topic_router or a storage path_router cannot route by such a key. PostgresEgress and RedisEgress drop only their own routing key, so any other such key reaches their rows as data. Rename a key such as __source__ to source to keep it as data.

docs.title: What Each Sink Writes
docs.text:
Every sink receives the events and telemetry above, and a when: labels sink receives the labels instead. What each writes differs:

Sink Writes ConsoleEgress one line per record, [TEL], [EVT] or [LBL] followed by the record without stream_type, in one INFO log call per batch, so only a batch's first line carries the logging format's prefix and the other lines are bare KafkaEgress the record as JSON, without stream_type unless include_stream_type=True; the message key is path_id for telemetry and key for an event. A label goes to event_topic with no key RedisEgress the record as JSON in one payload field, with any __stream__ key removed ParquetStorageEgress, JsonlStorageEgress, IcebergStorageEgress without a router, one flat row per event or label, with an event's value mapping unpacked into columns, and no telemetry; with a router, each record as the router leaves it PostgresEgress an event or telemetry record whose value is a mapping, routed by its __table__ key, which is removed, with sim_ts, timestamp, key as event_id, task and instance, or path_id, added to it, as Egress describes; a label as the columns sim_ts, timestamp, path, old, new and label, the last three as JSON text

In a flat row, a finished event's columns are its task's payload only: the queued and started rows of a task carry path_id and status, and its finished row has them null unless the payload holds them. Egress describes the file sinks.

docs.title: SimPy Compatibility
docs.text:
Every modelling feature of SimPy 4.1.2, 98 in all, with its status in YAML, the builder and the low-level API: native and checked, or not yet. A native feature is checked by conformance tests that run a plain SimPy 4.1.2 model and the same model in all three APIs, and compare event times, outcomes and balances. The page is generated from tests/conformance/register.yaml, the list the tests read, so a feature is native here only with its checks.

48 features are native and checked in all three APIs, 48 are not yet, and 2 are differences kept by design. Each feature that is not yet native becomes native in all three APIs in 0.23.0, as the Roadmap says.

The low-level API is SimPy with a few classes added, so most SimPy features work in it, those not yet checked included; SimPy and desflow explains how the two fit together. Where desflow differs from SimPy on purpose, the difference is listed under the table.

The sections are numbered by kind. C1 to C7 are SimPy's core operations, such as events, conditions, interrupts, resources and stores. S1 to S3 are support features desflow builds from those operations: breakdowns, schedules and replay. SimPy has no single call for them, so their conformance tests compare with the same behaviour written in plain SimPy.

Section Operations native in all three APIs C1: Events and Processes 9 C2: Wait for One or All 2 C3: Interrupts and Preemption 3 C4: Resources 5 C5: Stores and Containers 11 C6: Run Control 10 C7: Patience 2 S1: Breakdowns 1 S2: Schedules 1 S3: Replay 1 Not Yet none; 48 SimPy features to come Differences Kept by Design 2 differences

Under each feature, API details opens to show its SimPy construct, its form in YAML, the builder and the low-level API, and the conformance tests that check it.

docs.title: C1: Events and Processes
docs.text:
Waiting a fixed time, events a task can fire or fail, and processes: starting one, waiting for it, reading its return value or its failure, and inspecting an event or a process while it runs.

Timed wait: A task waits a set or sampled time, such as the time packing takes, before it goes on.

API details
  • SimPy: simpy.events.Timeout
  • YAML: a task with service and no resource
  • Builder: @app.task(service_id=...) with no resource
  • Low-level: yield env.timeout(delay)
  • Checks: test_c1_timed_wait
  • Taught on: Timed wait

Signal event success and value: One task fires a named signal with a value, and every task waiting for it wakes up and reads that value.

API details
  • SimPy: simpy.events.Event.succeed(value)
  • YAML: signals: [restocked], signal: restocked on the firing task and wait: {signal: restocked}
  • Builder: add_signal, @app.task(signal=...), wait={"signal": ...}, or context.signal(name).fire(value)
  • Low-level: Signal(env, name): yield signal.wait() and signal.fire(value)
  • Checks: test_c1_signal_event_success_and_value
  • Taught on: Signal event success and value

Signal event failure: A signal fires as a failure, and every task waiting for it fails with the same reason.

API details
  • SimPy: simpy.events.Event.fail(exception)
  • YAML: a failing task with signal; its waiters fail with its reason
  • Builder: the same, or context.signal(name).fail(reason)
  • Low-level: signal.fail(reason); waiters receive SignalFailed
  • Checks: test_c1_signal_event_failure
  • Taught on: Signal event failure

Start and wait for a process: A task starts a child flow, such as an inspection, and waits until it ends.

API details
  • SimPy: yield env.process(child())
  • YAML: wait: {task: inspect}
  • Builder: wait={"task": "inspect"}, or yield context.call("inspect")
  • Low-level: yield env.process(child())
  • Checks: test_c1_start_and_wait_for_a_process
  • Taught on: Start and wait for a process

Process return value: The task that waited for a child flow reads what the child produced.

API details
  • SimPy: a process's return value
  • YAML: wait.inspect.value.<field>, the last payload of the child flow
  • Builder: the same, or the value of context.call(...)
  • Low-level: value = yield env.process(child())
  • Checks: test_c1_process_return_value
  • Taught on: Process return value

Process failure: A failure inside a child flow reaches the task waiting for it, which can handle it or fail in turn.

API details
  • SimPy: an exception raised in a process reaches the process that waits for it
  • YAML: fail, fail_reason and on_fail on a task; a failure no on_fail handles fails the waiting task
  • Builder: the same, and a function that raises fails its task
  • Low-level: try: yield env.process(child()) and except
  • Checks: test_c1_process_failure, test_c1_process_failure_handled_by_on_fail
  • Difference: In YAML and the builder a failure no task waits for ends the entity's flow, publishes failed and is counted, and the run goes on; in SimPy, and in the low-level API, an exception nobody handles stops the run.
  • Taught on: Process failure

Event inspection: A condition reads whether a signal has fired, whether it succeeded, and its value.

API details
  • SimPy: Event.triggered, .processed, .ok, .value
  • YAML: signal.<name>.count, .ok and .value in a condition
  • Builder: context.signal(name).wait() and its SimPy attributes, or the signal's count, ok and value
  • Low-level: the same attributes of SimPy events and Signal
  • Checks: test_c1_event_inspection
  • Taught on: Event inspection

Process inspection: After a wait, a task reads whether a child flow has finished, whether it succeeded, and its value.

API details
  • SimPy: Process.is_alive, .triggered, .ok, .value
  • YAML: wait.<branch>.done, .ok and .value after the wait
  • Builder: the process context.spawn and context.call return
  • Low-level: the process env.process returns
  • Checks: test_c1_process_inspection
  • Taught on: Process inspection

Wait for a shared condition: A task waits until a condition on the model's state holds, such as stock reaching 5.

API details
  • SimPy: a loop over a fresh "changed" event
  • YAML: wait: {condition: level.stock >= 5}
  • Builder: wait={"condition": "level.stock >= 5"}
  • Low-level: env.watch_changes(check), or a SimPy loop
  • Checks: test_c1_wait_for_a_shared_condition
  • Taught on: Wait for a shared condition

docs.title: C2: Wait for One or All
docs.text:
Waiting for the first of several events, or for all of them, as SimPy's AnyOf and AllOf conditions do.

Wait for one event: A task waits for whichever of several events happens first, such as a delivery or a time limit.

API details
  • SimPy: simpy.events.AnyOf, a | b
  • YAML: wait: {any: {stock: {signal: restocked}, limit: {timeout: 3}}}
  • Builder: wait={"any": {...}}
  • Low-level: yield a | b
  • Checks: test_c2_wait_for_one_event, test_c2_wait_for_one_event_two_at_one_instant
  • Difference: Losing signal, timeout and condition branches are dropped when the wait ends; losing child flows keep running, as SimPy leaves processes running.
  • Taught on: Wait for one event

Wait for all events: A task waits until every one of several events has happened.

API details
  • SimPy: simpy.events.AllOf, a & b
  • YAML: wait: {all: {...}}
  • Builder: wait={"all": {...}}
  • Low-level: yield a & b
  • Checks: test_c2_wait_for_all_events, test_c2_wait_for_all_events_with_a_failing_branch
  • Taught on: Wait for all events

docs.title: C3: Interrupts and Preemption
docs.text:
Interrupting a task while it waits or while it is in service, and a higher-priority request taking a resource unit from a lower-priority user.

Interrupt while waiting: Another task or a scenario step interrupts a task while it is still in a queue.

API details
  • SimPy: simpy.Process.interrupt while the process waits for a request
  • YAML: interrupt: {task: waiter} on a scenario step or a task; on_interrupt on the task
  • Builder: context.interrupt("waiter"); @app.task(on_interrupt=...)
  • Low-level: process.interrupt(cause), caught as simpy.Interrupt
  • Checks: test_c3_interrupt_while_waiting
  • Taught on: Interrupt while waiting

Interrupt during service: A task is interrupted while it holds a resource, and resumes, restarts or abandons its work.

API details
  • SimPy: simpy.Process.interrupt while the process holds a unit
  • YAML: on_interrupt: resume, restart or abandon
  • Builder: @app.task(on_interrupt=...)
  • Low-level: except simpy.Interrupt, then request again
  • Checks: test_c3_interrupt_during_service, test_c3_two_interrupts_at_one_instant
  • Taught on: Interrupt during service

Priority preemption: A more urgent request takes a resource unit away from a less urgent user, who is interrupted.

API details
  • SimPy: simpy.resources.resource.PreemptiveResource
  • YAML: resources.<name>.preempt: true with queue: priority; preempt: false on a task opts out
  • Builder: add_resource(..., queue="priority", preempt=True)
  • Low-level: DynamicResource(..., queue="priority", preempt=True) and request(priority, preempt=True)
  • Checks: test_c3_priority_preemption, test_c3_priority_preemption_equal_priorities, test_c3_two_preemptions_at_one_instant, test_c3_preemption_tie_between_users, test_c3_priority_preemption_low_level
  • Taught on: Priority preemption

docs.title: C4: Resources
docs.text:
Requesting and releasing resource units, in order of arrival or of priority, cancelling a request before or after its grant, and holding several resources at once.

Ordinary request and release: A task takes one unit of a resource, such as a packer, waits in line if none is free, and gives it back when done.

API details
  • SimPy: simpy.resources.resource.Resource
  • YAML: resource: packers on a task
  • Builder: @app.task(resource_id="packers")
  • Low-level: with packers.request() as req: yield req
  • Checks: test_c4_ordinary_request_and_release
  • Taught on: Ordinary request and release

Priority request: Waiting requests are served by priority, the lowest number first, instead of in order of arrival.

API details
  • SimPy: simpy.resources.resource.PriorityResource
  • YAML: queue: priority on the resource and priority on a task
  • Builder: add_resource(..., queue="priority") and @app.task(priority=...)
  • Low-level: DynamicResource(..., queue="priority") and request(priority=...)
  • Checks: test_c4_priority_resource_request, test_c4_priority_request_with_mixed_preempt_flags
  • Difference: Equal priorities are served first in, first out, as in SimPy; desflow also offers fifo and lifo queues, under which a request's priority is ignored.
  • Taught on: Priority request

Cancel before a grant: A task leaves the queue before it is served, so it never takes a unit.

API details
  • SimPy: Request.cancel() before it is granted
  • YAML: patience, or an interrupt with on_interrupt: abandon
  • Builder: the same
  • Low-level: request.cancel(), or leaving the with block
  • Checks: test_c4_cancel_before_a_grant, test_c4_renege_ahead_of_a_preempting_request
  • Taught on: Cancel before a grant

Cancel after a grant: A task that already holds a unit stops early and gives the unit back.

API details
  • SimPy: Request.cancel() after the grant releases nothing; Resource.release(request) does
  • YAML: an interrupt with on_interrupt: abandon gives the unit back
  • Builder: the same
  • Low-level: request.cancel() releases nothing; resource.release(request)
  • Checks: test_c4_cancel_after_a_grant
  • Taught on: Cancel after a grant

Hold several resources: A task holds more than one resource at once, taken in a fixed order, and can hand them to the next task.

API details
  • SimPy: nested requests, each held while the next is awaited
  • YAML: resource: [picker, bench], acquired in that order; keep hands units to the next task
  • Builder: @app.task(resource_id=["picker", "bench"], keep=[...])
  • Low-level: nested with blocks
  • Checks: test_c4_hold_several_resources, test_c4_keep_hands_a_unit_to_the_next_task
  • Difference: A model whose tasks acquire two resources in opposite orders is refused when it is built, because those tasks could each wait for ever; SimPy runs it.
  • Taught on: Hold several resources

docs.title: C5: Stores and Containers
docs.text:
Putting and getting items in a store and amounts in a container, with capacity limits, priority items, filtered gets, cancelled puts and gets, and the order of puts and gets at the same time.

Bounded store put: A task adds an item to a store, and waits when the store is full.

API details
  • SimPy: simpy.resources.store.Store.put
  • YAML: put: {store: parcels} on a task
  • Builder: @app.task(put={"store": "parcels"})
  • Low-level: yield parcels.put(item)
  • Checks: test_c5_bounded_store_put
  • Taught on: Bounded store put

Bounded store get: A task takes an item from a store, and waits when the store is empty.

API details
  • SimPy: simpy.resources.store.Store.get
  • YAML: get: {store: parcels} on a task
  • Builder: @app.task(get={"store": "parcels"})
  • Low-level: item = yield parcels.get()
  • Checks: test_c5_bounded_store_get
  • Taught on: Bounded store get

Equal-time puts and gets: When items are added and taken at the same moment, waiting tasks are served in the same order as in SimPy.

API details
  • SimPy: simpy.resources.store.Store, one waiting get granted per trigger
  • YAML: get: {store: parcels} and put: {store: parcels} on tasks
  • Builder: @app.task(get={"store": "parcels"})
  • Low-level: yield parcels.put(item), item = yield parcels.get()
  • Checks: test_c5_equal_time_puts_and_gets_follow_simpy_store, test_c5_equal_time_puts_and_gets_as_tasks
  • Difference: While a get with a filter waits, the store grants as SimPy's FilterStore does, looking at every waiting get each time.
  • Taught on: Equal-time puts and gets

Bounded quantity put: A task adds an amount to a container, such as boxes to stock, and waits when there is no room.

API details
  • SimPy: simpy.resources.container.Container.put
  • YAML: put: {container: stock, amount: 2} on a task
  • Builder: @app.task(put={"container": "stock", "amount": 2})
  • Low-level: yield stock.put(2)
  • Checks: test_c5_bounded_quantity_put
  • Taught on: Bounded quantity put

Bounded quantity get: A task takes an amount from a container, and waits until there is enough.

API details
  • SimPy: simpy.resources.container.Container.get
  • YAML: get: {container: stock, amount: 1} on a task
  • Builder: @app.task(get={"container": "stock", "amount": 1})
  • Low-level: yield stock.get(1)
  • Checks: test_c5_bounded_quantity_get
  • Taught on: Bounded quantity get

Priority item storage: Items in a store come out by priority, the lowest number first, instead of in the order they went in.

API details
  • SimPy: simpy.resources.store.PriorityStore
  • YAML: stores.<name>.priority: true and a put with priority
  • Builder: add_store(..., priority=True) and put={"store": ..., "priority": ...}
  • Low-level: DynamicStore(..., priority=True) with simpy.PriorityItem
  • Checks: test_c5_priority_item_storage
  • Difference: Equal priorities come out in put order in the builder and YAML, which add a rising put order to the priority; a plain SimPy PriorityStore gives no order among equal priorities.
  • Taught on: Priority item storage

Filtered retrieval: A task takes only an item that matches a condition, such as a parcel for its own area.

API details
  • SimPy: simpy.resources.store.FilterStore.get(filter)
  • YAML: get: {store: parcels, filter: item.area == attr.area}
  • Builder: get={"store": "parcels", "filter": ...}, a condition or a function of the item
  • Low-level: parcels.get(filter=lambda item: ...)
  • Checks: test_c5_filtered_retrieval
  • Difference: A priority store takes no filter, because SimPy has no store that both ranks and filters.
  • Taught on: Filtered retrieval

Cancel store get: A task stops waiting for an item, for example when its patience runs out.

API details
  • SimPy: simpy.resources.base.Get.cancel()
  • YAML: patience on a task with a store get
  • Builder: @app.task(get={"store": ...}, patience=...)
  • Low-level: get.cancel()
  • Checks: test_c5_cancel_store_get
  • Taught on: Cancel store get

Cancel quantity get: A task stops waiting for an amount from a container.

API details
  • SimPy: simpy.resources.base.Get.cancel()
  • YAML: patience on a task with a container get
  • Builder: @app.task(get={"container": ...}, patience=...)
  • Low-level: get.cancel()
  • Checks: test_c5_cancel_quantity_get
  • Taught on: Cancel quantity get

Cancel store put: A task stops waiting for room in a full store.

API details
  • SimPy: simpy.resources.base.Put.cancel()
  • YAML: an interrupt with on_interrupt: abandon while the put waits
  • Builder: the same
  • Low-level: put.cancel()
  • Checks: test_c5_cancel_store_put
  • Taught on: Cancel store put

Cancel quantity put: A task stops waiting for room in a full container.

API details
  • SimPy: simpy.resources.base.Put.cancel()
  • YAML: an interrupt with on_interrupt: abandon while the put waits
  • Builder: the same
  • Low-level: put.cancel()
  • Checks: test_c5_cancel_quantity_put
  • Taught on: Cancel quantity put

docs.title: C6: Run Control
docs.text:
Starting a run from a given time and state, ending it at a time, at an event or on a condition, draining it, and stepping through it one event at a time.

Initial time: The simulation clock starts at a given time instead of 0.

API details
  • SimPy: simpy.core.Environment(initial_time=...)
  • YAML: simulation.initial_time
  • Builder: SimulationContext(..., initial_time=100)
  • Low-level: DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(initial_time=100)
  • Checks: test_c6_initial_time
  • Taught on: Initial time

Initial resources: Each resource starts with a given number of units.

API details
  • SimPy: simpy.resources.resource.Resource(capacity=...)
  • YAML: resources.<name>.current_cap
  • Builder: add_resource(name, current_cap=2, ...)
  • Low-level: CapacityConfig(current_cap=2, ...)
  • Checks: test_c6_initial_resources
  • Taught on: Initial resources

Initial inventory: Containers start with a given level, and stores with given items.

API details
  • SimPy: Container(init=...); items in a Store
  • YAML: containers.<name>.level and stores.<name>.items
  • Builder: add_container(..., level=6) and add_store(..., items=[...])
  • Low-level: ContainerConfig(level=6) and DynamicStore(..., items=[...])
  • Checks: test_c6_initial_inventory
  • Taught on: Initial inventory

Initial entity state: Each arriving entity, such as an order, starts with given attributes.

API details
  • SimPy: the attributes a process starts with
  • YAML: arrivals.<name>.attributes
  • Builder: add_arrival(..., attributes={...})
  • Low-level: the values a process is started with
  • Checks: test_c6_initial_entity_state
  • Taught on: Initial entity state

Stop at a time: The run ends at a given simulation time.

API details
  • SimPy: simpy.core.Environment.run(until=...)
  • YAML: run.until
  • Builder: app.run(until=...)
  • Low-level: env.run(until=...)
  • Checks: test_c6_stop_at_a_time
  • Taught on: Stop at a time

Stop at an event: The run ends when a given event happens, such as a closing signal, even before its end time.

API details
  • SimPy: simpy.core.Environment.run(until=event)
  • YAML: run.stop: {signal: closing} beside run.until
  • Builder: app.run(until=..., stop={"signal": "closing"}), a signal's name, or a function returning an event
  • Low-level: env.run(until=event)
  • Checks: test_c6_stop_at_an_event, test_c6_stop_at_an_event_at_the_same_instant_as_until
  • Difference: When the stop and until fall at the same time, until ends the run first, as SimPy's own until would.
  • Taught on: Stop at an event

Explicit stop condition: The run ends as soon as a condition on the model's state holds.

API details
  • SimPy: env.run(until=event) with a process that succeeds the event when the condition holds
  • YAML: run.stop: {condition: level.stock >= 5}
  • Builder: app.run(until=..., stop={"condition": "..."})
  • Low-level: env.watch_changes(check) and env.run(until=event)
  • Checks: test_c6_explicit_stop_condition
  • Taught on: Explicit stop condition

Stop arrivals and drain: New arrivals stop, and the run goes on until everything already in the model has finished.

API details
  • SimPy: interrupt the source, then env.run(until=env.all_of(entities))
  • YAML: run.drain: true or {limit: 1 h}; desflow run --drain
  • Builder: app.run(until=..., drain=True), or context.stop_arrivals()
  • Low-level: source.interrupt(), then env.run(until=env.all_of(processes))
  • Checks: test_c6_stop_arrivals_and_drain, test_c6_stop_arrivals_and_drain_with_a_limit
  • Taught on: Stop arrivals and drain

Step one event: The run advances one event at a time, so a script can watch each step.

API details
  • SimPy: simpy.core.Environment.step()
  • YAML: SimulationContext.from_yaml(path).start(), then .step()
  • Builder: app.start(), app.step(), app.close()
  • Low-level: env.step()
  • Checks: test_c6_step_one_event
  • Difference: A blueprint has no stepping key; its context, from from_yaml, steps as a builder context does.
  • Taught on: Step one event

Inspect next event time: A script reads when the next event will happen without running it.

API details
  • SimPy: simpy.core.Environment.peek()
  • YAML: SimulationContext.from_yaml(path).start(), then .peek()
  • Builder: app.peek()
  • Low-level: env.peek()
  • Checks: test_c6_inspect_next_event_time
  • Taught on: Inspect next event time

docs.title: C7: Patience
docs.text:
Customers who give up after waiting too long (reneging) and customers who do not join a queue that is too long (balking).

Reneging: A customer leaves the queue after waiting longer than their patience.

API details
  • SimPy: simpy.events.AnyOf of a request and a timeout
  • YAML: patience: 3 min on a task
  • Builder: @app.task(..., patience=180)
  • Low-level: yield req | env.timeout(patience), then req.triggered
  • Checks: test_c7_reneging, test_c7_reneging_tie_timeout_scheduled_after_the_grant, test_c7_reneging_tie_timeout_scheduled_before_the_grant, test_c7_reneged_request_leaves_the_queue, test_c7_patience_pauses_during_service
  • Taught on: Reneging

Balking: A customer does not join the queue at all when a condition holds, such as the queue being too long.

API details
  • SimPy: a check before Resource.request
  • YAML: balk: <condition> on a task
  • Builder: @app.task(..., balk="...")
  • Low-level: an if before the request
  • Checks: test_c7_balking
  • Taught on: Balking

docs.title: S1: Breakdowns
docs.text:
A resource that fails and is repaired, with the work it interrupts.

Breakdown and repair: A resource fails from time to time and is repaired, interrupting the work it was doing.

API details
  • SimPy: a repair process holding the machine on a PreemptiveResource
  • YAML: resources.<name>.breakdown: {time_to_failure, repair, work}
  • Builder: add_breakdown(resource, time_to_failure={...}, repair={...}, work=...)
  • Low-level: run_breakdowns(env, resource, sampler, work=...)
  • Checks: test_s1_failure_during_service, test_s1_failure_during_service_work_finishes, test_s1_planned_change_during_repair
  • Difference: The resource is down on a calendar clock, from the failure to the repair, even while it waits for the work in service to finish with work: finish.
  • Taught on: Breakdown and repair

docs.title: S2: Schedules
docs.text:
A schedule of times at which an arrival rate or a capacity changes during a run.

Finite schedules: Arrival rates or capacities change at set times during the run.

API details
  • SimPy: a process that changes values at set times, started before the others
  • YAML: scenario steps with at, path and value
  • Builder: add_scenario(steps) or add_step(at, path=..., value=...)
  • Low-level: run_scenario(env, steps, until=...)
  • Checks: test_s2_step_at_an_arrival_time
  • Difference: A step applies before every other event at its time, so the arrival gap drawn then uses the new value.
  • Taught on: Finite schedules

docs.title: S3: Replay
docs.text:
Arrivals read from a local CSV or Parquet file instead of drawn at random.

Local replay: Arrivals come from rows in a local CSV or Parquet file instead of a random distribution.

API details
  • SimPy: a loop over recorded rows, each a timeout to its time
  • YAML: arrivals.<name>.replay: {path, time, unit, fields, on_invalid}
  • Builder: add_arrival_replay(name, source, ...)
  • Low-level: read_trace(source, ...) and a SimPy loop over its rows
  • Checks: test_s3_replay_equal_times_invalid_rows_and_the_horizon
  • Taught on: Local replay

docs.title: Differences Kept by Design
docs.text:
• A run with no until (SimPy: core.Environment.run() returns when no event is left): A run with a sink or an ingress connector and no until runs for ever, because a live run has no end: the connectors keep events coming. Give it an until, with a drain when it should finish its work, or a stop that is sure to happen, or stop it with Ctrl+C.
  • Capacity 0 (SimPy: resources.resource.Resource(capacity=0) raises ValueError, and so do Store and Container): A resource, store or container may have a capacity of 0, at the start or later, because its capacity changes during a run: a shift with no packers, a shelf that is closed. At capacity 0 a resource grants no request, and a store or container accepts no put, until the capacity rises; a get still takes what a store or container holds.

docs.title: Statistic Names
docs.text: Every name the built-in statistics publish, at each level, generated by running the statistics in the code. Statistics explains the levels and how each value is computed. Each level publishes the names of the levels before it, and the new ones listed under it. <sim_id> is the simulation's id, <name> a resource, store or container, <task> a task, and <arrival> the arrival that started a flow's entities.

docs.title: none
docs.text: Publishes nothing: the statistics are off.

docs.title: minimal
docs.text: Name Measures <sim_id>.stats.resources.<name>.capacity units now <sim_id>.stats.resources.<name>.in_use units held by tasks; above capacity after a drop, until they finish <sim_id>.stats.resources.<name>.queue_length requests waiting now <sim_id>.stats.resources.<name>.utilization in_use as a percentage of capacity, now <sim_id>.stats.resources.<name>.down 1 while a resource with a breakdown is down, 0 otherwise <sim_id>.stats.stores.<name>.capacity items it can hold now <sim_id>.stats.stores.<name>.level items held now <sim_id>.stats.stores.<name>.getters_waiting tasks waiting to get an item <sim_id>.stats.stores.<name>.putters_waiting tasks waiting to put an item <sim_id>.stats.containers.<name>.capacity largest amount, now <sim_id>.stats.containers.<name>.level amount held now <sim_id>.stats.containers.<name>.getters_waiting tasks waiting to take an amount <sim_id>.stats.containers.<name>.putters_waiting tasks waiting to add an amount <sim_id>.stats.tasks.<task>.in_progress instances queued or started and not yet ended, now

docs.title: basic
docs.text: Name Measures <sim_id>.stats.resources.<name>.utilization_avg utilisation averaged over time, in percent <sim_id>.stats.resources.<name>.queue_length_avg requests waiting, averaged over time <sim_id>.stats.resources.<name>.downtime seconds a resource with a breakdown has been down so far <sim_id>.stats.resources.<name>.failures failures of a resource with a breakdown so far <sim_id>.stats.stores.<name>.level_avg items held, averaged over time <sim_id>.stats.containers.<name>.level_avg amount held, averaged over time <sim_id>.stats.tasks.<task>.finished instances finished so far <sim_id>.stats.tasks.<task>.balked instances that refused to join the queue; published once one does <sim_id>.stats.tasks.<task>.reneged instances that left the queue before they were served; published once one does <sim_id>.stats.tasks.<task>.failed instances that failed: their fail held, their function raised or their wait failed; published once one does <sim_id>.stats.tasks.<task>.interrupted interrupts delivered to instances, preemptions not included; published once one is <sim_id>.stats.tasks.<task>.preempted times a higher-priority request took an instance's unit; published once one does <sim_id>.stats.tasks.<task>.resumed times an interrupted instance got its units back and was served again; published once one does <sim_id>.stats.flows.<arrival>.finished entities that left the model, by the arrival that started them <sim_id>.stats.flows.<arrival>.started entities whose first task has started, by the arrival that started them <sim_id>.stats.flows.<arrival>.in_system entities in the model now: started, and not yet finished, failed or gone <sim_id>.stats.flows.<arrival>.failed entities whose flow ended in a failure no on_fail handled; published once one does

docs.title: YAML Format
docs.text:
Every key a blueprint accepts, section by section. YAML Blueprints describes how a file is read and where an error points, and each User Guide page shows its keys in use.

Every section is optional except simulation. Unknown keys are refused, so a misspelt key is reported with its line rather than ignored. A time is seconds or a duration such as 10 min, and an instant is now, a signed duration such as -1d, or an ISO datetime. ${VAR} and ${VAR:-default} read environment variables anywhere in the file.

Each section becomes one builder call:

A blueprint with logic in Python beside it, which the sections below refer to:

docs/snippets/yaml/hybrid.yaml
# The shop with its logic in Python. YAML keeps the blueprint and the
# experiment; shop_logic.py beside this file holds what YAML cannot express.
simulation:
  sim_id: Shop
  factor: 0
  random_seed: 1

egress:
  - type: Console
    # Only events reach the terminal; telemetry is dropped.
    when: !python shop_logic.events_only

resources:
  packers: {current_cap: 1, max_cap: 3}

services:
  packing: {dist: normal, mean: 4.0, std: 1.0}

arrivals:
  orders: {dist: exponential, rate: 0.2, spawn: pack_order}

tasks:
  pack_order:
    service: packing
    resource: packers
    # Called as choose_delivery(task_id, context) for every packed order.
    payload: !python shop_logic.choose_delivery

processes:
  # Called as breaks(context, resource="packers", every=50, duration=5).
  - function: !python shop_logic.breaks
    kwargs: {resource: packers, every: 50, duration: 5}

scenario:
  - {at: 1 min, path: Shop.arrival.orders.rate, value: 0.4}

run:
  until: 3 min

docs.title: simulation
docs.text:
The arguments of SimulationContext. Time and Pacing describes the clock.

Key Value sim_id required; the first part of every registry path and statistic name factor 1.0 follows the wall clock, 0 does not wait; 1.0 by default random_seed a whole number; without one, the run draws a seed and logs it logical_start_time the instant simulation time 0 maps to; the load time by default go_live_at the instant from which the run is paced in real time warmup a time, 0 or more, before which no sink receives a record and at which the statistics restart initial_time the simulation clock's reading when the run starts, in seconds or a duration; 0 by default timezone an IANA name, such as Australia/Melbourne, that timestamps are written in, with their offset; a logical_start_time or go_live_at without an offset, and now, are read in it; the zone of logical_start_time, or UTC, by default lag_interval simulation seconds or a duration between system.simulation.lag_seconds readings; 0 turns them off; by default off at factor: 0 and every second otherwise

docs.title: resources, stores and containers
docs.text:
name: {...} entries. Resources and Stores and Containers describe them.

Section Keys resources current_cap and max_cap, whole numbers; queue: fifo (the default), lifo or priority; preempt: true lets a lower priority value take a busy unit, with queue: priority; breakdown: {time_to_failure, repair, work}, two distributions and interrupt (the default) or finish, makes it fail and be repaired stores current_cap and max_cap, whole numbers of items; priority: true to return the lowest priority first; items, the items held at the start, [priority, item] pairs for a priority store containers current_cap and max_cap, the largest amount; level, the amount at the start, 0 by default

A store and a container cannot share a name.

docs.title: signals
docs.text: A list of names, each a signal that tasks fire with signal and wait for with wait: {signal: name}. Tasks and Processes describes them.

docs.title: variables
docs.text: name: value entries, any YAML value, each at the registry path <sim_id>.variables.<name>. Live Parameters describes them.

docs.title: services and arrivals
docs.text:
name: {dist, ...} entries: a distribution family and the parameters it takes. Time-valued parameters take durations, and rate is per second. Arrivals and Services shows each family, and Reference, Distributions lists their parameters and rules.

An arrival also takes:

Key Value spawn the task each arrival starts attributes a mapping each new entity starts with, read as attr.<name> replay in place of a distribution: {path, time, unit, fields, on_invalid}, a CSV or Parquet file relative to the blueprint whose rows arrive at their times; unit is ms, s (the default), min, h or timestamp, fields a list of columns or all (the default), on_invalid error (the default) or skip. Arrivals and Services describes it

docs.title: tasks
docs.text:
name: {...} entries, each built with @app.task. Tasks and Processes and Task Flow describe them.

Key Value service the service whose time the task takes; needed with a resource resource the resource the task holds while it works, or a list of them, acquired in the order listed keep resources in resource handed to the next task, which releases them once it starts payload required: the finished event's value, a mapping, or a !python function called as function(task_id, context) id_field adds the task id to a mapping payload under this key item_field adds the item the task's store get took to a mapping payload under this key attributes a list of entity attributes added to a mapping payload priority a number or an expression such as attr.tier, for a resource with queue: priority patience seconds, a duration or an expression: how long the task may wait for its wait, its resource and its get, all together, before it leaves and publishes reneged; it pauses while the task is served balk a condition checked before the task joins a queue; when it holds, the task publishes balked wait what the task waits for before its resource: {signal: name}, {task: name}, {timeout: ...}, {condition: ...}, or {any: {name: branch, ...}} or {all: {...}}; read after it as wait.<branch>.done, .ok and .value signal a signal under signals the task fires with its payload when it finishes, and fails when it fails fail a condition checked after the service, reading the task's own payload; when it holds the task publishes failed fail_reason the reason a failure publishes; the fail condition's text by default on_fail the task a failed instance goes to; without it the flow ends on_interrupt resume (the default), restart or abandon: what an interrupt or a preemption does on_interrupt_next the task an abandoned instance goes to preempt false keeps the task's requests from preempting; true by default interrupt {task, where, cause}: when the task finishes, interrupts every running instance of task whose where holds get {container: name, amount: ...} or {store: name}, with an optional filter condition for a store, which reads the item offered as item.<field>: taken after the resource, before the work put the same form, without a filter: added after the work; a store receives the payload, with an optional priority for a priority store next a task name; {when: [{condition, task}, ...], default: task}; or {weights: {task: number, ...}} set a mapping applied to the entity's attributes when the task finishes

An amount is a number or an expression, 1 when left out. A task with a service and no resource is a timed step; one with neither, and no get, takes no time.

docs.title: processes
docs.text: A list of !python generator functions, each written as {function: ..., kwargs: {...}} or as the bare reference, started as function(context, **kwargs); Python in a Blueprint shows them.

docs.title: telemetry
docs.text:
A list of custom readings, each {interval, function}: every interval simulation seconds, greater than 0, function(context) is called and publishes with context.publish. The built-in readings of resources, stores and containers come from stats instead.

docs/snippets/yaml/telemetry.yaml:telemetry
telemetry:
  # Every 5 simulation seconds, calls packers_report(context), which publishes
  # Shop.waiting_per_packer and Shop.arrival_rate with context.publish
  - interval: 5
    function: !python shop_logic.packers_report

docs.title: stats
docs.text: The built-in statistics, as a level, stats: basic, or as a mapping, stats: {level: all, interval: 1 min}. The level is none, minimal, basic, typical or all, and the interval, 10 seconds by default, is a time greater than 0. Statistics describes them.

docs.title: scenario
docs.text:
A list of steps, applied in time order on the simulation clock:

Key Value at the time of the step path a registry path, checked when the file loads; needs a value value the new value, which must convert to the type the path holds record a mapping, published as a ground-truth label to the when: labels sinks interrupt {task, where, cause}: interrupts every running instance of task whose where holds

A step needs a path and value, a record, an interrupt, or more than one. A step applies before every other event at its time; steps at the same time apply in the order written; a step at or after until never applies. Live Parameters shows scenarios and labels, and Time-varying Arrivals the boundaries.

docs.title: ingress and egress
docs.text:
Lists of connectors, each with a type and a config of the constructor's keyword arguments. type is one of the short names below, or a !python class from another package. A connector's module is imported only when a blueprint names it, so a blueprint that uses Kafka does not need the PostgreSQL driver; a missing package stops the load with its line and the pip install command, except Parquet and JSON Lines, which import PyArrow when they start writing.

Direction type Class Extra ingress Local LocalIngress none ingress Kafka KafkaIngress kafka ingress Postgres PostgresIngress postgres ingress Redis RedisIngress redis egress Console ConsoleEgress none egress Kafka KafkaEgress kafka egress Parquet ParquetStorageEgress parquet egress Jsonl JsonlStorageEgress parquet egress Iceberg IcebergStorageEgress iceberg egress Postgres PostgresEgress postgres egress Redis RedisEgress redis

An egress entry also takes when: history or live, both needing simulation.go_live_at, labels, or a !python function of one record; and batch_size and flush_interval, both greater than 0. Ingress and Egress describe them.

Settings that the Python API takes as objects are plain values:

type Setting Plain value Kafka topics Without a topic_router, event_topic and telemetry_topic are created when the run starts, with one partition each, if they do not exist. Parquet, Jsonl filesystem A mapping. type is local (the default) or s3, and the other keys are passed to PyArrow's S3FileSystem, such as endpoint_override, access_key, secret_key and region. An endpoint_override starting with http:// sets the scheme. A key whose value is empty is left out. Parquet, Jsonl default_path Without a path_router, each event is written there as one flat row, with its value mapping unpacked into columns, and telemetry is left out. It is a file name prefix, not a folder: each batch is a file of its own, named as Egress explains. Iceberg catalog A mapping of PyIceberg catalog properties, such as type, uri, warehouse and s3.endpoint, passed to load_catalog on the first write. An optional name key names the catalog. Iceberg default_table, schemas Without a table_router, each event is written to default_table as one flat row. schemas maps a table to its columns, each with a type: string, int, long, float, double, boolean, timestamp, timestamptz, date or binary. Postgres tables Tables created when the run starts, if they do not exist. Each maps to columns, a mapping of column name to SQL type, and an optional primary_key. table_name defaults to the table when tables names one.

An ISO time string bound for a timestamp or date column of Iceberg or PostgreSQL is converted before the write.

docs.title: batching
docs.text: The arguments of with_batching, the defaults for every sink: batch_size and flush_interval, and optionally max_queued_batches and drain_stall_seconds, all greater than 0. Egress describes them.

docs.title: run
docs.text: Key Value until a time greater than initial_time; desflow run --until overrides it stop ends the run before until when it happens: {signal: name}, the next firing of a signal, or {condition: ...}, the first moment a condition holds drain true stops the arrivals at until and runs on until no entity is left; {limit: 1 h} stops at the latest that long after until; desflow run --drain sets it before a list of !python functions called with no arguments before the run, for setup such as creating topics

docs.title: Include a File
docs.text: !include path puts a mapping from another YAML file in place, with the path relative to the file that names it, such as the settings desflow fit writes: packing: !include fitted/packing.yaml. !include {file: path, spawn: pack} adds keys to the file's mapping, such as the task an arrival spawns. The file is read with the same loader, so ${VAR}, !python and !include work in it, and a file that includes itself, directly or through another, is refused. Input Fitting shows it.

docs.title: Security
docs.text: A blueprint with no !python references is read entirely by yaml.SafeLoader, and loading it imports only the connector modules its type entries name; an !include reads another YAML file the same way and imports nothing itself. A file that references Python, directly or in a file it includes, runs the imports it names, so it is as trusted as a Python script: run blueprints from people you would take a script from. Python in a Blueprint explains.

docs.title: Changing Demand
docs.text:
Level: Intermediate

The shop's one packer packs an order in 1.5 seconds, and orders usually arrive at 0.4 a second. From 20 to 40 minutes a promotion brings 0.9 a second, more than one packer can pack. This page asks: what does a 20-minute rush do to waits, and does a second packer for the rush keep them short? It runs the hour with one packer through the rush and with two.

docs.title: What You Add
docs.text: A schedule: changes to the arrival rate and the number of packers at set times. The shop is the one from First Simulation, with packing at a constant 1.5 seconds.

docs.title: Write the Schedule
docs.text:
A schedule is a list of steps, each a registry path, a value and the simulation time it applies at. The rush is four steps: the rate and the packers change at 20 minutes and change back at 40:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/changing_demand.yaml:schedule
# The rush: 0.9 orders a second from 20 to 40 minutes, and RUSH_PACKERS for it
scenario:
  - {at: 20 min, path: Shop.arrival.orders.rate, value: 0.9}
  - {at: 20 min, path: Shop.resources.packers.current_cap, value: "${RUSH_PACKERS:-1}"}
  - {at: 40 min, path: Shop.arrival.orders.rate, value: 0.4}
  - {at: 40 min, path: Shop.resources.packers.current_cap, value: 1}

${RUSH_PACKERS:-1} reads the environment variable RUSH_PACKERS, so RUSH_PACKERS=2 desflow run changing_demand.yaml runs the second plan.

docs/snippets/tutorials/changing_demand.py:schedule
# The rush: 0.9 orders a second from 20 to 40 minutes, and rush_packers for it
.add_scenario(
    [
        {"at": "20 min", "path": "Shop.arrival.orders.rate", "value": 0.9},
        {
            "at": "20 min",
            "path": "Shop.resources.packers.current_cap",
            "value": rush_packers,
        },
        {"at": "40 min", "path": "Shop.arrival.orders.rate", "value": 0.4},
        {
            "at": "40 min",
            "path": "Shop.resources.packers.current_cap",
            "value": 1,
        },
    ]
)
docs/snippets/tutorials/changing_demand_low_level.py:schedule
def schedule(rush_packers):
    """The rush: 0.9 orders a second from 20 to 40 minutes, and rush_packers for it."""
    return [
        {"at": 1200, "path": "Shop.arrival.orders.rate", "value": 0.9},
        {
            "at": 1200,
            "path": "Shop.resources.packers.current_cap",
            "value": rush_packers,
        },
        {"at": 2400, "path": "Shop.arrival.orders.rate", "value": 0.4},
        {"at": 2400, "path": "Shop.resources.packers.current_cap", "value": 1},
    ]

run_scenario is the SimPy process that applies the steps:

docs/snippets/tutorials/changing_demand_low_level.py:run
# Each step applies before every other event at its time
env.process(run_scenario(env, schedule(rush_packers), until=3600))

The steps follow the simulation clock, so the schedule repeats exactly on every run and at any factor. A step at a time applies before every other event at that time: the order that arrives at 20 minutes draws its next gap from the rush rate. Time-varying Arrivals sets out these boundaries.

docs.title: Result
docs.text:
What does a 20-minute rush do to waits? With one packer, it builds a queue for the whole rush: the mean wait over the hour is 147.74 seconds and the longest 416.75 seconds, more than 6 minutes. A second packer for the rush keeps the mean at 0.74 seconds and the longest at 6.06. Both pack the same 1,978 orders:

The Builder and Low-level scripts print both plans:

1 in the rush: 1978 packed, mean wait 147.74 s, longest 416.75 s
2 in the rush: 1978 packed, mean wait  0.74 s, longest   6.06 s

docs.title: Why It Works
docs.text: During the rush one packer would need 0.9 × 1.5 = 1.35 seconds of packing every second, more than it has: 0.9 orders arrive a second and the packer finishes about 0.67, so the queue grows by about 0.23 orders a second for as long as the rush lasts. That is a finite overload: when the rush ends the load falls to 0.6, and the packer works the queue off, here by about 54 minutes. A load that stays at 1 or above is different: its queue grows for as long as the run lasts, and no run length gives a stable mean wait, as on Queues and Capacity. A finite overload has an answer, but it depends on the schedule: a mean over the hour mixes the quiet minutes with the rush, so report the longest wait, or the waits during the rush, beside it. With two packers the rush load is 0.68 a packer, and waits stay short.

docs.title: Full Files
docs.text:
Full files YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/changing_demand.yaml
# The Changing Demand tutorial: a 20-minute rush, with one packer or two.
# Run it with: desflow run changing_demand.yaml
# With a second packer for the rush: RUSH_PACKERS=2 desflow run changing_demand.yaml
simulation:
  sim_id: Shop
  factor: 0
  random_seed: 42

resources:
  packers: {current_cap: 1, max_cap: 2}

services:
  packing: {dist: constant, value: 1.5 s}

arrivals:
  orders: {dist: exponential, rate: 0.4, spawn: pack_order}

tasks:
  pack_order:
    service: packing
    resource: packers
    payload: {event_type: order_packed}

# The rush: 0.9 orders a second from 20 to 40 minutes, and RUSH_PACKERS for it
scenario:
  - {at: 20 min, path: Shop.arrival.orders.rate, value: 0.9}
  - {at: 20 min, path: Shop.resources.packers.current_cap, value: "${RUSH_PACKERS:-1}"}
  - {at: 40 min, path: Shop.arrival.orders.rate, value: 0.4}
  - {at: 40 min, path: Shop.resources.packers.current_cap, value: 1}

# Orders packed, and the mean and longest wait, at the end
stats: {level: typical, interval: 2 h}

egress:
  - type: Console

run:
  until: 1 h
docs/snippets/tutorials/changing_demand.py
"""The Changing Demand tutorial: a 20-minute rush, with one packer or two.

One packer and 1.5 seconds of packing; orders arrive at 0.4 a second, and at 0.9
from 20 to 40 minutes. Every record is printed to the terminal, and the script
prints the waits with one packer through the rush and with a second packer for it:
python changing_demand.py 2>/dev/null shows only those lines.
"""

import logging

from desflow import ConsoleEgress, SimulationContext

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
)


def shop(rush_packers: int) -> SimulationContext:
    """The shop of First Simulation, with a rush from 20 to 40 minutes."""
    app = (
        SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0, random_seed=42)
        .add_resource("packers", current_cap=1, max_cap=2)
        .add_service("packing", dist="constant", value=1.5)
        .add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=0.4)
        # The rush: 0.9 orders a second from 20 to 40 minutes, and rush_packers for it
        .add_scenario(
            [
                {"at": "20 min", "path": "Shop.arrival.orders.rate", "value": 0.9},
                {
                    "at": "20 min",
                    "path": "Shop.resources.packers.current_cap",
                    "value": rush_packers,
                },
                {"at": "40 min", "path": "Shop.arrival.orders.rate", "value": 0.4},
                {
                    "at": "40 min",
                    "path": "Shop.resources.packers.current_cap",
                    "value": 1,
                },
            ]
        )
        # Orders packed, and the mean and longest wait, at the end
        .with_stats("typical", interval=7200)
        .add_egress(ConsoleEgress())
    )

    @app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="packers")
    def pack_order(task_id: int):
        return {"event_type": "order_packed"}

    @app.arrival_loop("orders")
    def order_generator(context: SimulationContext):
        task_id = 0
        while True:
            # The gap is drawn from the rate in force now
            order = yield context.wait_for_arrival("orders")
            context.spawn(pack_order(task_id, entity=order))
            task_id += 1

    return app


def outcomes(rush_packers: int) -> dict:
    """Runs the hour and returns the orders packed and their waits."""
    app = shop(rush_packers)
    app.run(until="1 h")
    r = app.env.stats.readings()
    name = "Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.{}".format
    return {
        "finished": r[name("finished")],
        "wait_mean": r[name("wait_mean")],
        "wait_max": r[name("wait_max")],
    }


if __name__ == "__main__":
    for packers in (1, 2):
        r = outcomes(packers)
        print(
            f"{packers} in the rush: {r['finished']} packed, "
            f"mean wait {r['wait_mean']:5.2f} s, longest {r['wait_max']:6.2f} s"
        )
docs/snippets/tutorials/changing_demand_low_level.py
"""The Changing Demand tutorial: a 20-minute rush, with one packer or two.

One packer and 1.5 seconds of packing; orders arrive at 0.4 a second, and at 0.9
from 20 to 40 minutes. Every record is printed to the terminal, and the script
prints the waits with one packer through the rush and with a second packer for it:
python changing_demand_low_level.py 2>/dev/null shows only those lines.
"""

import itertools
import logging

from desflow import (
    CapacityConfig,
    ConsoleEgress,
    DistributionConfig,
    DynamicRealtimeEnvironment,
    DynamicResource,
    Sampler,
    SimParameter,
    run_scenario,
)

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
)

PARAMS = SimParameter(
    sim_id="Shop",
    arrival={"orders": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=0.4)},
    service={"packing": DistributionConfig(dist="constant", value=1.5)},
    resources={"packers": CapacityConfig(current_cap=1, max_cap=2)},
)


def schedule(rush_packers):
    """The rush: 0.9 orders a second from 20 to 40 minutes, and rush_packers for it."""
    return [
        {"at": 1200, "path": "Shop.arrival.orders.rate", "value": 0.9},
        {
            "at": 1200,
            "path": "Shop.resources.packers.current_cap",
            "value": rush_packers,
        },
        {"at": 2400, "path": "Shop.arrival.orders.rate", "value": 0.4},
        {"at": 2400, "path": "Shop.resources.packers.current_cap", "value": 1},
    ]


def pack_order(env, sampler, packers, key, task_id):
    path_id = "Shop.service.packing"

    def publish(value):
        env.publish_event(key, value, task="pack_order", instance=task_id)

    publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "queued"})
    env.stats.task_queued("pack_order", task_id)
    with packers.request() as request:
        yield request
        publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "started"})
        env.stats.task_started("pack_order", task_id)
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(env.registry.get_config(path_id)))
        publish({"event_type": "order_packed"})
        env.stats.task_finished("pack_order", task_id)


def order_generator(env, sampler, packers):
    arrival = env.registry.get_config("Shop.arrival.orders")
    for task_id in itertools.count():
        # The gap is drawn from the rate in force now
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(arrival))
        key = f"orders-{task_id + 1}"
        env.process(pack_order(env, sampler, packers, key, task_id))


def run(rush_packers=1, factor=0.0):
    env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=factor)
    env.registry.register_sim_parameter(PARAMS)
    env.setup_egress([ConsoleEgress()])
    # Orders packed, and the mean and longest wait, at the end
    env.setup_stats("Shop", "typical", interval=7200)
    packers = DynamicResource(env, "Shop", "packers")
    # Each step applies before every other event at its time
    env.process(run_scenario(env, schedule(rush_packers), until=3600))
    env.process(order_generator(env, Sampler(seed=42), packers))
    try:
        env.run(until=3600)
    finally:
        env.teardown()
    return env


def outcomes(rush_packers: int) -> dict:
    """Runs the hour and returns the orders packed and their waits."""
    r = run(rush_packers).stats.readings()
    name = "Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.{}".format
    return {
        "finished": r[name("finished")],
        "wait_mean": r[name("wait_mean")],
        "wait_max": r[name("wait_max")],
    }


if __name__ == "__main__":
    for packers in (1, 2):
        r = outcomes(packers)
        print(
            f"{packers} in the rush: {r['finished']} packed, "
            f"mean wait {r['wait_mean']:5.2f} s, longest {r['wait_max']:6.2f} s"
        )

docs.title: Choosing Inputs
docs.text:
Level: Basics

Packing takes 1.5 seconds on average. So far the shop has said exactly that: a constant 1.5 seconds. Real packing times vary, and a model is only as good as the times it draws. This page asks: which distribution fits packing times?

docs.title: What You Add
docs.text:
A packing time chosen from evidence. The model simulates the busy hour with 3 packers from Queues and Capacity. It gets four candidates for packing, all with a mean of 1.5 seconds, and runs the hour with each:

  • constant: the mean alone, as the shop had it;
  • exponential: the usual choice when nothing is known;
  • triangular: an expert's estimate;
  • empirical: times measured at the packing bench.

docs.title: An Expert's Range
docs.text:
Choosing a distribution for an input is called input modelling. Often there is no data yet, but someone who knows the work can say how long it takes at least, usually and at most. A triangular distribution takes exactly those three numbers, low, mode and high, and all three are required:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/choosing_inputs.yaml:triangular
# An expert's estimate: at least 1 s, usually 1.25 s, at most 2.25 s
triangular: {dist: triangular, low: 1 s, mode: 1.25 s, high: 2.25 s}
docs/snippets/tutorials/choosing_inputs.py:triangular
# An expert's estimate: at least 1 s, usually 1.25 s, at most 2.25 s
app.add_service("triangular", dist="triangular", low=1, mode=1.25, high=2.25)
docs/snippets/tutorials/choosing_inputs_low_level.py:triangular
# An expert's estimate: at least 1 s, usually 1.25 s, at most 2.25 s
TRIANGULAR = DistributionConfig(dist="triangular", low=1, mode=1.25, high=2.25)

Its mean is (low + mode + high) ÷ 3 = (1 + 1.25 + 2.25) ÷ 3 = 1.5 seconds. In a blueprint every time-valued parameter takes a duration such as 1.25 s or 2 min; a plain number is seconds.

docs.title: Measured Times
docs.text:
When times can be measured, use them. An empirical distribution draws from a list of measured values, each equally likely (or with weights, one per value). These are 40 packing times timed at the bench, with a mean of 1.5 seconds:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/choosing_inputs.yaml:empirical
# 40 packing times measured at the bench, in seconds
empirical:
  dist: empirical
  values: [1.5, 2.5, 2.4, 1.2, 1.3, 1.2, 1.8, 1.4, 2.0, 0.7,
           2.7, 1.4, 1.9, 1.4, 1.3, 1.8, 2.0, 1.4, 1.4, 1.9,
           1.1, 0.8, 1.7, 1.1, 0.7, 1.1, 1.2, 0.9, 0.8, 1.5,
           2.1, 1.3, 1.1, 1.7, 1.9, 1.3, 1.8, 2.2, 1.4, 1.1]
docs/snippets/tutorials/choosing_inputs.py:empirical
# 40 packing times measured at the bench, in seconds
measured = [
    1.5, 2.5, 2.4, 1.2, 1.3, 1.2, 1.8, 1.4, 2.0, 0.7,
    2.7, 1.4, 1.9, 1.4, 1.3, 1.8, 2.0, 1.4, 1.4, 1.9,
    1.1, 0.8, 1.7, 1.1, 0.7, 1.1, 1.2, 0.9, 0.8, 1.5,
    2.1, 1.3, 1.1, 1.7, 1.9, 1.3, 1.8, 2.2, 1.4, 1.1,
]  # fmt: skip
app.add_service("empirical", dist="empirical", values=measured)
docs/snippets/tutorials/choosing_inputs_low_level.py:empirical
# 40 packing times measured at the bench, in seconds
MEASURED = [
    1.5, 2.5, 2.4, 1.2, 1.3, 1.2, 1.8, 1.4, 2.0, 0.7,
    2.7, 1.4, 1.9, 1.4, 1.3, 1.8, 2.0, 1.4, 1.4, 1.9,
    1.1, 0.8, 1.7, 1.1, 0.7, 1.1, 1.2, 0.9, 0.8, 1.5,
    2.1, 1.3, 1.1, 1.7, 1.9, 1.3, 1.8, 2.2, 1.4, 1.1,
]  # fmt: skip
EMPIRICAL = DistributionConfig(dist="empirical", values=MEASURED)

The values are taken when the model is loaded. A list is not one number, so an empirical distribution has no registry path and does not change while the run goes on; the other distributions have one path per parameter, such as Shop.service.triangular.mode.

docs.title: Same Mean, Different Waits
docs.text:
All four candidates have the same mean, so the packers are equally busy with each: utilisation 0.9. Run the hour with each, and read the mean wait from the statistics at the typical level, which Measuring a Run explains:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/choosing_inputs.yaml:compare
tasks:
  pack_order:
    # The candidate comes from the PACKING variable, empirical when it is not set
    service: ${PACKING:-empirical}
    resource: packers
    payload: {event_type: order_packed}

# The mean wait of pack_order, published at the end
stats: {level: typical, interval: 1 h}

for packing in constant triangular empirical exponential; do
  PACKING=$packing desflow run choosing_inputs.yaml 2>&1 | grep wait_mean
done
docs/snippets/tutorials/choosing_inputs.py:compare
# The task packs with the candidate; the mean wait is read at the end
@app.task(service_id=packing, resource_id="packers")
def pack_order(task_id):
    return {"event_type": "order_packed"}

app.with_stats("typical", interval=3600)
docs/snippets/tutorials/choosing_inputs_low_level.py:compare
def pack_order(env, sampler, packers, packing, task_id):
    """One order, packed with the candidate called `packing`."""
    env.stats.task_queued("pack_order", task_id)
    with packers.request() as request:
        yield request
        env.stats.task_started("pack_order", task_id)
        service = env.registry.get_config(f"Shop.service.{packing}")
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(service))
    env.stats.task_finished("pack_order", task_id)

The Builder and Low-level scripts print one line per candidate; the YAML runs print the same numbers as the value of their wait_mean lines:

constant     mean wait  1.27 s
triangular   mean wait  1.28 s
empirical    mean wait  1.35 s
exponential  mean wait  2.37 s

A mean alone hides queues. With constant packing nobody holds a packer for long. With exponential packing a few orders take 4, 5 or 6 seconds, and everyone behind them waits: the mean wait almost doubles at the same utilisation.

docs.title: Result
docs.text:
Which distribution fits packing times? The empirical distribution, because it is the measured times themselves. On the left, the shapes of the four candidates; on the right, the mean wait each gives in the busy hour:

With the empirical distribution the mean wait is 1.35 seconds. The constant mean gives 1.27 seconds, 6% too short, and the exponential guess gives 2.37 seconds, 75% too long. The expert's triangle is close to the constant, because its range is narrower than the measured one.

docs.title: Why It Works
docs.text: In the busy hour the mean wait is roughly proportional to the square of the spread of the gaps between orders plus the square of the spread of the packing times, each spread measured relative to its mean (Kingman's approximation). The gaps are the same in all four runs, so only the packing spread differs: none for constant, a little for triangular, more for the measured times, and as much as the mean itself for exponential. A family fitted to the measured times, such as a gamma with their mean and standard deviation, takes other parameters, a shape and a scale; Arrivals and Services gives the formulas that turn a mean and a standard deviation into them, and lists each distribution with its parameters and rules. Fit the Inputs fits every family to the 40 times with desflow fit, Input Fitting describes its options and outcomes, and Fit a Distribution fits a column of your own. Distributions gives the mean and variance of each family.
