docs.title: Result
docs.text:
How do orders move through pick, pack and ship? Most go straight through, and a few go to backorder or are packed again. The run publishes the finished count of every task at the end, with stats: basic:

Task Finished in the hour pick_order 1,857 backorder 80 pack_order 1,849 ship_order 1,775

4.3% of picks led to backorder (80 of 1,857), and 4.0% of parcels were packed again (74 of 1,849 packs did not lead to a shipment). The weights ask for 5%; the run drew a few less.

docs.title: Why It Works
docs.text: In a flow, each task's arrival rate follows from the rates into it and the routing weights: this is flow balance. Every pack leads to a shipment with probability 0.95, so each order is packed 1 ÷ 0.95 = 1.05 times on average, and the packers see 5% more work than there are orders. A rework loop raises utilisation in the same way, which is why it belongs in the load you work out before running. Task Flow describes routing in full.

docs.title: Full Files
Interruptions
docs.text:
Level: Advanced

A quarter of the shop's orders are express, as in Priorities, but now an express order does not wait for the regular order being packed: it takes the packer at once. This page asks: what remains of a regular order's packing when an express order takes its packer, and which way of carrying on keeps regular orders waiting least? It compares three policies over an hour.

docs.title: What You Add
docs.text: A packer that can be preempted, an on_interrupt policy on regular orders: resume, restart or abandon, and a breakdown, which interrupts work in the same way. The shop is the one from Priorities: one packer, regular orders at 0.45 a second and express orders at 0.15, and 1.5 seconds of packing.

docs.title: Preemption
docs.text:
Priority so far decided only who goes next. Preemption also stops the work in progress: SimPy's PreemptiveResource takes a unit from the user with the highest priority value when a request with a lower one finds every unit busy, and that user's process receives an Interrupt. In desflow it is preempt: true on a resource whose queue is priority:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/interruptions.yaml:packers
resources:
  # An express order takes the packer from a regular one being packed
  packers: {current_cap: 1, max_cap: 4, queue: priority, preempt: true}
docs/snippets/tutorials/interruptions.py:packers
# An express order takes the packer from a regular one being packed
.add_resource(
    "packers", current_cap=1, max_cap=4, queue="priority", preempt=True
)
docs/snippets/tutorials/interruptions_low_level.py:packers
# An express order takes the packer from a regular one being packed
"packers": DynamicResource(
    env, "Shop", "packers", queue="priority", preempt=True
),

Equal priorities do not preempt, so one express order does not take the packer from another; SimPy's one exception, a user whose request with preempt: false was made at the same moment, does not arise here.

docs.title: Resume, Restart or Abandon
docs.text:
A preempted or interrupted task first gives back everything it holds and stops waiting for anything, as SimPy's with blocks do on the way out. Its on_interrupt then says what it does:

  • resume, the default: it queues again and, once it has the packer back, packs for the time it had left;
  • restart: it queues again and packs for a new time, drawn from the same seeded stream, as if the work were spoiled;
  • abandon: it ends, and its flow with it, unless on_interrupt_next names a task to go to.

It publishes preempted (or interrupted) when it loses the packer, and resumed when it has it again:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/interruptions.yaml:policy
pack_order:
  service: packing
  resource: packers
  priority: 1
  # What a regular order does when it loses the packer
  on_interrupt: ${POLICY:-resume}
  payload: {event_type: order_packed}

${POLICY:-resume} reads the environment variable POLICY, so POLICY=restart desflow run interruptions.yaml runs the second policy.

docs/snippets/tutorials/interruptions.py:policy
@app.task(
    service_id="packing",
    resource_id="packers",
    priority=1,
    # What a regular order does when it loses the packer
    on_interrupt=policy,
)
def pack_order(task_id: int):
    return {"event_type": "order_packed"}
docs/snippets/tutorials/interruptions_low_level.py:policy
def pack(env, sampler, shop, arrival, key, task_id, policy):
    """Packs one order; when it loses the packer, it follows `policy`."""
    task, priority = TASKS[arrival]
    path_id = "Shop.service.packing"

    def publish(value):
        env.publish_event(key, value, task=task, instance=task_id)

    publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "queued"})
    env.stats.task_queued(task, task_id)
    shop["running"].setdefault(task, []).append(env.active_process)
    remaining, started = None, False
    while True:
        request = shop["packers"].request(priority=priority)
        since = None
        try:
            yield request
            status = "resumed" if started else "started"
            publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": status})
            if started:
                env.stats.task_resumed(task, task_id)
            else:
                env.stats.task_started(task, task_id)
            started = True
            if remaining is None:
                remaining = sampler.sample(env.registry.get_config(path_id))
            since = env.now
            yield env.timeout(remaining)
            publish({"event_type": "order_packed" if priority else "express_packed"})
            env.stats.task_finished(task, task_id)
            shop["packers"].release(request)
            break
        except simpy.Interrupt as interrupt:
            request.cancel()
            shop["packers"].release(request)
            if since is not None:
                # resume serves what is left; restart draws a new packing time
                remaining = (
                    remaining - (env.now - since) if policy == "resume" else None
                )
            preempted = isinstance(interrupt.cause, Preempted)
            if preempted:
                value = {"status": "preempted", "resource": "packers"}
            else:
                value = {"status": "interrupted", "cause": interrupt.cause}
            publish({"path_id": path_id, **value})
            env.stats.task_interrupted(task, task_id, preempted=preempted)
            if policy == "abandon":
                env.stats.task_dropped(task, task_id)
                shop["running"][task].remove(env.active_process)
                return
    shop["running"][task].remove(env.active_process)
    env.stats.flow_finished(arrival)

The process catches simpy.Interrupt, whose cause is SimPy's Preempted for a preemption, gives back its request, and asks again. That loop is what on_interrupt writes for you.

The statistics count each preempted, interrupted and resumed; a resumed order's wait is the sum of its waits, and its packing time is the time it was packed:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/interruptions.yaml:watch
# Counts of preemptions and resumptions, and the mean wait and service, at the end
stats: {level: typical, interval: 1 h}
docs/snippets/tutorials/interruptions.py:watch
# Counts of preemptions and resumptions, and the mean wait and service, at the end
.with_stats("typical", interval=3600)
docs/snippets/tutorials/interruptions_low_level.py:watch
# Counts of preemptions and resumptions, and the mean wait and service, at the end
env.setup_stats("Shop", "typical", interval=3600)

docs.title: Interrupt a Task
docs.text:
Preemption is one source of interrupts; a model can send others. An interrupt names a task, and every instance of it that is running, waiting or being served, receives an interrupt with the cause given, and follows its on_interrupt. A where condition, such as attr.order == 3, limits it to the instances it holds for. Here the packer is called away at 30 minutes:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/interruptions.yaml:interrupt
scenario:
  # The packer is called away at 30 minutes: every regular order in the shop,
  # waiting or being packed, is interrupted
  - {at: 30 min, interrupt: {task: pack_order, cause: called away}}

A task can carry the same interrupt, applied when it finishes.

docs/snippets/tutorials/interruptions.py:interrupt
def called_away(context: SimulationContext):
    """The packer is called away at 30 minutes: every regular order in the shop,
    waiting or being packed, is interrupted."""
    yield context.env.timeout(1800)
    context.interrupt("pack_order", cause="called away")

app.add_process(called_away)

context.interrupt(task, where=None, cause=None) returns how many instances it reached; it never reaches the instance that calls it.

docs/snippets/tutorials/interruptions_low_level.py:interrupt
def called_away(env, shop):
    """The packer is called away at 30 minutes: every regular order in the shop,
    waiting or being packed, is interrupted."""
    yield env.timeout(1800)
    for process in list(shop["running"].get("pack_order", [])):
        process.interrupt("called away")

process.interrupt(cause) is SimPy's; the model keeps its own list of the processes it may interrupt.

docs.title: A Breakdown
docs.text:
A machine that fails interrupts the work it was doing in the same way. A resource's breakdown makes it fail at random times and be repaired: here a packing station fails about once a minute and takes 5 to 15 seconds to repair:

YAMLBuilderLow-level examples/yaml/breakdowns.yaml:station
resources:
  station:
    current_cap: 2
    max_cap: 3
    breakdown:
      # Calendar time from a repair, or the start, to the next failure.
      time_to_failure: {dist: exponential, rate: 0.0167}
      repair: {dist: uniform, low: 5 s, high: 15 s}
      # The orders being packed are interrupted, and follow their on_interrupt.
      work: interrupt
examples/builder/breakdowns_example.py:station
.add_resource("station", current_cap=2, max_cap=3)
.add_breakdown(
    "station",
    # Calendar time from a repair, or the start, to the next failure
    time_to_failure={"dist": "exponential", "rate": 0.0167},
    repair={"dist": "uniform", "low": 5, "high": 15},
    # The orders being packed are interrupted, and follow their on_interrupt
    work="interrupt",
)
examples/low-level/breakdowns_example.py:station
breakdowns={
    "station": BreakdownConfig(
        # Calendar time from a repair, or the start, to the next failure
        time_to_failure=DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=0.0167),
        repair=DistributionConfig(dist="uniform", low=5, high=15),
        # The orders being packed are interrupted
        work="interrupt",
    )
},

run_breakdowns(env, station, sampler) is the SimPy process that puts the station down and repairs it.

With work: interrupt, each order being packed when the station fails receives an interrupt whose cause is breakdown and follows its on_interrupt, as a preempted order does. During the repair the station's effective capacity is 0, so no order starts, while its current_cap keeps the planned value; a change to it during the repair sets the capacity the station returns to. With work: finish, the orders being packed finish, and only new work waits for the repair. Breakdowns checks the downtime of the example.

docs.title: Result
docs.text:
What remains of a regular order's packing when an express order takes its packer? With resume, the time it had left: 344 preemptions cost regular orders a mean wait of 8.12 seconds. With restart, nothing: each preempted order packs again from the start, preemptions rise to 393, and the mean wait triples to 25.03 seconds. With abandon, the order is lost: 313 are, and the 1,294 packed orders wait only 3.60 seconds, because the queue loses everyone who was preempted:

The Builder and Low-level scripts print all three:

resume : 344 preempted, 1607 packed, mean wait  8.12 s, mean packing 1.50 s
restart: 393 preempted, 1606 packed, mean wait 25.03 s, mean packing 1.69 s
abandon: 313 preempted, 1294 packed, mean wait  3.60 s, mean packing 1.50 s

docs.title: Why It Works
docs.text: Under restart the packer spends part of its time on packing that is thrown away, so it does more work for the same orders: the mean time packed rises from 1.50 to 1.69 seconds, the load nears what one packer can do, and waits grow fast, as on Queues and Capacity. resume loses no work, so its waits are close to those of plain priority. abandon looks best only because the mean leaves out the orders it lost; count them beside it. Resources describes preemption, and Tasks and Processes the task's steps.

docs/snippets/tutorials/interruptions.py
"""The Interruptions tutorial: express orders take the packer from regular ones.

One packer, regular orders at 0.45 a second and express orders at 0.15, and 1.5
seconds of packing. Every record is printed to the terminal, and the script prints
what preemption did to regular orders under each policy at the end:
python interruptions.py 2>/dev/null shows only those lines.
"""

import logging

from desflow import ConsoleEgress, SimulationContext

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
)


def shop(policy: str = "resume") -> SimulationContext:
    """The shop, where a regular order follows `policy` when it loses the packer."""
    app = (
        SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0, random_seed=42)
        # An express order takes the packer from a regular one being packed
        .add_resource(
            "packers", current_cap=1, max_cap=4, queue="priority", preempt=True
        )
        .add_service("packing", dist="constant", value=1.5)
        # 0.6 orders a second in all, one in four of them express
        .add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=0.45)
        .add_arrival("express", dist="exponential", rate=0.15)
        # Counts of preemptions and resumptions, and the mean wait and service, at the end
        .with_stats("typical", interval=3600)
        .add_egress(ConsoleEgress())
    )

    @app.task(
        service_id="packing",
        resource_id="packers",
        priority=1,
        # What a regular order does when it loses the packer
        on_interrupt=policy,
    )
    def pack_order(task_id: int):
        return {"event_type": "order_packed"}


    @app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="packers", priority=0)
    def pack_express(task_id: int):
        return {"event_type": "express_packed"}

    for arrival, task, name in (
        ("orders", pack_order, "pack_order"),
        ("express", pack_express, "pack_express"),
    ):

        def loop(context: SimulationContext, arrival=arrival, task=task, name=name):
            while True:
                entity = yield context.wait_for_arrival(arrival)
                context.spawn(task(context.next_instance(name), entity=entity))

        app.arrival_loop(arrival)(loop)

    def called_away(context: SimulationContext):
        """The packer is called away at 30 minutes: every regular order in the shop,
        waiting or being packed, is interrupted."""
        yield context.env.timeout(1800)
        context.interrupt("pack_order", cause="called away")

    app.add_process(called_away)
    return app


def outcomes(policy: str) -> dict:
    """Runs one hour and returns what preemption did to regular orders."""
    app = shop(policy)
    app.run(until="1 h")
    readings = app.env.stats.readings()
    name = "Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.{}".format
    return {
        "preempted": readings[name("preempted")],
        "interrupted": readings.get(name("interrupted"), 0),
        "finished": readings[name("finished")],
        "wait_mean": readings[name("wait_mean")],
        "service_mean": readings[name("service_mean")],
    }


if __name__ == "__main__":
    for policy in ("resume", "restart", "abandon"):
        r = outcomes(policy)
        print(
            f"{policy:<7}: {r['preempted']} preempted, {r['finished']} packed, "
            f"mean wait {r['wait_mean']:5.2f} s, mean packing {r['service_mean']:4.2f} s"
        )
docs/snippets/tutorials/interruptions_low_level.py
"""The Interruptions tutorial: express orders take the packer from regular ones.

One packer, regular orders at 0.45 a second and express orders at 0.15, and 1.5
seconds of packing. Every record is printed to the terminal, and the script prints
what preemption did to regular orders under each policy at the end:
python interruptions_low_level.py 2>/dev/null shows only those lines.
"""

import itertools
import logging

import simpy
from simpy.resources.resource import Preempted

from desflow import (
    CapacityConfig,
    ConsoleEgress,
    DistributionConfig,
    DynamicRealtimeEnvironment,
    DynamicResource,
    Sampler,
    SimParameter,
)

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
)

PARAMS = SimParameter(
    sim_id="Shop",
    arrival={
        # 0.6 orders a second in all, one in four of them express
        "orders": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=0.45),
        "express": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=0.15),
    },
    service={"packing": DistributionConfig(dist="constant", value=1.5)},
    resources={"packers": CapacityConfig(current_cap=1, max_cap=4)},
)
TASKS = {"orders": ("pack_order", 1), "express": ("pack_express", 0)}


def pack(env, sampler, shop, arrival, key, task_id, policy):
    """Packs one order; when it loses the packer, it follows `policy`."""
    task, priority = TASKS[arrival]
    path_id = "Shop.service.packing"

    def publish(value):
        env.publish_event(key, value, task=task, instance=task_id)

    publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "queued"})
    env.stats.task_queued(task, task_id)
    shop["running"].setdefault(task, []).append(env.active_process)
    remaining, started = None, False
    while True:
        request = shop["packers"].request(priority=priority)
        since = None
        try:
            yield request
            status = "resumed" if started else "started"
            publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": status})
            if started:
                env.stats.task_resumed(task, task_id)
            else:
                env.stats.task_started(task, task_id)
            started = True
            if remaining is None:
                remaining = sampler.sample(env.registry.get_config(path_id))
            since = env.now
            yield env.timeout(remaining)
            publish({"event_type": "order_packed" if priority else "express_packed"})
            env.stats.task_finished(task, task_id)
            shop["packers"].release(request)
            break
        except simpy.Interrupt as interrupt:
            request.cancel()
            shop["packers"].release(request)
            if since is not None:
                # resume serves what is left; restart draws a new packing time
                remaining = (
                    remaining - (env.now - since) if policy == "resume" else None
                )
            preempted = isinstance(interrupt.cause, Preempted)
            if preempted:
                value = {"status": "preempted", "resource": "packers"}
            else:
                value = {"status": "interrupted", "cause": interrupt.cause}
            publish({"path_id": path_id, **value})
            env.stats.task_interrupted(task, task_id, preempted=preempted)
            if policy == "abandon":
                env.stats.task_dropped(task, task_id)
                shop["running"][task].remove(env.active_process)
                return
    shop["running"][task].remove(env.active_process)
    env.stats.flow_finished(arrival)


def order_generator(env, sampler, shop, arrival, policy):
    config = env.registry.get_config(f"Shop.arrival.{arrival}")
    for task_id in itertools.count():
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(config))
        key = f"{arrival}-{task_id + 1}"
        env.process(pack(env, sampler, shop, arrival, key, task_id, policy))


def called_away(env, shop):
    """The packer is called away at 30 minutes: every regular order in the shop,
    waiting or being packed, is interrupted."""
    yield env.timeout(1800)
    for process in list(shop["running"].get("pack_order", [])):
        process.interrupt("called away")


def run(policy="resume", until=3600, factor=0.0):
    env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=factor)
    env.registry.register_sim_parameter(PARAMS)
    env.setup_egress([ConsoleEgress()])
    # Counts of preemptions and resumptions, and the mean wait and service, at the end
    env.setup_stats("Shop", "typical", interval=3600)
    shop = {
        # An express order takes the packer from a regular one being packed
        "packers": DynamicResource(
            env, "Shop", "packers", queue="priority", preempt=True
        ),
        "running": {},
    }
    sampler = Sampler(seed=42)
    env.process(order_generator(env, sampler, shop, "orders", policy))
    env.process(order_generator(env, sampler, shop, "express", policy))
    env.process(called_away(env, shop))
    try:
        env.run(until=until)
    finally:
        env.teardown()
    return env


def outcomes(policy: str) -> dict:
    """Runs one hour and returns what preemption did to regular orders."""
    readings = run(policy).stats.readings()
    name = "Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.{}".format
    return {
        "preempted": readings[name("preempted")],
        "interrupted": readings.get(name("interrupted"), 0),
        "finished": readings[name("finished")],
        "wait_mean": readings[name("wait_mean")],
        "service_mean": readings[name("service_mean")],
    }


if __name__ == "__main__":
    for policy in ("resume", "restart", "abandon"):
        r = outcomes(policy)
        print(
            f"{policy:<7}: {r['preempted']} preempted, {r['finished']} packed, "
            f"mean wait {r['wait_mean']:5.2f} s, mean packing {r['service_mean']:4.2f} s"
        )

Next, Competing Resources asks what happens while an order holds one resource and waits for another.

docs.title: Local Replay
docs.text:
Level: Intermediate

The shop recorded every order of one morning, 09:00 to 10:00 on 1 October 2026: 1,963 orders, 0.545 a second on average. A model with exponential gaps at that rate says one packer keeps waits short. This page asks: what does the shop do with the same orders, at the times they were really placed? It replays the recorded morning and compares it with the model.

docs.title: What You Add
docs.text:
A replayed arrival: arrivals taken from the rows of a file instead of a distribution. The shop is the one from First Simulation, with packing at a constant 1.5 seconds. The recorded orders are local_replay_orders.csv, one row per order; download it into the folder that holds the blueprint and the scripts:

ordered_at,order_id,items
2026-10-01T09:00:00.3,A10001,2
2026-10-01T09:00:02.0,A10002,2

docs.title: Replay the Rows
docs.text:
Each row becomes one arrival at its time, and the fields named in fields become the order's attributes. unit says what the time column holds: ms, s, min or h from the start of the run, or timestamp, a date and time read from the run's logical_start_time, here 09:00 on the recorded day:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/tutorials/local_replay.yaml:replay
arrivals:
  orders:
    # Each row is one order, at its recorded time, carrying its order_id and items
    replay:
      path: local_replay_orders.csv
      time: ordered_at
      unit: timestamp
      fields: [order_id, items]
      # A row without a valid time is left out, with a warning naming it
      on_invalid: skip
    spawn: pack_order

The path is relative to the blueprint.

docs/snippets/tutorials/local_replay.py:replay
# Each row is one order, at its recorded time, carrying its order_id and items
app.add_arrival_replay(

docs/snippets/tutorials/local_replay_low_level.py:replay
def replayed_orders(env, sampler, packers):
    """Starts one order at each row's time, carrying its order_id and items."""
    rows = read_trace(
        TRACE,
        time="ordered_at",
        unit="timestamp",
        fields=["order_id", "items"],
        # A row without a valid time is left out, with a warning naming it
        on_invalid="skip",
        start=START,
    )
    for task_id, row in enumerate(rows):
        # A row at or after the end of the run never arrives
        yield env.timeout(row.time - env.now)
        key = f"orders-{task_id + 1}"
        env.process(pack_order(env, sampler, packers, key, task_id, row.fields))

read_trace reads and checks the rows; each row has its simulation time, its row number and its fields.

The rows are read and checked when the run starts:

  • Rows must be in time order. The first row out of order stops the run, named with its row number.
  • Rows at equal times arrive at that time in the order of the file. Times are recorded to a tenth of a second, so 74 rows of the recorded morning have the same time as the row above them.

  • A row without a valid time stops the run, unless on_invalid is skip: then it is left out with a warning. Row 501 of the recorded morning has no time:

    Skipped row 501, which has no valid ordered_at: ''

  • A row before the start of the run stops it; rows at or after until never arrive. The file holds 19 orders after 10:00, which this run leaves out.

  • After the last row the arrival stops, with one INFO line, and the run goes on until until.

A Parquet file works the same way and needs the parquet extra.

docs.title: Result
docs.text:
What does the shop do with the orders of the real morning? Something the model does not show. Replayed, the orders wait 91.31 seconds on average and up to 295.40 seconds; the model at the same mean rate waits 2.57 seconds on average and at most 14.34. The recorded morning holds two bursts, at 09:15 and 09:40, of three minutes each. Each builds a queue that the packer clears only by about 32 and 54 minutes:

The Builder and Low-level scripts print both runs:

recorded: 1962 packed, mean wait 91.31 s, longest 295.40 s
modelled: 1905 packed, mean wait  2.57 s, longest  14.34 s

docs.title: Why It Works
docs.text: A mean rate says how many orders come in an hour, not when they come. Exponential gaps spread the orders evenly over the hour, with small random clusters; the recorded morning has bursts that push the load above one packer for minutes at a time, a finite overload like the rush of Changing Demand. Replaying the recorded rows keeps the bursts, so it shows waits the fitted model cannot. Use a replay to check a model against the data it was fitted to: when the two disagree, the arrivals are not exponential at one rate, and the model needs a schedule, as on Time-varying Arrivals, or the replay itself.

docs/snippets/tutorials/local_replay.py
"""The Local Replay tutorial: a recorded morning of orders, against a model of it.

One packer and 1.5 seconds of packing. The orders of 09:00 to 10:00 on 1 October
2026 arrive at their recorded times from local_replay_orders.csv; a second run
draws exponential gaps at the same mean rate, 0.545 orders a second. Every record
is printed to the terminal, and the script prints the waits of both runs:
python local_replay.py 2>/dev/null shows only those lines.
"""

import logging
from datetime import datetime
from pathlib import Path

from desflow import ConsoleEgress, SimulationContext

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
)

TRACE = Path(__file__).resolve().parent / "local_replay_orders.csv"


def shop(replay: bool) -> SimulationContext:
    """One packer, with the recorded orders or with a model of them."""
    app = (
        SimulationContext(
            sim_id="Shop",
            factor=0,
            random_seed=42,
            # Simulation time 0 is 09:00 on the recorded day
            logical_start_time=datetime(2026, 10, 1, 9, 0),
        )
        .add_resource("packers", current_cap=1, max_cap=2)
        .add_service("packing", dist="constant", value=1.5)
        # Orders packed, and the mean and longest wait, at the end
        .with_stats("typical", interval=7200)
        .add_egress(ConsoleEgress())
    )
    if replay:
        # Each row is one order, at its recorded time, carrying its order_id and items
        app.add_arrival_replay(
            "orders",
            TRACE,
            time="ordered_at",
            unit="timestamp",
            fields=["order_id", "items"],
            # A row without a valid time is left out, with a warning naming it
            on_invalid="skip",
        )
    else:
        # The same mean rate: 1,963 orders in the hour
        app.add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=0.545)

    @app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="packers")
    def pack_order(task_id: int):
        return {"event_type": "order_packed"}

    @app.arrival_loop("orders")
    def order_generator(context: SimulationContext):
        task_id = 0
        while True:
            # The wait for the next row, as for any other arrival
            order = yield context.wait_for_arrival("orders")
            context.spawn(pack_order(task_id, entity=order))
            task_id += 1


    return app


def outcomes(replay: bool) -> dict:
    """Runs the hour and returns the orders packed and their waits."""
    app = shop(replay)
    app.run(until="1 h")
    r = app.env.stats.readings()
    name = "Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.{}".format
    return {
        "finished": r[name("finished")],
        "wait_mean": r[name("wait_mean")],
        "wait_max": r[name("wait_max")],
    }


if __name__ == "__main__":
    for replay in (True, False):
        r = outcomes(replay)
        label = "recorded" if replay else "modelled"
        print(
            f"{label}: {r['finished']} packed, "
            f"mean wait {r['wait_mean']:5.2f} s, longest {r['wait_max']:6.2f} s"
        )

"""The Local Replay tutorial: a recorded morning of orders, against a model of it.

One packer and 1.5 seconds of packing. The orders of 09:00 to 10:00 on 1 October
2026 arrive at their recorded times from local_replay_orders.csv; a second run
draws exponential gaps at the same mean rate, 0.545 orders a second. Every record
is printed to the terminal, and the script prints the waits of both runs:
python local_replay_low_level.py 2>/dev/null shows only those lines.
"""

import itertools
import logging
from datetime import datetime
from pathlib import Path

from desflow import (
    CapacityConfig,
    ConsoleEgress,
    DistributionConfig,
    DynamicRealtimeEnvironment,
    DynamicResource,
    Sampler,
    SimParameter,
    read_trace,
)

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
)

TRACE = Path(__file__).resolve().parent / "local_replay_orders.csv"
START = datetime(2026, 10, 1, 9, 0)  # simulation time 0 is 09:00 on the recorded day
PARAMS = SimParameter(
    sim_id="Shop",
    # The same mean rate: 1,963 orders in the hour
    arrival={"orders": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=0.545)},
    service={"packing": DistributionConfig(dist="constant", value=1.5)},
    resources={"packers": CapacityConfig(current_cap=1, max_cap=2)},
)


def pack_order(env, sampler, packers, key, task_id, fields):
    path_id = "Shop.service.packing"

    def publish(value):
        env.publish_event(key, value, task="pack_order", instance=task_id)

    publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "queued"})
    env.stats.task_queued("pack_order", task_id)
    with packers.request() as request:
        yield request
        publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "started"})
        env.stats.task_started("pack_order", task_id)
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(env.registry.get_config(path_id)))
        publish({"event_type": "order_packed"})
        env.stats.task_finished("pack_order", task_id)


def replayed_orders(env, sampler, packers):
    """Starts one order at each row's time, carrying its order_id and items."""
    rows = read_trace(
        TRACE,
        time="ordered_at",
        unit="timestamp",
        fields=["order_id", "items"],
        # A row without a valid time is left out, with a warning naming it
        on_invalid="skip",
        start=START,
    )
    for task_id, row in enumerate(rows):
        # A row at or after the end of the run never arrives
        yield env.timeout(row.time - env.now)
        key = f"orders-{task_id + 1}"
        env.process(pack_order(env, sampler, packers, key, task_id, row.fields))


def modelled_orders(env, sampler, packers):
    arrival = env.registry.get_config("Shop.arrival.orders")
    for task_id in itertools.count():
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(arrival))
        key = f"orders-{task_id + 1}"
        env.process(pack_order(env, sampler, packers, key, task_id, {}))


def run(replay=True, factor=0.0):
    env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=factor, logical_start_time=START)
    env.registry.register_sim_parameter(PARAMS)
    env.setup_egress([ConsoleEgress()])
    # Orders packed, and the mean and longest wait, at the end
    env.setup_stats("Shop", "typical", interval=7200)
    packers = DynamicResource(env, "Shop", "packers")
    orders = replayed_orders if replay else modelled_orders
    env.process(orders(env, Sampler(seed=42), packers))
    try:
        env.run(until=3600)
    finally:
        env.teardown()
    return env


def outcomes(replay: bool) -> dict:
    """Runs the hour and returns the orders packed and their waits."""
    r = run(replay).stats.readings()
    name = "Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.{}".format
    return {
        "finished": r[name("finished")],
        "wait_mean": r[name("wait_mean")],
        "wait_max": r[name("wait_max")],
    }


if __name__ == "__main__":
    for replay in (True, False):
        r = outcomes(replay)
        label = "recorded" if replay else "modelled"
        print(
            f"{label}: {r['finished']} packed, "
            f"mean wait {r['wait_mean']:5.2f} s, longest {r['wait_max']:6.2f} s"
        )

Next, Comparing Designs asks whether a fourth packer cuts the mean wait, and by how much.

docs.title: Measuring a Run
docs.text:
Level: Basics

Most of the last three pages read one number, the mean wait. A run knows much more: how busy the packers were, how long the queue was, how many orders were packed, and how long the slowest one waited. This page asks: what does a run tell me?

docs.title: What You Add
docs.text: stats: typical, the built-in statistics at the level that includes waits. The model simulates the busy hour with 3 packers and the measured packing times that Choosing Inputs chose.

docs.title: Switch On Statistics
docs.text:
desflow keeps statistics about a run as it goes, and publishes them as telemetry every 10 simulation seconds and once more at the end. They are off by default, because most runs only generate data. A level switches them on, and each level answers one more question:

Level Question it answers Adds none nothing (the default) minimal What is happening now? each resource's capacity, in_use, queue_length and utilization, and each task's in_progress basic How much got done, and how busy was it? finished counts, each arrival's started and in_system, and utilization_avg and queue_length_avg over time typical How long did orders take? each task's wait_mean, wait_max, service_mean and service_max all How long did the slowest take? each task's wait_p50, wait_p95 and wait_p99, and the same for service

Each level includes the ones above it. Switch on typical:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/measuring_a_run.yaml:stats
# Counts, time averages, and the mean and maximum wait and service, every 10 s
stats: typical
docs/snippets/tutorials/measuring_a_run.py:stats
# Counts, time averages, and the mean and maximum wait and service, every 10 s
.with_stats("typical")
docs/snippets/tutorials/measuring_a_run_low_level.py:stats
# Counts, time averages, and the mean and maximum wait and service, every 10 s
env.setup_stats("Shop", "typical", interval=10)

The environment keeps the statistics in env.stats. Resources report their own changes, but a low-level process has no task for desflow to watch, so it reports each step itself: env.stats.task_queued, task_started and task_finished with the task's name and instance id, and flow_started and flow_finished when the order enters and leaves the shop. The full file below shows them.

The statistics are telemetry, so they reach every sink, and they can also be read in Python at the end of the run:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/measuring_a_run.yaml:read
# The statistics are telemetry, so every sink receives them
egress:
  - type: Console
docs/snippets/tutorials/measuring_a_run.py:read
if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run(until="1 h")
    # The statistics are telemetry, so the console printed them; read them here too
    for name, value in app.env.stats.readings().items():
        print(f"{name} = {value}")
docs/snippets/tutorials/measuring_a_run_low_level.py:read
if __name__ == "__main__":
    env = run()
    # The statistics are telemetry, so the console printed them; read them here too
    for name, value in env.stats.readings().items():
        print(f"{name} = {value}")

Every name has the same form, <sim_id>.stats.<kind>.<name>.<statistic>, such as Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.wait_mean. These are the statistics published at the end of the hour:

[TEL] {'sim_ts': 3600.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.resources.packers.capacity', 'value': 3}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 3600.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.resources.packers.in_use', 'value': 3}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 3600.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.resources.packers.queue_length', 'value': 8}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 3600.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.resources.packers.utilization', 'value': 100.0}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 3600.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.resources.packers.utilization_avg', 'value': 86.56336659179189}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 3600.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.resources.packers.queue_length_avg', 'value': 2.405756864104584}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 3600.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.in_progress', 'value': 11}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 3600.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.finished', 'value': 6250}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 3600.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.wait_mean', 'value': 1.3816663590146558}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 3600.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.wait_max', 'value': 9.378296391499589}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 3600.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.service_mean', 'value': 1.4953759999999972}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 3600.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.service_max', 'value': 2.7000000000000455}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 3600.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.flows.orders.finished', 'value': 6250}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 3600.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.flows.orders.started', 'value': 6261}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 3600.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.flows.orders.in_system', 'value': 11}

tasks.pack_order.finished counts the orders the task finished, and flows.orders.finished counts the orders that left the shop, named by the arrival that started them; with one task the two are equal. flows.orders.started counts the orders that entered, 6,261, and flows.orders.in_system the 11 still in the shop when the hour ended, which tasks.pack_order.in_progress also counts: the mean wait describes the orders that started packing, and End Conditions shows what a run leaves out when it ends. The mean wait is 1.38 seconds, not the 1.35 seconds of the empirical candidate in Choosing Inputs, although both use the same 40 measured packing times. The service is now called packing, so it draws from its own stream, service.packing, and the times come in another order; Randomness and Seeds explains why.

docs.title: Counts and Averages Over Time
docs.text:
The statistics are of two kinds. A count, such as finished, adds one for each order. An average over time, such as utilization_avg or queue_length_avg, weighs each value by how long it lasted. Look at the area under the number of busy packers:

desflow adds the area every time the value changes, so the average is exact at any moment. A reading taken now and then, such as every 10 seconds, sees only the value at that instant. The queue in the first five minutes of the hour shows the difference:

The queue rises and falls many times between two readings, and a handful of readings can land on high points by chance. Here they average 2.60 orders, while the queue held 2.19 orders on average over the same five minutes.

docs.title: Wait and Service
docs.text:
The time each order spends in the shop has two parts, both measured from the task's own events:

  • wait runs from queued to started: the time spent waiting for a packer;
  • service runs from started to the finished event: the time spent being packed.

service_mean is 1.50 seconds, the mean of the measured times, and service_max is 2.7 seconds, the longest of them, so the model draws what it was given. wait_max is 9.38 seconds: one order waited almost seven times as long as the average one.

docs.title: Result
docs.text: What does a run tell me? One hour of the busy shop tells you that the packers were busy 86.6% of the time on average, the queue held 2.41 orders on average, an order waited 1.38 seconds on average and 9.38 seconds at most, and 6,250 orders were packed.

docs.title: Why It Works
docs.text: The numbers check each other. Little's Law says that the average number waiting equals the rate at which orders arrive times the average time each waits. 6,250 orders in 3,600 seconds is 1.74 a second, and 1.74 × 1.38 = 2.40, which is queue_length_avg. The utilisation checks the same way: 1.74 orders a second × 1.50 seconds ÷ 3 packers = 0.87. A set of statistics that fails a check like this one points to a mistake in the model or in how it is read. Statistics describes how each one is computed, and the Statistics reference lists every name each level publishes.

        publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "started"})
        env.stats.task_started("pack_order", task_id)
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(env.registry.get_config(path_id)))
        publish({"event_type": "order_packed"})
    env.stats.task_finished("pack_order", task_id)
    env.stats.flow_finished("orders")  # the order leaves the shop


def order_generator(env, sampler, packers):
    arrival = env.registry.get_config("Shop.arrival.orders")
    task_id = 0
    while True:
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(arrival))
        env.stats.flow_started("orders")  # the order enters the shop
        env.process(pack_order(env, sampler, packers, f"orders-{task_id + 1}", task_id))
        task_id += 1


def run(until=3600, factor=0.0):
    env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=factor)
    env.registry.register_sim_parameter(PARAMS)
    env.setup_egress([ConsoleEgress()])
    # Counts, time averages, and the mean and maximum wait and service, every 10 s
    env.setup_stats("Shop", "typical", interval=10)
    packers = DynamicResource(env, "Shop", "packers")
    env.process(order_generator(env, Sampler(seed=42), packers))
    try:
        env.run(until=until)
    finally:
        env.teardown()
    return env


if __name__ == "__main__":
    env = run()
    # The statistics are telemetry, so the console printed them; read them here too
    for name, value in env.stats.readings().items():
        print(f"{name} = {value}")

Next, Trusting Results asks whether one run is enough.

docs.title: Parameter Sweeps
docs.text:
Level: Intermediate

Comparing Designs found that a fourth packer cuts the busy hour's mean wait from 2.48 to 0.27 seconds, at 1.8 orders a second. That rate is an estimate, and demand moves from day to day. This page asks: how much does the answer depend on the arrival rate? It runs both designs at four rates around the estimate.

docs.title: What You Add
docs.text: A sweep in the experiment: a registry path and the values it takes. The model and the two designs are those of Comparing Designs.

docs.title: Sweep One Input
docs.text:
A sweep runs every variant at every value of its paths. Here that is two variants at four rates, 8 designs, each run 20 times with the same 20 seeds:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/parameter_sweeps_experiment.yaml:sweep
variants:
  three: {}
  four: {Shop.resources.packers.current_cap: 4}
# Each variant at each rate: 8 designs, all run with the same 20 seeds
sweep:
  Shop.arrival.orders.rate: [1.6, 1.7, 1.8, 1.9]
docs/snippets/tutorials/parameter_sweeps.py:sweep
"variants": {"three": {}, "four": {"Shop.resources.packers.current_cap": 4}},
# Each variant at each rate: 8 designs, all run with the same 20 seeds
"sweep": {"Shop.arrival.orders.rate": [1.6, 1.7, 1.8, 1.9]},
docs/snippets/tutorials/parameter_sweeps_low_level.py:sweep
"variants": {"three": {}, "four": {"Shop.resources.packers.current_cap": 4}},
# Each variant at each rate: 8 designs, all run with the same 20 seeds
"sweep": {"Shop.arrival.orders.rate": [1.6, 1.7, 1.8, 1.9]},

Changing one input while every other stays as it is shows how sensitive the answer is to that input. This is one-factor sensitivity. A sweep with two paths runs every combination of their values, so its size is the product of the list lengths.

Run it with desflow experiment parameter_sweeps_experiment.yaml, or python parameter_sweeps.py and python parameter_sweeps_low_level.py. Each design's name is its variant followed by its swept value, such as three Shop.arrival.orders.rate=1.9, and results.csv and summary.csv have a column for the swept path. The mean wait of each design, with the 95% half-width:

Orders a second Three packers (s) Four packers (s) 1.6 0.97 ± 0.07 0.17 ± 0.01 1.7 1.47 ± 0.14 0.21 ± 0.01 1.8 2.48 ± 0.32 0.27 ± 0.01 1.9 5.55 ± 1.01 0.35 ± 0.02

docs.title: Result
docs.text: How much does the answer depend on the arrival rate? With three packers, a great deal: 1.9 orders a second, about 6% above the estimate, more than doubles the mean wait to 5.55 seconds, and 1.6 orders a second cuts it to 0.97. With four packers the mean wait stays under 0.35 seconds at every rate. So the decision to add a packer holds whatever the demand within this range, while the three-packer wait cannot be predicted well without a better estimate of the rate.

docs.title: Why It Works
docs.text: Three packers that take 1.5 seconds an order on average pack 2 orders a second at most. At 1.9 orders a second they are busy 95% of the time, and close to that limit a small rise in demand makes the queue much longer, so the wait grows faster than the rate. Four packers stay below 72% busy at every rate in the sweep, far from their limit. Every design ran with the same seeds, so the differences between rows come from the rate, not from chance. The intervals widen with the rate, because a busier shop varies more from run to run.

docs.title: Patience
docs.text:
Level: Intermediate

The shop now takes 0.7 orders a second, and its one packer packs one every 1.5 seconds, so orders arrive faster than they can be packed. A real customer does not wait for ever: one whose order has not started within 30 seconds cancels it. And the courier leaves at the hour, so the shop takes no new orders in the last five minutes. This page asks: which orders leave or refuse to join, and what does that do to the wait of the others? It measures the hour with a patience of 30 seconds and without one.

docs.title: What You Add
docs.text: A patience and a balk condition on the packing task. The shop is the one from First Simulation: one packer and 1.5 seconds of packing, run for an hour, with orders at 0.7 a second.

docs.title: Leave After a Wait
docs.text:
An entity that leaves a queue after waiting too long reneges. In SimPy it waits for whichever comes first, the unit or a timeout, with the | of two events (an AnyOf), then checks which one happened. In desflow it is the task's patience: how long the task may wait, for its wait, then its resource and then its get from a store or container, before it leaves the queue and publishes reneged. It counts waiting time only and pauses while the task is served, as SimPy's pattern does when a preempted process waits again with the patience it has left:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/patience.yaml:patience
# A customer cancels an order not started within 30 seconds
patience: ${PATIENCE:-30 s}

${PATIENCE:-30 s} reads the environment variable PATIENCE, 30 seconds when it is not set, so PATIENCE="1 h" desflow run patience.yaml runs the hour with no limit that matters. patience takes seconds, a duration, or an expression such as attr.patience, so each order can bring its own.

docs/snippets/tutorials/patience.py:patience
# A customer cancels an order not started within 30 seconds
patience=patience,

patience is 30 here, in seconds; it also takes a duration, as in YAML: patience="30 s". A distribution's parameters in the builder take seconds only.

docs/snippets/tutorials/patience_low_level.py:patience
# A customer cancels an order not started within 30 seconds
yield request | env.timeout(patience)
if not request.triggered:
    # Leaving the with block takes the request out of the queue
    publish("reneged")
    env.stats.task_reneged("pack_order", task_id)
    return

request | env.timeout(patience) is SimPy's AnyOf: it happens when either event does. request.triggered is true once the unit is granted. Leaving the with block takes a waiting request out of the queue at once, so the packer is never granted to an order that has gone. SimPy and desflow describes events and conditions.

A reneged order publishes reneged in place of started and its finished event, and adds nothing to the wait statistics, because it was never served.

A grant and a patience can fall at the same instant: the packer finishes the previous order at exactly the moment the next order's 30 seconds run out. desflow then does what plain SimPy does, which depends on which of the two events was scheduled first; the Reneging and Balking guide shows both cases.

docs.title: Refuse to Join
docs.text:
An entity that does not join a queue at all balks. In SimPy it is an if before the request. In desflow it is the task's balk, a condition checked before the task joins the queue; when it holds, the task publishes balked and never asks for the resource. Here t, the simulation time, stops new orders in the last five minutes:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/patience.yaml:balk
# The courier leaves at the hour, so the last 5 minutes take no new orders
balk: t >= 3300
docs/snippets/tutorials/patience.py:balk
# The courier leaves at the hour, so the last 5 minutes take no new orders
balk="t >= 3300",
docs/snippets/tutorials/patience_low_level.py:balk
# The courier leaves at the hour, so the last 5 minutes take no new orders
if env.now >= 3300:
    publish("balked")
    env.stats.task_balked("pack_order", task_id)
    return

The condition reads the names every expression reads, such as attr.<name> for the order's own attributes and level.<name> for a store or container; Task Flow lists them.

docs.title: Count Who Left
docs.text:
With statistics at basic and above, each task publishes how many instances reneged and balked, as Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.reneged and .balked, once the first one happens. typical adds the mean and longest wait of the orders that were served:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/patience.yaml:watch
# Counts of finished, reneged and balked orders, and the mean wait, at the end
stats: {level: typical, interval: 1 h}
docs/snippets/tutorials/patience.py:watch
# Counts of finished, reneged and balked orders, and the mean wait, at the end
.with_stats("typical", interval=3600)
docs/snippets/tutorials/patience_low_level.py:watch
# Counts of finished, reneged and balked orders, and the mean wait, at the end
env.setup_stats("Shop", "typical", interval=3600)

A low-level process counts its own outcomes with env.stats.task_reneged(task, instance) and env.stats.task_balked(task, instance), as the full file below does.

docs.title: Result
docs.text:
Which orders leave or refuse to join, and what does that do to the others? With a patience of 30 seconds, 69 orders leave the queue during the hour, and the mean wait of the packed orders falls from 72.16 seconds to 14.57 seconds; no packed order waits more than 30 seconds. In both runs the 194 orders that arrive in the last five minutes refuse to join. The wait of each packed order over the hour shows why:

The Builder and Low-level scripts print both runs:

patience 30 s: 2173 packed, 69 reneged, 194 balked, mean wait 14.57 s
patience none: 2242 packed, 0 reneged, 194 balked, mean wait 72.16 s

docs.title: Why It Works
docs.text: Orders arrive at 0.7 a second and bring 1.05 seconds of packing each second, more than one packer can do, so without patience the queue grows and every order waits longer than the one before. Patience removes the orders that have waited longest, which keeps the queue short for the rest: the shop packs 69 fewer orders, and every order it packs waits less. The mean wait of packed orders is then no longer the whole story, because it leaves out the orders that left; report the reneged and balked counts beside it. Statistics describes what each count measures.

docs/snippets/tutorials/patience.py
"""The Patience tutorial: orders leave after waiting too long, and none join near closing.

One packer, 0.7 orders a second and 1.5 seconds of packing. Every record is printed
to the terminal, and the script prints what happened to the orders with a patience
of 30 seconds and with none at the end: python patience.py 2>/dev/null shows only
those lines.
"""

import logging

from desflow import ConsoleEgress, SimulationContext

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
)


def shop(patience: float = 30) -> SimulationContext:
    """The shop, where a customer waits at most `patience` seconds."""
    app = (
        SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0, random_seed=42)
        .add_resource("packers", current_cap=1, max_cap=4)
        .add_service("packing", dist="constant", value=1.5)
        # 0.7 orders a second: more than one packer can pack
        .add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=0.7)
        # Counts of finished, reneged and balked orders, and the mean wait, at the end
        .with_stats("typical", interval=3600)
        .add_egress(ConsoleEgress())
    )

    @app.task(
        service_id="packing",
        resource_id="packers",
        # A customer cancels an order not started within 30 seconds
        patience=patience,
        # The courier leaves at the hour, so the last 5 minutes take no new orders
        balk="t >= 3300",
    )
    def pack_order(task_id: int):
        return {"event_type": "order_packed"}


    @app.arrival_loop("orders")
    def order_generator(context: SimulationContext):
        task_id = 0
        while True:
            order = yield context.wait_for_arrival("orders")
            context.spawn(pack_order(task_id, entity=order))
            task_id += 1

    return app


def outcomes(patience: float) -> dict:
    """Runs one hour and returns what happened to the orders, and the mean wait."""
    app = shop(patience)
    app.run(until="1 h")
    readings = app.env.stats.readings()
    name = "Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.{}".format
    return {
        outcome: readings.get(name(outcome), 0)
        for outcome in ("finished", "reneged", "balked", "wait_mean")
    }


if __name__ == "__main__":
    for patience, label in ((30, "30 s"), (3600, "none")):
        result = outcomes(patience)
        print(
            f"patience {label:>4}: {result['finished']} packed, "
            f"{result['reneged']} reneged, {result['balked']} balked, "
            f"mean wait {result['wait_mean']:5.2f} s"
        )
docs/snippets/tutorials/patience_low_level.py
"""The Patience tutorial: orders leave after waiting too long, and none join near closing.

One packer, 0.7 orders a second and 1.5 seconds of packing. Every record is printed
to the terminal, and the script prints what happened to the orders with a patience
of 30 seconds and with none at the end: python patience_low_level.py 2>/dev/null
shows only those lines.
"""

import logging

from desflow import (
    CapacityConfig,
    ConsoleEgress,
    DistributionConfig,
    DynamicRealtimeEnvironment,
    DynamicResource,
    Sampler,
    SimParameter,
)

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
)

PARAMS = SimParameter(
    sim_id="Shop",
    # 0.7 orders a second: more than one packer can pack
    arrival={"orders": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=0.7)},
    service={"packing": DistributionConfig(dist="constant", value=1.5)},
    resources={"packers": CapacityConfig(current_cap=1, max_cap=4)},
)


def pack_order(env, sampler, packers, key, task_id, patience):
    path_id = "Shop.service.packing"

    def publish(status):
        value = {"path_id": path_id, "status": status}
        env.publish_event(key, value, task="pack_order", instance=task_id)

    # The courier leaves at the hour, so the last 5 minutes take no new orders
    if env.now >= 3300:
        publish("balked")
        env.stats.task_balked("pack_order", task_id)
        return
    publish("queued")
    env.stats.task_queued("pack_order", task_id)
    with packers.request() as request:
        # A customer cancels an order not started within 30 seconds
        yield request | env.timeout(patience)
        if not request.triggered:
            # Leaving the with block takes the request out of the queue
            publish("reneged")
            env.stats.task_reneged("pack_order", task_id)
            return
        publish("started")
        env.stats.task_started("pack_order", task_id)
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(env.registry.get_config(path_id)))
        value = {"event_type": "order_packed"}
        env.publish_event(key, value, task="pack_order", instance=task_id)
    env.stats.task_finished("pack_order", task_id)


def order_generator(env, sampler, packers, patience):
    arrival = env.registry.get_config("Shop.arrival.orders")
    task_id = 0
    while True:
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(arrival))
        key = f"orders-{task_id + 1}"
        env.process(pack_order(env, sampler, packers, key, task_id, patience))
        task_id += 1


def run(patience=30, until=3600, factor=0.0):
    env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=factor)
    env.registry.register_sim_parameter(PARAMS)
    env.setup_egress([ConsoleEgress()])
    # Counts of finished, reneged and balked orders, and the mean wait, at the end
    env.setup_stats("Shop", "typical", interval=3600)
    packers = DynamicResource(env, "Shop", "packers")
    sampler = Sampler(seed=42)
    env.process(order_generator(env, sampler, packers, patience))
    try:
        env.run(until=until)
    finally:
        env.teardown()
    return env


def outcomes(patience: float) -> dict:
    """Runs one hour and returns what happened to the orders, and the mean wait."""
    readings = run(patience).stats.readings()
    name = "Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.{}".format
    return {
        outcome: readings.get(name(outcome), 0)
        for outcome in ("finished", "reneged", "balked", "wait_mean")
    }


if __name__ == "__main__":
    for patience, label in ((30, "30 s"), (3600, "none")):
        result = outcomes(patience)
        print(
            f"patience {label:>4}: {result['finished']} packed, "
            f"{result['reneged']} reneged, {result['balked']} balked, "
            f"mean wait {result['wait_mean']:5.2f} s"
        )

Reneging and Balking shows the same two decisions in a shop example, with ties and how to check that every order is accounted for. Next, Interruptions asks what remains of an order's packing when an express order takes its packer.

docs.title: Priorities
docs.text:
Level: Intermediate

A quarter of the shop's orders are now express: the customer paid for speed. With one packer and 0.6 orders a second, every order waits about 5 seconds. This page asks: can express orders jump the queue? And what does that cost the others?

docs.title: What You Add
docs.text: An express arrival whose task has priority: 0, while regular orders keep priority: 1, and a packer that serves its queue by priority. The shop is the one from First Simulation, one packer and 1.5 seconds of packing, with regular orders at 0.45 a second and express orders at 0.15, run for an hour.

docs.title: Order the Queue
docs.text:
Which waiting entity a resource serves next is its queue discipline. The usual one is first in, first out (FIFO); others are last in, first out (LIFO), and by priority. Look at four requests that join a queue while the packer is busy, and the order each discipline serves them in:

SimPy has a PriorityResource for the priority discipline, and a PriorityStore for items. In desflow every resource has a queue: fifo (the default), lifo or priority. Under priority the lowest number goes first, and requests with the same priority are served first in, first out:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/priorities.yaml:queue
resources:
  # The packer serves the lowest priority first, the oldest first among equals
  packers: {current_cap: 1, max_cap: 4, queue: priority}
docs/snippets/tutorials/priorities.py:queue
# The packer serves the lowest priority first, the oldest first among equals
app.add_resource("packers", current_cap=1, max_cap=4, queue=queue)
docs/snippets/tutorials/priorities_low_level.py:queue
# The packer serves the lowest priority first, the oldest first among equals
packers = DynamicResource(env, "Shop", "packers", queue=queue)

docs.title: Give Express Orders Priority
docs.text:
Each task gives its requests a priority. Express orders get 0, so they are served before any regular order that is waiting; regular orders get 1:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/priorities.yaml:priority
tasks:
  pack_order:
    service: packing
    resource: packers
    priority: 1
    payload: {event_type: order_packed}
  pack_express:
    service: packing
    resource: packers
    priority: 0  # served before any regular order that is waiting
    payload: {event_type: express_packed}

Here each task has a fixed number. A priority can also be an expression read from the entity's attributes, which Task Flow describes, such as priority: attr.priority, so each order gets its own. A priority on a task whose resource does not have queue: priority is refused when the file loads, so to run the shop under fifo, remove queue: priority and both priority lines.

docs/snippets/tutorials/priorities.py:priority
@app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="packers", priority=rank(1))
def pack_order(task_id: int):
    return {"event_type": "order_packed"}

# Served before any regular order that is waiting
@app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="packers", priority=rank(0))
def pack_express(task_id: int):
    return {"event_type": "express_packed"}

rank gives each task its priority under priority and none under fifo, because a priority on a resource of another order is refused when the run starts. A task's priority can also be an expression such as priority="attr.tier", or a function of the task id and the entity's attributes, such as priority=lambda task_id, attributes: attributes["tier"], so each order gets its own; the attributes exist before the order joins the queue, while its payload does not.

docs/snippets/tutorials/priorities_low_level.py:priority
# Express orders are served before any regular order that is waiting
TASKS = {"orders": ("pack_order", 1), "express": ("pack_express", 0)}
docs/snippets/tutorials/priorities_low_level.py:request
# Under fifo and lifo the priority is ignored
with packers.request(priority=priority) as request:

In the low-level API each request carries its priority. A resource whose queue is fifo or lifo ignores it, which is how the same code runs under both orders.

Both kinds of order use the same packer, so they share one queue. The built-in statistics, which Statistics describes, keep the mean wait of each task apart: Shop.stats.tasks.pack_express.wait_mean and Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.wait_mean.

docs.title: Starvation
docs.text: Priority has a price. A regular order is served only when no express order is waiting, so every express order that arrives while it waits pushes it back. As the shop gets busier this grows quickly: with a quarter of orders express, the regular wait is 2.50 seconds at 0.5 orders a second in all, 3.98 at 0.55 and 6.94 at 0.6, while express orders wait less than a second at all three. If express orders alone kept the packer busy, regular orders would never be served at all: they would starve.

docs.title: Result
docs.text:
Can express orders jump the queue? Yes, and the regular orders pay for it. The scripts print the mean wait of each kind of order under each queue order:

fifo     pack_express mean wait  5.84 s
fifo     pack_order   mean wait  5.32 s
priority pack_express mean wait  0.84 s
priority pack_order   mean wait  6.94 s

Under priority, express orders wait 0.84 seconds on average instead of 5.84. Regular orders pay for it: 6.94 seconds instead of 5.32.

docs.title: Why It Works
docs.text: Priority does not make the packer faster, so it cannot remove waiting; it only decides who waits. Weighted by how many orders of each kind arrive, the mean wait is 0.75 × 5.32 + 0.25 × 5.84 = 5.45 seconds under fifo and 0.75 × 6.94 + 0.25 × 0.84 = 5.41 seconds under priority: almost the same total, shared out differently. Resources describes how the queue orders requests. The same queue in plain SimPy, a PriorityResource, serves these requests in the same order, ties included, and the tests check it in all three ways of writing (SimPy Compatibility). Items can be ranked too: a priority store returns the parcel with the lowest priority first, which Stores and Containers describes; a resource's priority decides who is served, a store's decides which item is taken.

"""The Priorities tutorial: express orders go before regular ones, builder.

One packer, regular orders at 0.45 a second and express orders at 0.15, and 1.5
seconds of packing. Every record is printed to the terminal, and the script prints
the mean wait of each kind of order under each queue order at the end:
python priorities.py 2>/dev/null shows only those lines.
"""

import logging

from desflow import ConsoleEgress, SimulationContext

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
)


def shop(queue: str = "priority") -> SimulationContext:
    """The shop with the packer's queue in `queue` order."""

    def rank(value):
        # A priority counts only under the priority order, and the other orders
        # refuse one, so under fifo the tasks have none
        return value if queue == "priority" else None

    app = (
        SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0, random_seed=42)
        .add_service("packing", dist="constant", value=1.5)
        # 0.6 orders a second in all, one in four of them express
        .add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=0.45)
        .add_arrival("express", dist="exponential", rate=0.15)
        .with_stats("typical", interval=3600)  # the mean wait of each task
        .add_egress(ConsoleEgress())
    )
    # The packer serves the lowest priority first, the oldest first among equals
    app.add_resource("packers", current_cap=1, max_cap=4, queue=queue)

    @app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="packers", priority=rank(1))
    def pack_order(task_id: int):
        return {"event_type": "order_packed"}

    # Served before any regular order that is waiting
    @app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="packers", priority=rank(0))
    def pack_express(task_id: int):
        return {"event_type": "express_packed"}


    def loop(arrival, task):
        def generator(context: SimulationContext):
            task_id = 0
            while True:
                order = yield context.wait_for_arrival(arrival)
                context.spawn(task(task_id, entity=order))
                task_id += 1

        return generator

    app.arrival_loop("orders")(loop("orders", pack_order))
    app.arrival_loop("express")(loop("express", pack_express))
    return app


def mean_waits(queue: str) -> dict:
    """Runs one hour and returns the mean wait of each task."""
    app = shop(queue)
    app.run(until="1 h")
    readings = app.env.stats.readings()
    return {
        task: readings[f"Shop.stats.tasks.{task}.wait_mean"]
        for task in ("pack_express", "pack_order")
    }


if __name__ == "__main__":
    for queue in ("fifo", "priority"):
        for task, wait in mean_waits(queue).items():
            print(f"{queue:<8} {task:<12} mean wait {wait:5.2f} s")
docs/snippets/tutorials/priorities_low_level.py
"""The Priorities tutorial: express orders go before regular ones, low-level.

One packer, regular orders at 0.45 a second and express orders at 0.15, and 1.5
seconds of packing. Every record is printed to the terminal, and the script prints
the mean wait of each kind of order under each queue order at the end:
python priorities_low_level.py 2>/dev/null shows only those lines.
"""

import logging

from desflow import (
    CapacityConfig,
    ConsoleEgress,
    DistributionConfig,
    DynamicRealtimeEnvironment,
    DynamicResource,
    Sampler,
    SimParameter,
)

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
)

PARAMS = SimParameter(
    sim_id="Shop",
    arrival={
        # 0.6 orders a second in all, one in four of them express
        "orders": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=0.45),
        "express": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=0.15),
    },
    service={"packing": DistributionConfig(dist="constant", value=1.5)},
    resources={"packers": CapacityConfig(current_cap=1, max_cap=4)},
)
# Express orders are served before any regular order that is waiting
TASKS = {"orders": ("pack_order", 1), "express": ("pack_express", 0)}


def pack(env, sampler, packers, arrival, key, task_id):
    task, priority = TASKS[arrival]
    path_id = "Shop.service.packing"

    def publish(value):
        env.publish_event(key, value, task=task, instance=task_id)

    publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "queued"})
    env.stats.task_queued(task, task_id)
    # Under fifo and lifo the priority is ignored
    with packers.request(priority=priority) as request:
        yield request
        publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "started"})
        env.stats.task_started(task, task_id)
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(env.registry.get_config(path_id)))
        event = "express_packed" if arrival == "express" else "order_packed"
        publish({"event_type": event})
    env.stats.task_finished(task, task_id)


def order_generator(env, sampler, packers, arrival):
    config = env.registry.get_config(f"Shop.arrival.{arrival}")
    task_id = 0
    while True:
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(config))
        key = f"{arrival}-{task_id + 1}"
        env.process(pack(env, sampler, packers, arrival, key, task_id))
        task_id += 1


def run(queue="priority", until=3600, factor=0.0):
    env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=factor)
    env.registry.register_sim_parameter(PARAMS)
    env.setup_egress([ConsoleEgress()])
    env.setup_stats("Shop", "typical", interval=3600)  # the mean wait of each task
    # The packer serves the lowest priority first, the oldest first among equals
    packers = DynamicResource(env, "Shop", "packers", queue=queue)
    sampler = Sampler(seed=42)
    env.process(order_generator(env, sampler, packers, "orders"))
    env.process(order_generator(env, sampler, packers, "express"))
    try:
        env.run(until=until)
    finally:
        env.teardown()
    return env


def mean_waits(queue: str) -> dict:
    """Runs one hour and returns the mean wait of each task."""
    readings = run(queue).stats.readings()
    return {
        task: readings[f"Shop.stats.tasks.{task}.wait_mean"]
        for task in ("pack_express", "pack_order")
    }


if __name__ == "__main__":
    for queue in ("fifo", "priority"):
        for task, wait in mean_waits(queue).items():
            print(f"{queue:<8} {task:<12} mean wait {wait:5.2f} s")

docs.title: Process Interaction
docs.text:
Level: Intermediate

Packed orders now wait for a courier, who comes every 10 minutes and takes every order that is waiting. An order that waits too long goes by post instead, which costs more and takes longer. This page asks: when does a waiting order resume, and how long must it be allowed to wait so that most orders go by courier? It compares limits of 5 and 8 minutes over an 8-hour day.

docs.title: What You Add
docs.text: A signal, courier_left, that the courier fires as it leaves, and a dispatch task that waits for either the signal or its limit, whichever comes first. The shop is the one from First Simulation: one packer, an order every 2 seconds on average and 1.5 seconds of packing.

docs.title: A Signal
docs.text:
So far a process has waited for time, a resource or an item. Processes can also wait for each other. In SimPy one process yields an event, and another succeeds it; every process waiting for the event resumes. desflow gives such an event a name, a signal: declared once, fired by a task when it finishes, and fired again later, each firing waking every waiter that waits at that moment:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/process_interaction.yaml:signal
signals:
  # Fired by the courier as it leaves with every order that waits for it
  - courier_left
docs/snippets/tutorials/process_interaction.py:signal
# Fired by the courier as it leaves with every order that waits for it
app.add_signal("courier_left")
docs/snippets/tutorials/process_interaction_low_level.py:signal
# Fired by the courier as it leaves with every order that waits for it
"courier_left": Signal(env, "courier_left"),

Signal holds one pending SimPy Event. wait() returns it, and fire(value) succeeds it and puts a fresh one in its place, so a process that starts waiting after a firing waits for the next one. SimPy and desflow describes events.

The courier arrives every 10 minutes, and its task fires the signal with its payload:

couriers: {dist: constant, value: 10 min, spawn: collect}
docs/snippets/yaml/process_interaction.yaml:collect
collect:
  payload: {event_type: courier_left}
  # Fires courier_left with this payload, so every waiting order resumes
  signal: courier_left

# A courier every 10 minutes
.add_arrival("couriers", dist="constant", value=600)

@app.task(signal="courier_left")
def collect(task_id: int):
    return {"event_type": "courier_left"}

# A courier every 10 minutes
"couriers": DistributionConfig(dist="constant", value=600),
docs/snippets/tutorials/process_interaction_low_level.py:collect
def collect(env, shop, key, ids):
    """Fires courier_left with the payload, so every waiting order resumes."""
    task_id = next(ids["collect"])
    payload = {"event_type": "courier_left"}
    publish(env, key, "collect", task_id, payload)
    env.stats.task_finished("collect", task_id)
    shop["courier_left"].fire(payload)
    env.stats.flow_finished("couriers")
    yield env.timeout(0)

docs.title: Wait for the First of Two
docs.text:
A packed order waits for the courier or for its limit. SimPy waits for the first of several events with a | b, an AnyOf; desflow's wait takes the same with any and a name for each branch. After the wait, wait.<branch>.done says whether that branch happened, so next can route on it:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/process_interaction.yaml:dispatch
dispatch:
  # The courier's departure, or the limit, whichever comes first
  wait:
    any:
      courier: {signal: courier_left}
      limit: {timeout: "${LIMIT:-5 min}"}
  payload: {event_type: dispatched}
  # wait.courier.done is true when the courier came before the limit
  next:
    when: [{condition: wait.courier.done, task: by_courier}]
    default: by_post

"${LIMIT:-5 min}" reads the environment variable LIMIT, 5 minutes when it is not set, so LIMIT="8 min" desflow run process_interaction.yaml runs the longer limit.

docs/snippets/tutorials/process_interaction.py:dispatch
@app.task(
    # The courier's departure, or the limit, whichever comes first
    wait={
        "any": {"courier": {"signal": "courier_left"}, "limit": {"timeout": limit}}
    },
    # wait.courier.done is true when the courier came before the limit
    next={
        "when": [{"condition": "wait.courier.done", "task": "by_courier"}],
        "default": "by_post",
    },
)
def dispatch(task_id: int):
    return {"event_type": "dispatched"}
docs/snippets/tutorials/process_interaction_low_level.py:dispatch
def dispatch(env, shop, key, ids):
    task_id = next(ids["dispatch"])
    publish(env, key, "dispatch", task_id, {"status": "queued"})
    env.stats.task_queued("dispatch", task_id)
    # The courier's departure, or the limit, whichever comes first
    courier = shop["courier_left"].wait()
    done = yield env.any_of([courier, env.timeout(shop["limit"])])
    publish(env, key, "dispatch", task_id, {"status": "started"})
    env.stats.task_started("dispatch", task_id)
    publish(env, key, "dispatch", task_id, {"event_type": "dispatched"})
    env.stats.task_finished("dispatch", task_id)
    # The courier came before the limit when its event is in the AnyOf's value
    task = "by_courier" if courier in done else "by_post"
    env.process(send(env, key, task, ids))

env.any_of([...]) is the AnyOf; its value holds the events that happened, so courier in done is the YAML's wait.courier.done.

The task publishes queued when it starts waiting and started when the wait ends, so its wait statistics measure the time waiting for the courier:

docs.title: Result
docs.text:
When does a waiting order resume? When the courier leaves, if that is within its limit, and at the limit otherwise. With a limit of 5 minutes, 6,952 orders go by courier and 7,020 by post; with a limit of 8 minutes, 11,005 go by courier and 2,872 by post, and the mean wait for dispatch rises from 225.3 to 288.2 seconds:

The Builder and Low-level scripts print both runs:

limit 5 min: 6952 by courier, 7020 by post, mean wait  225.3 s
limit 8 min: 11005 by courier, 2872 by post, mean wait  288.2 s

docs.title: Why It Works
docs.text: Orders are packed at random moments, so the time from packing to the next courier is spread evenly over the 10 minutes between couriers. A limit of 5 minutes catches the courier for half the orders, and a limit of 8 minutes for 8 in 10, which is what the runs show. Every waiting order resumes at the same firing, which is why the courier takes them all at once. Tasks and Processes describes every kind of wait, and Wait for One or All shows ties and failures.
