docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
Data first. The values are read, missing ones counted and left out, and invalid ones refused or, with --drop-invalid, counted and left out. They are converted to seconds. Then each family is checked against the data before it is fitted: enough values, positive values where the family needs them, and not a constant column.

Maximum likelihood, location at 0. desflow's families have no location parameter: a gamma or a Weibull starts at 0. scipy can fit a location too, which moves the start of the distribution to wherever the data suggests: for the 40 packing times plus one outlier of 120 seconds, a free location puts a gamma's start at 0.70 seconds, the smallest value, with a shape of 0.21 and a scale of 81, which desflow cannot use. So the location of exponential, gamma, weibull and lognormal is fixed at 0, and each fit is converted to desflow's parameters:

Family Fitted with desflow's parameters exponential scipy.stats.expon.fit(x, floc=0) rate = 1 ÷ scale normal scipy.stats.norm.fit(x) mean, std lognormal scipy.stats.lognorm.fit(x, floc=0) the variable's mean = scale × e^(s²/2) and std = mean × √(e^(s²) − 1) truncated_normal the likelihood of scipy.stats.truncnorm with low fixed, maximised by scipy.optimize.minimize mean, std, low uniform scipy.stats.uniform.fit(x) low, high triangular scipy.stats.triang.fit(x) low, mode, high gamma scipy.stats.gamma.fit(x, floc=0) shape, scale weibull scipy.stats.weibull_min.fit(x, floc=0) shape, scale constant every value is the same value empirical the values, or numpy.histogram with --bins values, or edges and counts

Each fit runs on its own, so one that fails is a row, not a crash.

Checks. Every fitted result is checked before it can be chosen: each parameter must be finite and within the family's rules, the same rules a blueprint's distribution is checked against, and the family's mean and standard deviation, from desflow's own formulas, must be within --tolerance of the data's. A result that fails is rejected with the reason. Some bad fits pass these checks: the three values 1.0, 1.0000001 and 1.0000002 fitted to a gamma give a shape of 1.4 × 10¹⁴ and a scale of 7.1 × 10⁻¹⁵, with the right mean and spread, which is why --min-count exists.

Diagnostics. For each fitted family: the log-likelihood of the data, AIC computed as 2k − 2 × log-likelihood, where k counts the fitted parameters (a fixed location does not count), and the Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic and p-value from scipy.stats.kstest. The p-value assumes the parameters were known in advance; they were estimated from the same data, so it is approximate and tends to be too high. empirical has no AIC.

Plot. The generated values are drawn through desflow's Sampler, seeded, with the same smallest delay a run applies, so the plot shows what a run draws and repeats exactly.

docs.title: Stability and Limits
docs.text:
• Size of the extra. Measured in new Python 3.12 environments on macOS, scipy 1.18.1 takes about 70 MB installed with uv and about 100 MB with pip, which also compiles bytecode, and 20 to 37 MB to download, depending on the platform. matplotlib and its dependencies, beyond the NumPy desflow already needs, add about 55 MB with uv and about 70 MB with pip. That is why fitting is not in the base install.
  • Local files only. The command reads a CSV file. Reading from a database or an object store, and automated selection beyond the lowest AIC, come later.
  • A fit is not a validation. A family that fits the data well can still change the model's answer, and a model whose inputs fit can still answer the question badly. Compare the model's output with the real system's, as Experiments does.
  • One column at a time. Each column is fitted on its own, so a dependence between two inputs, such as larger orders taking longer to pack, is not captured.

docs.title: Live Parameters: SimulationRegistry
docs.text: Every parameter of a run can change while the run goes on: an arrival rate, a number of packers, a stock level. This page shows how to name a parameter, the ways to change it, how to record what a change was for, and what happens to a value once it arrives.

docs.title: What It Is
docs.text: Every run has one SimulationRegistry, at env.registry. It maps dot-notation paths, such as Shop.resources.packers.current_cap, to the values the simulation reads. A scenario, an ingress connector or a process changes a parameter by updating its path, and the simulation follows the change without restarting. Changing a parameter takes three steps:

docs.title: Find the Path
docs.text:
A path is the sim_id, the kind of parameter, its name and the field:

Declared with Paths an arrival or a service <sim_id>.arrival.<name>.<parameter> and <sim_id>.service.<name>.<parameter>, one per scalar parameter of its family: .rate for an exponential, .mean and .std for a normal, .low, .mode and .high for a triangular, and so on; an empirical has none a resource <sim_id>.resources.<name>.current_cap and .max_cap a container <sim_id>.containers.<name>.current_cap, .max_cap and .level a store <sim_id>.stores.<name>.current_cap and .max_cap a variable <sim_id>.variables.<name>

Arrivals and Services lists each family's parameters. An update to a path that does not exist, including a parameter the family does not take, is logged as a warning and ignored, so a misspelt path changes nothing. compile_parameters() returns the SimParameter a SimulationContext will register, which shows the names to use:

docs/snippets/pages/live_parameters.py:compile
print(app.compile_parameters())

In the low-level API you register the parameters yourself, and read a value with registry.get(path).value:

docs/snippets/pages/registry.py:paths
params = SimParameter(
    sim_id="Shop",
    arrival={"orders": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=0.5)},
    service={"packing": DistributionConfig(dist="normal", mean=3.0, std=0.5)},
    resources={"packers": CapacityConfig(current_cap=2, max_cap=5)},
    containers={"stock": ContainerConfig(current_cap=100, max_cap=100, level=40)},
    variables={"conveyor_speed": 1.5},
)
env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=0.0)
env.registry.register_sim_parameter(params)
# Registered paths include:
#   Shop.arrival.orders.rate
#   Shop.service.packing.mean, Shop.service.packing.std
#   Shop.resources.packers.current_cap, Shop.resources.packers.max_cap
#   Shop.containers.stock.current_cap, .max_cap and .level
#   Shop.variables.conveyor_speed
print(env.registry.get("Shop.resources.packers.current_cap").value)  # 2

docs.title: Send a Value
docs.text:
Each source of a change suits a different job and lands at a different moment:

Source Use it for Lands at a scenario: YAML scenario, builder add_scenario, low-level run_scenario an experiment that must repeat exactly the exact simulation time given LocalIngress a local run with changes after set wall-clock delays a wall-clock delay from the start KafkaIngress, RedisIngress, PostgresIngress an operator or another program steering a running model when the message arrives a process calling env.registry.update a change that depends on the state of the simulation when the process makes it

Ingress gives the message each connector reads. A process changes a value directly:

docs/snippets/pages/registry.py:update
env.registry.update("Shop.resources.packers.current_cap", 3)  # applied
env.registry.update("Shop.resources.packers.current_cap", 9)  # stored as 5, the max_cap
env.registry.update("Shop.service.packing.std", -1.0)  # refused, the old 0.5 stays
env.registry.update("Shop.resources.lath.current_cap", 3)  # no such path: ignored
env.registry.update("Shop.service.packing.rate", 2.0)  # normal has no rate: ignored
env.registry.update("Shop.containers.stock.level", 150)  # stored as 100, the capacity

docs.title: Script an Experiment
docs.text:
A blueprint's scenario lists changes, each with the simulation time it applies at. Here a second packer starts at 30 seconds, orders arrive twice as fast from one minute, and the extra packer leaves at two minutes:

docs/snippets/yaml/scenario.yaml
# The first blueprint with a scripted experiment: a second packer starts at 30 s,
# orders arrive twice as fast from 1 min, and the extra packer leaves at
# 2 min. Every change lands at exactly that simulation time, on every run.
simulation:
  sim_id: Shop
  factor: 0
  random_seed: 1

egress:
  - type: Console

resources:
  packers: {current_cap: 1, max_cap: 3}

services:
  packing: {dist: normal, mean: 4 s, std: 1 s}

arrivals:
  orders: {dist: exponential, rate: 0.2, spawn: pack_order}

tasks:
  pack_order:
    service: packing
    resource: packers
    payload: {event_type: order_packed}

# The packers' capacity and queue every 10 seconds, to see each change land
stats: minimal

scenario:
  - {at: 30, path: Shop.resources.packers.current_cap, value: 2}
  - {at: 1 min, path: Shop.arrival.orders.rate, value: 0.4}
  - {at: 2 min, path: Shop.resources.packers.current_cap, value: 1}

run:
  until: 3 min

The builder and the low-level API take the same steps, as a list of mappings. Here are the steps of the changing_demand example in each API:

YAMLBuilderLow-level examples/yaml/changing_demand.yaml:schedule
scenario:
  # The rush: twice the orders, and a second packer, from 120 to 180 seconds
  - {at: 120, path: Shop.arrival.orders.rate, value: 0.8}
  - {at: 120, path: Shop.resources.packers.current_cap, value: 2}
  - {at: 180, path: Shop.arrival.orders.rate, value: 0.4}
  - {at: 180, path: Shop.resources.packers.current_cap, value: 1}
examples/builder/changing_demand_example.py:schedule
# The rush: twice the orders, and a second packer, from 120 to 180 seconds
app.add_scenario(
    [
        {"at": 120, "path": "Shop.arrival.orders.rate", "value": 0.8},
        {"at": 120, "path": "Shop.resources.packers.current_cap", "value": 2},
        {"at": 180, "path": "Shop.arrival.orders.rate", "value": 0.4},
        {"at": 180, "path": "Shop.resources.packers.current_cap", "value": 1},
    ]
)

add_step(at, path=..., value=..., record=...) adds one step.

examples/low-level/changing_demand_example.py:schedule
# The rush: twice the orders, and a second packer, from 120 to 180 seconds
SCHEDULE = [
    {"at": 120, "path": "Shop.arrival.orders.rate", "value": 0.8},
    {"at": 120, "path": "Shop.resources.packers.current_cap", "value": 2},
    {"at": 180, "path": "Shop.arrival.orders.rate", "value": 0.4},
    {"at": 180, "path": "Shop.resources.packers.current_cap", "value": 1},
]

env.process(run_scenario(env, SCHEDULE, until=300)) applies them; until is the run's end, as a step there never applies.

A scenario is not a connector. It is a SimPy process that waits on the simulation clock, so each step lands at exactly its at, on every run and at any factor, including 0. A step applies before every other event at its time, so an arrival gap drawn at that moment uses the new value; steps at the same time apply in the order written, and a step at or after until never applies. Time-varying Arrivals shows each case. Every path of a blueprint's scenario is checked against the model's registry when the file loads, so a misspelt path stops the load with its line; the builder checks its paths when the run starts. LocalIngress waits on the wall clock instead, and an unknown path is only logged when it is due. A scenario and an ingress connector can run together, so a scripted baseline can run while an operator steers over Kafka; when both change the same path, the later write wins.

docs.title: Record What a Change Was For
docs.text:
A detector or an agent that watches the data is scored against what really happened. A scenario step with a record publishes a ground-truth record of it: stream_type: "label", with the step's path, the value before (old) and after (new), and the step's record mapping as label. A step can have a record and no path, for something that happened outside the model, and then path, old and new are null.

docs/snippets/yaml/ground_truth.yaml:record
scenario:
  # Changes the rate and publishes a ground-truth record of the change
  - at: 30
    path: Shop.arrival.orders.rate
    value: 1.5
    record: {fault: order_surge, cause: flash sale}
  # A record with no change, such as a fault planted outside the model
  - at: 45
    record: {fault: label_printer_offline}

Labels go only to sinks with when: labels, and those sinks receive nothing else, so the labels never reach the pipeline under test and a scorer reads them apart from the data:

docs/snippets/yaml/ground_truth.yaml:sinks
egress:
  # The data under test: events and telemetry, and no label
  - type: Console
  # The labels only, for a scorer that checks what a detector found
  - type: Jsonl
    config: {default_path: labels/labels.jsonl}
    when: labels

The labels sink writes one file per batch under labels/, such as labels/labels_1a2b3c4d.jsonl, with one line per label:

{"stream_type":"label","sim_ts":30.0,"timestamp":"...","path":"Shop.arrival.orders.rate","old":0.5,"new":1.5,"label":{"fault":"order_surge","cause":"flash sale"}}
{"stream_type":"label","sim_ts":45.0,"timestamp":"...","path":null,"old":null,"new":null,"label":{"fault":"label_printer_offline"}}

In Python, env.publish_label(label, path=..., old=..., new=...) publishes one, and add_egress(sink, when="labels") or setup_egress(..., labels=[...]) makes a labels sink, as the measuring example shows.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
Registration. run(), or register_sim_parameter in the low-level API, flattens the SimParameter into the registry: one DynamicValue per path, holding the value and a change signal, and beside them the configuration objects the paths belong to, such as each DistributionConfig.

An update. registry.update(path, value) applies one change. The checks run in order, and an accepted value reaches the parts that read it:

  • A path that does not exist is logged as a warning, and the update is ignored.
  • A value of another type is converted to the type the path holds, so the string "5" sent to an integer path becomes 5; Python's conversion is used, so 2.5 sent to an integer path becomes 2. A value that cannot be converted is logged as an error and ignored.
  • A distribution parameter is checked on a copy of its configuration, by the rules used at build. One out of range is logged as an error, and the old value stays.
  • A current_cap outside 0 to max_cap, or a container level outside 0 to current_cap, is stored clamped to that range, with a warning. A lower max_cap clamps the stored current_cap the same way.
  • A value equal to the current one changes nothing.
  • Otherwise the value is stored, and the attribute of the configuration object is set too, found by splitting the path at its last dot: Shop.service.packing.mean sets mean on the object at Shop.service.packing. That is why the Sampler, which reads that object at every draw, sees the new value.

Change Signal. Each value has a SimPy Store with one slot as its signal. An update puts a token in it if it is empty, and wait_for_change() waits for that token, so several changes before a waiter wakes give one signal, and one waiting process takes it. Resources, stores and containers already wait on their own paths, so wait only on paths nothing else waits on, such as variables:

docs/snippets/pages/registry.py:wait
def watch_speed(env):
    """Logs the conveyor speed every time it changes."""
    speed = env.registry.get("Shop.variables.conveyor_speed")
    while True:
        yield speed.wait_for_change()
        print(f"t={env.now}: conveyor speed is now {speed.value}")


env.process(watch_speed(env))

A container's level changes with every put and get as well; the registry keeps that level so a reader sees it, without signalling the container again.

docs.title: Under Live Changes
docs.text:
What follows a change:

  • Distributions. The next draw uses the new value. The arrival already being waited for keeps its gap, and a task that has drawn its service time keeps it.
  • Resources, stores and containers. The capacity follows at once, and a container's level follows its path, as Resources and Stores and Containers describe.
  • Variables. The new value is stored; a process reads it with env.registry.get(path).value.

A change is easiest to see in the telemetry. With stats: minimal, the scenario above shows the second packer land:

[TEL] {'sim_ts': 20.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.resources.packers.capacity', 'value': 1}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 30.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.resources.packers.capacity', 'value': 1}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 40.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.resources.packers.capacity', 'value': 2}

The reading at 30 seconds still shows 1: the resource applies a change within the same simulation instant, but after the step that made it, and the reading was taken first. The builder publishes the same readings with with_stats:

docs/snippets/pages/live_parameters.py:telemetry
# The packers' capacity, in use, queue and utilization every 2 seconds
app.with_stats("minimal", interval=2.0)

docs.title: Stability and Limits
docs.text:
• An unknown path is a warning, not an error, for an ingress message or a process; only a scenario is checked when it loads.
  • A family is fixed. There is no path that turns a normal into an exponential; that is a new model.
  • Several changes, one signal. A process waiting on a path wakes once for several changes made before it runs, and reads the latest value.
  • Ingress lands on the wall clock. A message's change lands at whatever simulation time the run has reached when it arrives; a change that must happen at an exact simulation time is a scenario step.

docs.title: Low-level API
docs.text:
This page writes a simulation with SimPy and the environment directly: a packing team with a stock of boxes and a store of packed orders, every step written by hand. It builds on SimPy and desflow, which describes the SimPy constructs, and on Builder API, which writes the same kind of model for you.

Use the low-level API when you need what the builder does not do: resources created while the run goes on, as in Dynamic Topology, or events and interactions of your own shape. A builder or blueprint model can also start a low-level process with add_process, as Tasks and Processes shows.

A low-level script takes these steps, in this order:

docs.title: Create the Environment
docs.text:
docs/snippets/pages/low_level.py:imports
import logging

from desflow import (
    CapacityConfig,
    ConsoleEgress,
    ContainerConfig,
    DistributionConfig,
    DynamicContainer,
    DynamicRealtimeEnvironment,
    DynamicResource,
    DynamicStore,
    Sampler,
    SimParameter,
    time_to_seconds,
)
docs/snippets/pages/low_level.py:environment
env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=0.0)  # unpaced; 1.0 follows the wall clock

factor sets the pacing: 1.0 follows the wall clock, and 0.0 runs as fast as possible. logical_start_time and go_live_at work as Time and Pacing describes.

docs.title: Register the Parameters
docs.text:
docs/snippets/pages/low_level.py:parameters
env.registry.register_sim_parameter(
    SimParameter(
        sim_id="Shop",
        arrival={"orders": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=0.5)},
        service={"packing": DistributionConfig(dist="normal", mean=1.5, std=0.3)},
        resources={"packers": CapacityConfig(current_cap=1, max_cap=3)},
        containers={"boxes": ContainerConfig(current_cap=100, max_cap=100, level=100)},
        stores={"finished": CapacityConfig(current_cap=50, max_cap=50)},
        variables={"boxes_per_order": 1.0},
    )
)

One SimParameter holds every parameter of one simulation under its sim_id. Registering it gives each value a path, such as Shop.arrival.orders.rate, and only the registered paths exist. Live Parameters lists the paths.

docs.title: Attach the Connectors
docs.text:
docs/snippets/pages/low_level.py:connectors
env.setup_egress([ConsoleEgress()])  # starts the egress thread
# env.setup_ingress([KafkaIngress(...)]) would start the ingress thread
env.setup_stats("Shop", "basic", interval=60)  # readings and counts every minute

setup_egress starts the egress thread, which writes every record the processes publish. setup_ingress starts the ingress thread for parameter changes from outside, and setup_stats switches on the built-in statistics. Egress lists the arguments of setup_egress, including a warm-up and labels sinks.

docs.title: Create Resources, Containers and Stores
docs.text:
docs/snippets/pages/low_level.py:resources
packers = DynamicResource(env, "Shop", "packers")  # reads Shop.resources.packers.*
boxes = DynamicContainer(env, "Shop", "boxes")  # starts at its level, 100
finished = DynamicStore(env, "Shop", "finished")
sampler = Sampler(seed=42)  # a random stream per distribution, from one seed

Each reads its capacity from the registry when it is created, so the parameters must be registered first, and adds itself to the statistics. Sampler(seed=42) gives each registered distribution a random stream of its own, so a run repeats exactly, as Arrivals and Services describes.

docs.title: Write the Processes
docs.text:
A process is a SimPy generator: it yields to wait, and publishes records as it goes. This one does what @app.task does in the builder, with a box from stock and a store for the result. It publishes each event with the entity key, the task's name and its instance id, and reports each step to the statistics:

docs/snippets/pages/low_level.py:order
def order(env, key, task_id):
    """One order: queue for a packer, take a box, pack, then store the result."""
    path_id = "Shop.service.packing"

    def publish(value):
        env.publish_event(key, value, task="pack_order", instance=task_id)

    publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "queued"})
    env.stats.task_queued("pack_order", task_id)  # what @app.task reports for you
    with packers.request() as request:
        yield request
        count = env.registry.get("Shop.variables.boxes_per_order").value
        yield boxes.get(count)  # waits if the stock is too low
        publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "started"})
        env.stats.task_started("pack_order", task_id)
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(env.registry.get_config(path_id)))
        yield finished.put({"order": key})
        publish({"event_type": "order_packed"})
    env.stats.task_finished("pack_order", task_id)
    env.stats.flow_finished("orders")

The service time is drawn once the order has a packer and a box, from the configuration the registry holds at that moment, so a change made while it waited still applies to it.

The arrival loop keeps the configuration object rather than a copy of the rate, so the next draw uses whatever rate the registry holds. It gives each order its key, orders-1, orders-2:

docs/snippets/pages/low_level.py:arrivals
def arrivals(env):
    gap = env.registry.get_config("Shop.arrival.orders")  # the live config object
    task_id = 0
    while True:
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(gap))  # each draw reads the current rate
        env.process(order(env, f"orders-{task_id + 1}", task_id))  # the entity key
        task_id += 1

A reading of your own is a process that publishes at an interval; publish_telemetry uses the name exactly as given:

docs/snippets/pages/low_level.py:telemetry
def telemetry(env):
    """A reading of your own, beside the built-in statistics."""
    while True:
        env.publish_telemetry("Shop.boxes_per_packer", boxes.level / packers.capacity)
        yield env.timeout(10.0)

A process can also change the simulation itself, through the registry, as a connector or a scenario would:

docs/snippets/pages/low_level.py:control
def refill_and_rush(env):
    """Refills boxes every minute, and doubles arrivals after five minutes."""
    while True:
        yield env.timeout(60.0)
        missing = boxes.capacity - boxes.level
        if missing > 0:  # SimPy refuses a put of 0
            yield boxes.put(missing)
        if env.now >= 300 and env.registry.get("Shop.arrival.orders.rate").value < 1.0:
            env.registry.update("Shop.arrival.orders.rate", 1.0)
            env.registry.update("Shop.resources.packers.current_cap", 2)

docs.title: Start the Processes and Run
docs.text:
docs/snippets/pages/low_level.py:start
env.process(arrivals(env))
env.process(telemetry(env))
env.process(refill_and_rush(env))
docs/snippets/pages/low_level.py:run
logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
)
try:
    env.run(until=time_to_seconds("10 min"))  # until is in simulation seconds
finally:
    env.teardown()  # flushes the buffers and stops the threads

ConsoleEgress writes each record as a log line at INFO level, so logging is switched on first. env.run is SimPy's, so until is a number of simulation seconds; time_to_seconds converts a duration such as "10 min". teardown in finally publishes the last statistics, flushes the last records and stops both threads, even when the run stops with Ctrl+C or an error.

docs.title: What It Does for You
docs.text: Little: the environment paces the clock, holds the registry, writes records on the egress thread and keeps the statistics that setup_stats switches on. Everything else is your code. Builder API lists what SimulationContext.run() writes for you on top of the same steps.

docs.title: Errors and Limits
docs.text:
Nothing is checked before the run as a whole. Each call checks only what it reads, when it runs:

  • An unregistered path raises KeyError when a resource, a process or a registry.get asks for it, so register the parameters before creating anything that reads them.
  • A record without egress is dropped. Until setup_egress runs, publish_event and publish_telemetry do nothing, without an error.
  • A Sampler() with no seed draws nothing at random. Every sample is the distribution's mean (for a truncated_normal, its mean or its low, whichever is higher), so give it a seed.

The low-level API has no limits of its own: anything SimPy can model, a process can do.

docs.title: Full Script
docs.text:
Full script

The complete file, which the documentation tests run:

docs/snippets/pages/low_level.py
"""A complete low-level simulation, as the Low-level API page explains it step by step.

One packing team with a stock of boxes and a store of packed orders. Run it with
`python low_level.py`: it runs unpaced for 10 simulation minutes and prints every record
to the terminal.
"""

import logging

from desflow import (
    CapacityConfig,
    ConsoleEgress,
    ContainerConfig,
    DistributionConfig,
    DynamicContainer,
    DynamicRealtimeEnvironment,
    DynamicResource,
    DynamicStore,
    Sampler,
    SimParameter,
    time_to_seconds,
)

env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=0.0)  # unpaced; 1.0 follows the wall clock

env.registry.register_sim_parameter(
    SimParameter(
        sim_id="Shop",
        arrival={"orders": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=0.5)},
        service={"packing": DistributionConfig(dist="normal", mean=1.5, std=0.3)},
        resources={"packers": CapacityConfig(current_cap=1, max_cap=3)},
        containers={"boxes": ContainerConfig(current_cap=100, max_cap=100, level=100)},
        stores={"finished": CapacityConfig(current_cap=50, max_cap=50)},
        variables={"boxes_per_order": 1.0},
    )
)

env.setup_egress([ConsoleEgress()])  # starts the egress thread
# env.setup_ingress([KafkaIngress(...)]) would start the ingress thread
env.setup_stats("Shop", "basic", interval=60)  # readings and counts every minute

packers = DynamicResource(env, "Shop", "packers")  # reads Shop.resources.packers.*
boxes = DynamicContainer(env, "Shop", "boxes")  # starts at its level, 100
finished = DynamicStore(env, "Shop", "finished")
sampler = Sampler(seed=42)  # a random stream per distribution, from one seed


def order(env, key, task_id):
    """One order: queue for a packer, take a box, pack, then store the result."""
    path_id = "Shop.service.packing"

    def publish(value):
        env.publish_event(key, value, task="pack_order", instance=task_id)

    publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "queued"})
    env.stats.task_queued("pack_order", task_id)  # what @app.task reports for you
    with packers.request() as request:
        yield request
        count = env.registry.get("Shop.variables.boxes_per_order").value
        yield boxes.get(count)  # waits if the stock is too low
        publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "started"})
        env.stats.task_started("pack_order", task_id)
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(env.registry.get_config(path_id)))
        yield finished.put({"order": key})
        publish({"event_type": "order_packed"})
    env.stats.task_finished("pack_order", task_id)
    env.stats.flow_finished("orders")


def arrivals(env):
    gap = env.registry.get_config("Shop.arrival.orders")  # the live config object
    task_id = 0
    while True:
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(gap))  # each draw reads the current rate
        env.process(order(env, f"orders-{task_id + 1}", task_id))  # the entity key
        task_id += 1


def telemetry(env):
    """A reading of your own, beside the built-in statistics."""
    while True:
        env.publish_telemetry("Shop.boxes_per_packer", boxes.level / packers.capacity)
        yield env.timeout(10.0)


def refill_and_rush(env):
    """Refills boxes every minute, and doubles arrivals after five minutes."""
    while True:
        yield env.timeout(60.0)
        missing = boxes.capacity - boxes.level
        if missing > 0:  # SimPy refuses a put of 0
            yield boxes.put(missing)
        if env.now >= 300 and env.registry.get("Shop.arrival.orders.rate").value < 1.0:
            env.registry.update("Shop.arrival.orders.rate", 1.0)
            env.registry.update("Shop.resources.packers.current_cap", 2)


env.process(arrivals(env))
env.process(telemetry(env))
env.process(refill_and_rush(env))

if __name__ == "__main__":
    logging.basicConfig(
        level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
    )
    try:
        env.run(until=time_to_seconds("10 min"))  # until is in simulation seconds
    finally:
        env.teardown()  # flushes the buffers and stops the threads
    assert (
        packers.capacity == 2
        and env.registry.get("Shop.arrival.orders.rate").value == 1.0
    )
    assert len(finished.items) > 0

docs.title: Replications
docs.text: One run of a model is one sample: another seed draws other times and gives other values. Replications run the same model with many seeds and summarise each built-in statistic with a mean and a confidence interval. This page shows how to run them from the command line and from Python, in each of the three ways to write a model, what they return and send to the sinks, and how the seeds and intervals are made.

docs.title: What It Is
docs.text: A replication is one run of the model with a seed of its own. N replications give N independent values of each built-in statistic, such as the mean wait of a task. Their mean is the estimate, and the half-width of its confidence interval says how precise it is: with 95% confidence, the true value lies within the mean plus or minus the half-width. Trusting Results shows on the shop why one run is not an answer and how to choose the number of replications.

docs.title: Run Replications
docs.text:
Give the model, the number of replications, the seed they are spawned from and the time the arrivals stop:

YAMLBuilderLow-level 
desflow run replications.yaml --replications 20 --measure tasks.pack.wait_mean

--seed overrides simulation.random_seed, and --until overrides run.until, as for one run. --level sets the confidence level (0.95 when it is not given), --workers runs replications at once, each in its own process, and --drain drains every replication, as run.drain: true does. The command prints the summary, the seed of each replication and the command that repeats one. The blueprint's own warmup applies to every replication:

examples/yaml/replications.yaml:seed
# The replications' seeds are spawned from this one; --seed overrides it
random_seed: 42
warmup: 3 min
docs/snippets/pages/replications.py:builder
# shop is a function returning a new SimulationContext, called once per run
result = replicate(shop, 3, seed=42, until="1 h", warmup="3 min", measures=MEASURES)

shop is a function with no arguments that returns a new SimulationContext, such as the example's, because each replication starts from a new context. A blueprint path works here too.

docs/snippets/pages/replications.py:low-level
def model(env, sampler):
    """Builds the shop in the environment it is given, drawing from sampler."""
    env.registry.register_sim_parameter(PARAMS)
    env.process(orders(env, sampler, DynamicResource(env, "Shop", "packers")))


def low_level():
    shop = LowLevelModel(model, sim_id="Shop")
    return replicate(shop, 3, seed=42, until=3600, warmup=180, measures=MEASURES)

LowLevelModel names a function that builds the model in the environment and with the sampler it is given, and the sim_id its statistics are published under. The function registers the parameters, builds the resources and starts the processes; it sets up no statistics, because replicate does, and no sinks. Its tasks report their steps to env.stats, as Statistics shows.

replicate takes these options:

Option What it sets Default n how many replications, 2 or more seed the seed the replications' seeds are spawned from; None draws one and logs it until where each replication's arrivals stop, in seconds or a duration such as "1 h"; the replication ends there unless stop ends it earlier or drain runs on a blueprint's run.until stop ends each replication when it happens, as for run(): {"signal": name}, a signal's name, or {"condition": "..."}; for a LowLevelModel, a function of the environment that returns the event a blueprint's run.stop drain at until, stop the arrivals and run each replication on until no entity is left: True, or {"limit": "1 h"}; a LowLevelModel is drained when its function returns its arrival processes and reports its entities with env.stats.flow_started and flow_finished a blueprint's run.drain warmup the end of each replication's warm-up the model's own measures the statistics to summarise every statistic the run publishes, at least up to typical level the confidence level of the half-widths 0.95 workers replications run at once, each in its own process 1 overrides registry paths and the values every replication starts with, such as {"Shop.resources.packers.current_cap": 3}, set in the order given; a value the registry would refuse or clamp is refused, so a max_cap below the current current_cap needs current_cap set first none

docs.title: Choose the Measures
docs.text:
A measure is a statistic's published name without the sim id and stats, such as tasks.pack.wait_mean for Shop.stats.tasks.pack.wait_mean; Reference, Statistics lists them. Each replication keeps the statistics level its measures need, whatever level the model sets: basic for counts and time averages, typical for means and maxima of waits and services, and all for percentiles. A higher level the model sets stays.

A name that no replication publishes is refused, with the names the model does publish. A count that is published only once it is above 0, such as reneged, is 0 in a replication without one. A mean with no observation in a replication, such as the wait of a task that never started, is refused with the replication's number rather than left out.

docs.title: Read the Result
docs.text:
replicate, imported with from desflow import replicate, returns a Replications. Its summary has one row per measure, a mapping with measure, n, mean, half_width and level, and the interval runs from mean - half_width to mean + half_width; its table has one row per replication and measure, with the replication's number and seed; seeds lists the seeds in order:

docs/snippets/pages/replications.py:read
print(result.summary_text())  # each measure's n, mean and half-width
for row in result.summary:  # measure, n, mean, half_width and level
    low, high = row["mean"] - row["half_width"], row["mean"] + row["half_width"]
    print(f"{row['measure']}: {low:.2f} to {high:.2f} ({row['level']:.0%})")
print(result.seeds)  # replication i ran with seeds[i - 1]
for row in result.table:  # one row per replication and measure
    print(row["replication"], row["seed"], row["measure"], row["value"])

The summary of the three replications above:

measure                               n          mean    half-width (95%)
tasks.pack.wait_mean                  3          4.16                2.22
resources.packers.utilization_avg     3         78.51               4.363

Three replications give a wide interval; Trusting Results shows how to choose enough.

docs.title: Repeat One Replication
docs.text: Each replication's seed is a plain integer, recorded in seeds and in every row of the table, so any replication repeats on its own: desflow run shop.yaml --seed <its seed>, random_seed in a builder context, or Sampler(seed=...) in the low-level API, with the same end time, drain and warm-up. That run publishes its event records, which replications do not.

docs.title: What the Sinks Receive
docs.text:
When the model has sinks, a blueprint's egress or a builder's add_egress, they receive the result once, as telemetry stamped at the end time: each replication's value, then each measure's mean, half-width and count. A low-level model has no sinks of its own. These are the records a Console sink receives from the three replications above:

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
Seeds. The replications' seeds are numpy.random.SeedSequence(seed).spawn(n), each turned into one plain integer. The same seed gives the same list, and a longer list starts with the shorter one, so 40 replications begin with the 10 that n=10 runs. Within a replication each distribution draws from a random sequence of its own, as in any run (Randomness and Seeds).

One replication. Each replication builds the model again: it reads the blueprint, calls the factory, or calls the low-level function with a new environment and sampler. It runs unpaced, at factor 0, with no ingress, no egress and no statistics timer, applies the warm-up and the overrides before the clock starts, and reads env.stats.readings() at its end. A blueprint's run.before functions run once per replication, and once more when the model has sinks, for the build that sends them the result.

Intervals. The half-width is t × s ÷ √n, where s is the sample standard deviation of the n values and t the Student t quantile at (1 + level) ÷ 2 with n − 1 degrees of freedom. desflow computes the quantile itself, from the t distribution's cumulative probability by bisection, so replications need nothing beyond a base install; the tests check it against a published table.

Workers. With workers above 1, replications run in a pool of that many processes. Each process imports the model, so it must be a blueprint path or a function defined at the top of a module; a lambda or a function defined inside another function is refused with that reason. The values are the same as with one worker.

Sinks. When the model has sinks, it is built once more after the last replication, with its sinks but without its ingress and with the clock at the end time, and is not run. Its own statistics are switched off, so the sinks receive only the result. A model without sinks is not built again.

docs.title: Stability and Limits
docs.text:
• No event records. Replications send no event records: twenty streams of orders with different seeds in one sink could not be told apart. Repeat one replication with its seed to get its records.
  • Independent seeds only. Every replication of one call has its own seed. Comparing two designs with the same seeds, and checking that their random streams line up, is an experiment's job (Experiments).
  • Same model each time. A builder factory must return a new context on every call; a context that has run keeps its entity counters and is not a new replication.
  • Built-in statistics only. A replication summarises the built-in statistics at its end. Readings of your own, published with context.publish, are not summarised.
  • Steady state and terminating runs. The warm-up applies to each replication. A run with a natural start and end, such as a shop day, keeps its empty start and needs no warm-up.

docs.title: Resources: DynamicResource
docs.text: A resource is what an entity must hold while it works, and may have to wait for. This page shows how to declare one, how its queue is ordered, how it hands out units, and what happens when its capacity changes during a run.

docs.title: What It Is
docs.text: A resource is a number of identical units: packers, packing benches, checkout lanes, loading bays. A task asks for one unit, waits in the resource's queue while every unit is busy, holds the unit while it works, and gives it back. How many units there are is the resource's capacity, and it can change while the run goes on, as when packers go on a break.

docs.title: Declare a Resource
docs.text:
A resource has a current_cap, the number of units now, and a max_cap, the most a live change can set. run() builds a DynamicResource for each one the context declares; in the low-level API you build it after registering the parameters:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/resources.yaml:queue-order
resources:
  # fifo (the default), lifo or priority; priority serves the lowest number first,
  # and equal priorities first in, first out
  packers: {current_cap: 1, max_cap: 4, queue: priority}
docs/snippets/pages/resources.py:declare
app = SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0.0)
# fifo (the default), lifo or priority
app.add_resource("packers", current_cap=1, max_cap=4, queue="priority")
docs/snippets/pages/resources.py:resource
packers = DynamicResource(env, "Shop", "packers")  # capacity from the registry: 2


def order(env, order_id):
    with packers.request() as request:
        yield request  # waits until a unit is free
        yield env.timeout(10.0)  # holds the unit for 10 s
    # leaving the with block releases the unit

packers.request() is an event that happens when a unit is granted, and leaving the with block gives the unit back. A request whose with block is left before it is granted, for example after a timeout, is cancelled and never takes a unit.

docs.title: Queue Order
docs.text:
queue sets the order in which a resource serves the requests waiting for it:

  • fifo, the default: the oldest first;
  • lifo: the newest first;
  • priority: the lowest priority number first, and the oldest first among equal priorities.

Four requests that join while the only unit is busy are served in these orders:

docs/snippets/pages/resources.py:queue-order
def served_order(queue):
    """Four requests join while the only bench is busy; returns who is served when."""
    env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=0.0)
    env.registry.register_sim_parameter(
        SimParameter(
            sim_id="Shop",
            resources={"benches": CapacityConfig(current_cap=1, max_cap=1)},
        )
    )
    bench = DynamicResource(env, "Shop", "benches", queue=queue)
    served = []

    def use(name, priority, after=0.0):
        yield env.timeout(after)
        # The priority counts only under the priority order
        with bench.request(priority=priority) as request:
            yield request
            served.append(name)
            yield env.timeout(1.0)

    env.process(use("first", 1))  # takes the bench at once
    for name, priority in [
        ("orders-1", 1),
        ("express-1", 0),
        ("orders-2", 1),
        ("express-2", 0),
    ]:
        env.process(use(name, priority, after=0.1))  # all join while it is busy
    env.run(until=10)
    return served[1:]


for queue in ("fifo", "lifo", "priority"):
    print(f"{queue:<8} {', '.join(served_order(queue))}")

fifo     orders-1, express-1, orders-2, express-2
lifo     express-2, orders-2, express-1, orders-1
priority express-1, express-2, orders-1, orders-2
capacity 2, in use 4

The last line is the capacity drop that Under Live Changes describes, below. The same four requests, drawn:

docs.title: Task Priority
docs.text:
Under queue: priority, each task gives its requests a priority: a number, the same for every run of the task; an expression, read when the task joins the queue, such as attr.tier for the entity's attribute tier; or, in the builder, a function of the task id and the entity's attributes. The attributes exist before the request queues, and the task's own payload does not, so a priority cannot read it; an expression can read the previous task's payload as payload.<field>. The lowest priority is served first, and equal priorities first in, first out, which is the order of SimPy's PriorityResource: it ranks a request by (priority, time, not preempt), so among equal priorities and times a request that may preempt goes before one with preempt: false. The tests check it, ties included, in all three APIs (SimPy Compatibility).

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/resources.yaml:priority
tasks:
  pack_order:
    service: packing
    resource: packers
    # A number, or an expression read when the order joins the queue
    priority: attr.tier
    payload: {event_type: order_packed}
docs/snippets/pages/resources.py:priority
app = (
    SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0.0, random_seed=42)
    .add_resource("packers", current_cap=1, max_cap=4, queue="priority")
    .add_service("packing", dist="constant", value=1.5)
    .add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=0.5, attributes={"tier": 2})
)


# Each order's own priority, from its attributes, when it joins the queue;
# a number or an expression such as "attr.tier" works too
@app.task(
    service_id="packing",
    resource_id="packers",
    priority=lambda task_id, attributes: attributes["tier"],
)
def pack_order(task_id: int):
    return {"event_type": "order_packed"}

A low-level process passes the priority to the request: packers.request(priority=entity.attributes["tier"]), as the queue-order example above does. A resource whose queue is fifo or lifo ignores it.

A priority on a task whose resource does not have queue: priority is refused: when the blueprint loads, or when run() starts. Priorities shows what priority does to waits.

docs.title: Preemption
docs.text:
On a resource with preempt: true, which needs queue: priority, a request that finds every unit busy takes a unit from a task of a higher priority value, as SimPy's PreemptiveResource does. The task that loses the unit is chosen by SimPy's rule: the user whose (priority, request time, may not preempt) sorts last, and only when that sorts after the new request, so equal priorities do not preempt; the one exception is a user whose request was made at the same moment as the new one with preempt: false, which sorts after a request that may preempt. The task publishes preempted with the resource's name and follows its on_interrupt, as an interrupt would (Interruptions); a task with preempt: false never takes a unit this way. The interruptions example lets express orders preempt regular ones:

YAMLBuilderLow-level examples/yaml/interruptions.yaml:packers
# A lower priority value takes the packer from a higher one.
packers: {current_cap: 1, max_cap: 4, queue: priority, preempt: true}
examples/yaml/interruptions.yaml:pack
tasks:
  pack:
    service: packing
    resource: packers
    priority: attr.priority
    # A preempted or interrupted order queues again and serves what it had left.
    on_interrupt: resume
    payload: {event_type: order_packed}
    attributes: [priority]
examples/builder/interruptions_example.py:packers
# A lower priority value takes the packer from a higher one
.add_resource("packers", current_cap=1, max_cap=4, queue="priority", preempt=True)
examples/builder/interruptions_example.py:pack
@app.task(
    service_id="packing",
    resource_id="packers",
    priority="attr.priority",
    # A preempted or interrupted order queues again and serves what it had left
    on_interrupt="resume",
)
def pack(task_id, context, entity):
    return {"event_type": "order_packed", "priority": entity.attributes["priority"]}
examples/low-level/interruptions_example.py:pack
def pack(env, sampler, shop, key, priority, task_id):
    """Packs one order; a preemption or an interrupt sends it back to the queue
    with the packing time it had left."""
    path_id = "Shop.service.packing"

    def publish(value):
        env.publish_event(key, value, task="pack", instance=task_id)

    env.stats.flow_started(key.rsplit("-", 1)[0])  # the order enters the shop
    publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "queued"})
    env.stats.task_queued("pack", task_id)
    remaining, started = None, False
    shop["packing"].append(env.active_process)
    while True:
        request = shop["packers"].request(priority=priority)
        since = None
        try:
            yield request
            if not started:
                started = True
                publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "started"})
                env.stats.task_started("pack", task_id)
            else:
                publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "resumed"})
                env.stats.task_resumed("pack", task_id)
            if remaining is None:
                remaining = sampler.sample(env.registry.get_config(path_id))
            since = env.now
            yield env.timeout(remaining)
            payload = {"event_type": "order_packed", "priority": priority}
            publish(payload)
            env.stats.task_finished("pack", task_id)
            shop["packers"].release(request)
            break
        except simpy.Interrupt as interrupt:
            request.cancel()
            shop["packers"].release(request)  # nothing to give back if preempted
            if since is not None:
                remaining -= env.now - since
            if isinstance(interrupt.cause, Preempted):
                value = {
                    "path_id": path_id,
                    "status": "preempted",
                    "resource": "packers",
                }
                publish(value)
                env.stats.task_interrupted("pack", task_id, preempted=True)
            else:
                value = {"path_id": path_id, "status": "interrupted"}
                publish({**value, "cause": interrupt.cause})
                env.stats.task_interrupted("pack", task_id)
    shop["packing"].remove(env.active_process)
    env.stats.flow_finished(key.rsplit("-", 1)[0])

DynamicResource(env, "Shop", "packers", queue="priority", preempt=True) builds the resource, and request(priority, preempt=True) asks for a unit; the process that loses its unit receives simpy.Interrupt with a SimPy Preempted cause, whose resource, by and usage_since say what happened.

docs.title: Cancel and Release
docs.text:
A task that leaves a queue cancels its request, so the request is never granted later: patience that runs out, an interrupt, and an on_interrupt: abandon all do. Once a unit is granted, the task gives it back when it finishes, when it is interrupted, and when it is preempted (the preempting task has it then). In the low-level API these are SimPy's calls:

docs/snippets/pages/resource_cancel.py:cancel
held = packers.request()  # granted at once: the packer was free
waiting = packers.request()  # waits behind it

waiting.cancel()  # leaves the queue at once; it is never granted
held.cancel()  # granted already, so this releases nothing, as in SimPy
assert packers.in_use == 1 and packers.queue.items == []

packers.release(held)  # gives the packer back
packers.release(held)  # a second release does nothing

request.cancel() takes a waiting request out of the queue and does nothing to a granted one, and packers.release(request) gives a granted unit back once; releasing it again, or releasing a request that was never granted, gives nothing back. A with block does both on its way out, as in SimPy.

docs.title: Several Resources
docs.text:
A task can hold several resources at once: resource: [picker, bench] asks for a picker, then, while it holds the picker, for the bench. The task is served once it holds all of them, and it releases all of them when it finishes. While it waits for the bench it holds the picker: the holding is partial, and nothing is granted to several resources at once. patience covers the whole acquisition, and an interrupt gives back every unit held.

A task can also hand a unit to the next task of its flow with keep: the next task holds it from the start and gives it back once it publishes started, so an order keeps the picker until it is on the packing bench. The competing-resources example does both:

YAMLBuilderLow-level examples/yaml/competing_resources.yaml:tasks
tasks:
  pick:
    service: picking
    resource: picker
    # The picker stays with the order until pack has started.
    keep: [picker]
    payload: {event_type: order_picked}
    next: pack
  pack:
    service: packing
    resource: bench
    payload: {event_type: order_packed}
  wrap:
    service: wrapping
    # Holds the picker, then the bench too: acquired in this order.
    resource: [picker, bench]
    payload: {event_type: gift_wrapped}
examples/builder/competing_resources_example.py:tasks
# The picker stays with the order until pack has started
@app.task(service_id="picking", resource_id="picker", keep=["picker"], next="pack")
def pick(task_id, context):
    return {"event_type": "order_picked"}


@app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="bench")
def pack(task_id, context):
    return {"event_type": "order_packed"}


# Holds the picker, then the bench too: acquired in this order
@app.task(service_id="wrapping", resource_id=["picker", "bench"])
def wrap(task_id, context):
    return {"event_type": "gift_wrapped"}
examples/low-level/competing_resources_example.py:tasks
def pick(shop, key):
    """Picks an order and keeps the picker for pack, which gives it back."""
    env, stats = shop.env, shop.env.stats
    task_id, publish, status, duration = shop.step(key, "pick", "picking")
    stats.flow_started("orders")  # the order enters the shop
    status("queued")
    stats.task_queued("pick", task_id)
    picker = shop.picker.request()
    yield picker
    status("started")
    stats.task_started("pick", task_id)
    yield env.timeout(duration())
    publish({"event_type": "order_picked"})
    stats.task_finished("pick", task_id)
    env.process(pack(shop, key, picker))


def pack(shop, key, picker):
    env, stats = shop.env, shop.env.stats
    task_id, publish, status, duration = shop.step(key, "pack", "packing")
    status("queued")
    stats.task_queued("pack", task_id)
    with shop.bench.request() as bench:
        yield bench
        status("started")
        stats.task_started("pack", task_id)
        shop.picker.release(picker)  # the order is on the bench
        yield env.timeout(duration())
        publish({"event_type": "order_packed"})
        stats.task_finished("pack", task_id)
    stats.flow_finished("orders")


def wrap(shop, key):
    """Holds the picker, then the bench too: acquired in this order."""
    env, stats = shop.env, shop.env.stats
    task_id, publish, status, duration = shop.step(key, "wrap", "wrapping")
    stats.flow_started("gifts")
    status("queued")
    stats.task_queued("wrap", task_id)
    with shop.picker.request() as picker:
        yield picker
        with shop.bench.request() as bench:
            yield bench
            status("started")
            stats.task_started("wrap", task_id)
            yield env.timeout(duration())
            publish({"event_type": "gift_wrapped"})
            stats.task_finished("wrap", task_id)
    stats.flow_finished("gifts")

In the low-level API several resources are nested requests, and a handoff is a request released by the next process.

One order of acquisition. Two tasks that acquire the same two resources in opposite orders can each hold one and wait for ever for the other. desflow refuses such a model when it is built, naming both tasks: every task, keep handoffs included, must acquire shared resources in one order. Competing Resources shows what a partial holding costs.

docs.title: Breakdowns
docs.text:
A breakdown makes a resource fail at random and be repaired. time_to_failure is the time from the start, or from a repair, to the next failure, on calendar time, busy or idle; repair is how long a repair takes. While the resource is down its effective capacity is 0 and no request is granted:

YAMLBuilderLow-level examples/yaml/breakdowns.yaml:station
resources:
  station:
    current_cap: 2
    max_cap: 3
    breakdown:
      # Calendar time from a repair, or the start, to the next failure.
      time_to_failure: {dist: exponential, rate: 0.0167}
      repair: {dist: uniform, low: 5 s, high: 15 s}
      # The orders being packed are interrupted, and follow their on_interrupt.
      work: interrupt
examples/builder/breakdowns_example.py:station
.add_resource("station", current_cap=2, max_cap=3)
.add_breakdown(
    "station",
    # Calendar time from a repair, or the start, to the next failure
    time_to_failure={"dist": "exponential", "rate": 0.0167},
    repair={"dist": "uniform", "low": 5, "high": 15},
    # The orders being packed are interrupted, and follow their on_interrupt
    work="interrupt",
)
examples/low-level/breakdowns_example.py:station
breakdowns={
    "station": BreakdownConfig(
        # Calendar time from a repair, or the start, to the next failure
        time_to_failure=DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=0.0167),
        repair=DistributionConfig(dist="uniform", low=5, high=15),
        # The orders being packed are interrupted
        work="interrupt",
    )
},

Start run_breakdowns(env, station, sampler, work="interrupt") as a SimPy process beside the arrivals. station.fail() and station.repair() put a resource down and back by hand.

work says what happens to the tasks being served: interrupt, the default, interrupts each with the cause breakdown, and it follows its on_interrupt; finish lets them finish. Each failure and repair publishes an event keyed by the resource's name, with status down or repaired and reason: failure. Breakdowns checks the downtime of the example, and Interruptions explains on_interrupt.

docs.title: Registry Paths and Readings
docs.text: Each resource has two registry paths, <sim_id>.resources.<name>.current_cap and .max_cap, which a scenario, an ingress message or a process can change; Live Parameters explains how. A resource that breaks down adds <sim_id>.breakdown.<name>.time_to_failure and .repair, its two distributions. With statistics at the minimal level or above, each resource publishes four readings, such as Shop.stats.resources.packers.utilization: capacity, in_use, queue_length and utilization, the busy units as a percentage of the capacity; one that breaks down adds down, 1 while it is down. Statistics lists what the other levels add, among them downtime and failures.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
A DynamicResource grants units the way SimPy's Resource does, with two lists: queue, the waiting requests ranked by the queue order and a sequence number, so requests that rank the same are served in the order they arrived, and users, the granted requests. A request is granted when it is made if a unit is free and nothing waits ahead of it. Otherwise it waits, and each release grants the head of the queue when its release event is processed, one event later, as SimPy's Release does:

Because each step is the one SimPy takes, two events at the same simulation time are granted in SimPy's order: a waiting order whose patience runs out at the instant a unit is released reneges or is served exactly as it would in plain SimPy. in_use counts users: it goes up when a request is granted and down when a unit is released.

A waiting request leaves the queue at once when it is cancelled, which a with block does when it is left before the grant; request.cancel() does the same by hand. packers.release(request) gives a granted unit back. Cancelling a granted request releases nothing, and releasing a request twice, or one never granted, gives nothing back, as in SimPy. Every release still tries the head of the queue when its release event is processed, as SimPy's does: when a request that reneged was the head, the request behind it may then be granted or preempt a user.

SimPy and desflow. SimPy's Resource serves requests in the order they arrive, and PriorityResource by priority. Both take their capacity when they are created and keep it: capacity has no setter, so assigning a new one raises AttributeError (SimPy 4.1). desflow builds its own resource so the capacity can follow the registry and the queue order can be chosen; the request() call and the with block are SimPy's, so code written for SimPy works unchanged. SimPy and desflow compares the two.

docs.title: Under Live Changes
docs.text:
A change to current_cap takes effect at once, without stopping any work:

  • Growing grants waiting requests at once, up to the new capacity.
  • Shrinking stops nothing. The units still busy above the new capacity are owed: each one given back brings the busy count down, and no waiting task starts until the busy count is within the new capacity.
  • Growing again before the owed units are given back cancels them first, so only the rest of the rise grants waiting requests.
  • A current_cap outside 0 to max_cap is clamped to that range, with a warning.
  • Lowering max_cap lowers the capacity with it. A current_cap above the new max_cap is stored as max_cap, with a warning.
  • During a repair the capacity is 0 and current_cap keeps the planned value. A change to it sets the capacity the resource returns to and does not end the repair.

The example below takes three of five packers off the floor while four orders are being packed: the capacity is 2 at once, and in_use stays 4 until two orders finish. The animation steps through it:

docs/snippets/pages/resources.py:shrink
def capacity_drop(env):
    """Takes 3 of 5 packers off the floor at t=5 s. Orders being packed are not stopped."""
    env.registry.update("Shop.resources.packers.current_cap", 5)
    yield env.timeout(5.0)
    env.registry.update("Shop.resources.packers.current_cap", 2)
    yield env.timeout(0.1)  # the resource applies the change in its own process
    print(f"capacity {packers.capacity}, in use {packers.in_use}")

Until the owed units finish, in_use is above capacity, and the utilization reading is above 100.

docs.title: Stability and Limits
docs.text:
• Utilisation decides waits. A resource whose load is at or above its capacity has a queue that grows for as long as the run lasts; Queues and Capacity shows how to work it out.
  • Priority needs queue: priority. A task priority on a resource of another order is a load error, while a low-level request's priority is ignored under fifo and lifo.
  • Priority can starve. Under priority, a request with a high number is served only when no lower number is waiting; if the low numbers alone keep the resource busy, it is never served.
  • One order of acquisition. A model whose tasks acquire two resources in opposite orders is refused; Several Resources explains why.
  • A shrink never stops work. Lowering current_cap lets busy units finish. Work in progress stops only for an interrupt, a preemption or a breakdown: Interruptions, and Breakdowns for a machine that fails.
  • A preempted task queues again. With resume or restart it joins the back of its priority among the waiting requests, as a new SimPy request does; the time it waited before counts in its wait.

Amounts and items that tasks take and add, rather than hold, are Stores and Containers.

docs.title: Built-in Statistics
docs.text: A run can measure itself: how busy each resource was, how long tasks waited, how many entities finished. This page shows how to switch the statistics on, what each level publishes and costs, how each value is computed, and how to add readings of your own.

docs.title: What It Is
docs.text: The built-in statistics are measures that desflow keeps while the run goes on and publishes as telemetry, under fixed names such as Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.wait_mean. They need no code of yours in the builder or YAML, and they reach every sink like any other telemetry. They are off by default, because most runs only generate data. Measuring a Run reads them on the shop.

docs.title: Choose a Level
docs.text:
A level switches them on. Each level publishes what the levels before it publish, and answers one more question:

Level Question Adds none nothing; the default minimal What is happening now? resources: capacity, in_use, queue_length, utilization, and down for one that breaks down; stores and containers: capacity, level, getters_waiting, putters_waiting; tasks: in_progress basic How much got done, and how busy was it? tasks and flows: finished; flows: started and in_system; tasks: balked, reneged, failed, interrupted, preempted and resumed, and flows: failed, once one happens; resources: utilization_avg, queue_length_avg, and downtime and failures for one that breaks down; stores and containers: level_avg typical How long did tasks take? tasks: wait_mean, wait_max, service_mean, service_max all How long did the slowest take? tasks: wait_p50, wait_p95, wait_p99, service_p50, service_p95, service_p99

They are published every interval of simulation time, 10 seconds when it is not given, starting one interval after the start, and once more at the end of the run:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/statistics.yaml:levels
# none (the default), minimal, basic, typical or all, each adding to the one before;
# published every interval of simulation time and once at the end
stats: {level: typical, interval: 1 min}

stats: typical is the short form, with the 10-second interval. The interval takes seconds or a duration.

docs/snippets/pages/built_in_statistics.py:builder-levels
# none (the default), minimal, basic, typical or all, each adding to the one before;
# published every interval of simulation seconds and once at the end
app.with_stats("typical", interval=60)
docs/snippets/pages/built_in_statistics.py:low-level-levels
env.setup_stats("Shop", "typical", interval=60)  # before or after the resources

Resources, stores and containers add themselves to env.stats when they are built. Tasks are your own processes, so each reports its steps:

docs/snippets/pages/built_in_statistics.py:low-level-report
# A low-level task reports its own steps to the statistics
env.stats.task_queued("pack_order", task_id)
with packers.request() as request:
    yield request
    env.stats.task_started("pack_order", task_id)
    yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(env.registry.get_config(path_id)))
env.stats.task_finished("pack_order", task_id)
env.stats.flow_finished("orders")  # the order leaves the shop

docs.title: Read the Names
docs.text:
Every statistic is published as telemetry named <sim_id>.stats.<kind>.<name>.<statistic>, where the kind is resources, stores, containers, tasks or flows. A flow is named by the arrival that started its entities: Shop.stats.flows.orders.finished counts the orders that left the model. Reference, Statistics lists every name with what it measures. These are the statistics the blueprint above publishes at the end of its two minutes:

[TEL] {'sim_ts': 120.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.resources.packers.capacity', 'value': 2}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 120.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.resources.packers.in_use', 'value': 2}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 120.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.resources.packers.queue_length', 'value': 6}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 120.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.resources.packers.utilization', 'value': 100.0}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 120.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.resources.packers.utilization_avg', 'value': 90.79208653095155}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 120.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.resources.packers.queue_length_avg', 'value': 1.9083531344309013}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 120.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.in_progress', 'value': 8}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 120.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.finished', 'value': 70}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 120.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.wait_mean', 'value': 2.7959715976263215}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 120.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.wait_max', 'value': 11.22214686679115}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 120.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.service_mean', 'value': 3.0335617388528364}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 120.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.service_max', 'value': 6.357944038555676}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 120.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.flows.orders.finished', 'value': 70}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 120.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.flows.orders.started', 'value': 78}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 120.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.flows.orders.in_system', 'value': 8}

In Python the same values are in env.stats.readings(), by name, during or after the run:

docs/snippets/pages/built_in_statistics.py:low-level-read
# Every statistic the level publishes, by its published name
readings = env.stats.readings()
print(f"mean wait {readings['Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.wait_mean']:.2f} s")

app.env.stats.readings() gives the same from a builder or YAML run.

docs.title: Which Entities a Count Covers
docs.text:
Every entity that arrives belongs to one population when the statistics are read, and each population has its counts, from basic unless noted. A mean wait or service time covers only the instances that reached that step, so report the counts beside it:

Population Which entities Counts completed left the model after their last task flows.<arrival>.finished; tasks.<task>.finished per task still present started and not yet ended when the statistics are read flows.<arrival>.in_system; tasks.<task>.in_progress, the instances queued or started, from minimal rejected refused to join a queue, as their balk held tasks.<task>.balked abandoned left a queue when their patience ran out, or ended by an interrupt under on_interrupt: abandon tasks.<task>.reneged; an abandoned flow leaves in_system without adding to finished or failed, and tasks.<task>.interrupted counts the interrupts failed ended in a failure that no on_fail handled flows.<arrival>.failed; tasks.<task>.failed counts failed instances warm-up-crossing started before the warm-up ended and ended after it in finished, and in the wait and service times with their whole wait, but not in started

Without a warm-up, started is finished plus in_system plus the entities that balked, reneged, failed or were abandoned. A warm-up starts started, finished, failed and the outcome counts again from zero and leaves in_system and in_progress as they are, so after it finished also counts the warm-up-crossing entities and can be larger than started. End Conditions counts each population of a run.

docs.title: Add Readings of Your Own
docs.text:
Anything else is a custom reading: a function called at an interval of simulation time, which publishes with context.publish(name, value) as <sim_id>.<name>. It can read resources, stores, containers or any registry value.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/statistics.yaml:custom
telemetry:
  # Readings of your own: called as packers_report(context) every 30 seconds
  - interval: 30
    function: !python shop_logic.packers_report

The function is in shop_logic.py, beside the blueprint:

docs/snippets/yaml/shop_logic.py:packers-report
def packers_report(context):
    """A custom reading: orders waiting per packer, and the live arrival rate."""
    packers = context.get_resource("packers")
    waiting = len(packers.queue.items)
    context.publish("waiting_per_packer", waiting / max(packers.capacity, 1))
    rate = context.env.registry.get(f"{context.sim_id}.arrival.orders.rate").value
    context.publish("arrival_rate", rate)  # as Shop.arrival_rate
docs/snippets/pages/built_in_statistics.py:builder-custom
@app.telemetry_loop(interval=30.0)
def packers_report(context: SimulationContext):
    """Readings of your own: orders waiting per packer, and the live arrival rate."""
    packers = context.get_resource("packers")
    waiting = len(packers.queue.items)
    context.publish("waiting_per_packer", waiting / max(packers.capacity, 1))
    rate = context.env.registry.get("Shop.arrival.orders.rate").value
    context.publish("arrival_rate", rate)  # as Shop.arrival_rate

A process that loops, publishes with env.publish_telemetry(name, value) and waits with env.timeout(interval) does the same.

docs.title: Example: Measuring a Run
docs.text:
The measuring example publishes every statistic of the packers and the pack task every 5 minutes, leaves out a 3-minute warm-up, and sends a ground-truth record when packing slows down, to a sink of its own. It needs no Docker service and ends on its own.

examples/builder/measuring_example.py:fault
def slow_packing(context):
    """Packing slows from 4 to 4.8 seconds on average at 12 minutes, with its label."""
    yield context.env.timeout(720)
    path = "Shop.service.packing.scale"
    registry = context.env.registry
    old = registry.get(path).value
    registry.update(path, 1.2)
    context.env.publish_label(
        {"fault": "slow_packing", "cause": "new packing material"},
        path=path,
        old=old,
        new=registry.get(path).value,
    )


app.add_process(slow_packing)
