docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
The environment keeps one Statistics object, env.stats, which collects nothing until a level above none is set. Its timer publishes every value at each interval, and the teardown publishes them once more.

Readings now. capacity, in_use, queue_length and level are read from the object at the moment of publishing. in_use counts the units held by tasks, so after a capacity drop it can be above capacity, and utilization, in_use ÷ capacity × 100, above 100.

Breakdowns. A resource with a breakdown reads down now: 1 while it is down, 0 otherwise. downtime adds the length of each down period, and of one still going on, and failures adds one at each failure; Breakdowns checks both against the events.

Averages over time. utilization_avg, queue_length_avg and level_avg weigh each value by how long it lasted. Each resource, store and container reports every change, and the statistics add the area under the value since the last change, so the average is exact at any moment rather than sampled:

Counts. finished adds one when a task instance finishes, and a flow's finished adds one when an entity's last task has no next task. A flow's started adds one when an entity's first task instance begins, before its balk check and its queue, whether or not it is then served, and in_system is the number of its entities in the model now, started and not yet finished, failed or gone; so started is finished plus in_system plus the entities that balked, reneged, failed or were abandoned. A task's in_progress is the number of its instances queued or started and not yet ended, now. A low-level process reports entities with env.stats.flow_started(arrival) and, for one that leaves without finishing or failing, env.stats.flow_ended(arrival). A task's balked adds one when an instance refuses to join its queue, reneged when one leaves the queue after its patience, and failed when one fails (Failures); a flow's failed adds one when an entity's flow ends in a failure no on_fail handles. interrupted and preempted add one for each interrupt or preemption an instance receives, and resumed when it is served again. Each is published once it is above 0. A balked, reneged or failed instance adds no wait or service time. An interrupted instance that resumes adds one wait, the sum of all its waits, and one service time, the time it was served. A low-level process counts them with env.stats.task_balked(task, instance), env.stats.task_reneged(task, instance), env.stats.task_failed(task, instance), env.stats.flow_failed(arrival), env.stats.task_interrupted(task, instance, preempted=...) and env.stats.task_resumed(task, instance).

Wait and service. The wait of a task instance runs from its queued step to its started step, and its service from started to finished; a task that never queues, such as a timed step, waits 0. typical keeps a count, a total and a maximum of each, so their cost does not grow with the run. all keeps every observation and computes the percentiles exactly with NumPy's percentile at each publication, so its memory grows with the number of tasks.

Warm-up. A run's warmup resets every statistic once, at that time: the averages start again from zero area, and the counts and observations from zero. An instance that was queued before the reset and starts after it counts with its whole wait. Time and Pacing describes the warm-up.

docs.title: Stability and Limits
docs.text:
• Cost. minimal reads a few values at each publication. basic adds a little work at every change of a resource, store or container. typical adds a little at every task step. all keeps every wait and service time in memory for the whole run; use it for runs of thousands of tasks, not for a generator that runs for days.
  • One way to get resource readings. Before 0.21.0, a telemetry entry could publish <resource>.<reading> by name. That shortcut is gone: stats: minimal publishes the same readings, under Shop.stats.resources.<name>.<reading>. telemetry now takes only a function, for readings of your own.
  • One run is one sample. The statistics describe one run with one seed. Values from the same run are not independent of each other, and another seed gives other values; Trusting Results shows what that means for a result, and Replications run a model with many seeds.
  • A task appears once it has run. A task's statistics are published from the first time it starts, at typical and all, or finishes, at basic.

docs.title: Stores and Containers: DynamicStore and DynamicContainer
docs.text: A resource is held and given back. Stores and containers hold things that tasks take away and add: items, or an amount. This page shows how to declare them, how tasks put and get, and what a live change does.

docs.title: What It Is
docs.text:
• A store holds items, each one a value of its own: parcels on a shelf waiting for a courier, orders in a buffer. A task puts an item in, and another takes the oldest out.
  • A container holds an amount: boxes in a bin, fuel in a tank, a stock level. A task takes some, and another adds some.

Both have a capacity. A task that takes waits while there is not enough, and a task that adds waits while there is no room. Stock uses a container in the shop.

docs.title: Declare Them
docs.text:
A container has a current_cap, its capacity, the largest amount it holds; a max_cap, the largest capacity a live change can set; and a level, the amount it holds when the run starts, 0 when left out. A store has a current_cap and a max_cap, in whole items, and starts empty unless it lists items (Start With Items and Serve by Priority). run() builds a DynamicContainer and a DynamicStore for each one the context declares; a store and a container cannot share a name.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/stores_containers.yaml:container
containers:
  # An amount: room for 100 boxes, 20 when the run starts
  stock: {current_cap: 100, max_cap: 100, level: 20}
docs/snippets/yaml/stores_containers.yaml:store
stores:
  # Items: room for 5 parcels, empty when the run starts
  parcels: {current_cap: 5, max_cap: 10}
docs/snippets/pages/stores_containers.py:builder-container
# An amount: room for 100 boxes, 20 when the run starts
app.add_container("stock", current_cap=100, max_cap=100, level=20)
docs/snippets/pages/stores_containers.py:builder-store
# Items: room for 5 parcels, empty when the run starts
app.add_store("parcels", current_cap=5, max_cap=10)
docs/snippets/pages/stores_containers.py:low-level-container
env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=0.0)
env.registry.register_sim_parameter(
    SimParameter(
        sim_id="Shop",
        # An amount: room for 100 boxes, 20 when the run starts
        containers={"stock": ContainerConfig(current_cap=100, max_cap=100, level=20)},
        # Items: room for 5 parcels, empty when the run starts
        stores={"parcels": CapacityConfig(current_cap=5, max_cap=10)},
    )
)
stock = DynamicContainer(env, "Shop", "stock")  # starts at the level above, 20
parcels = DynamicStore(env, "Shop", "parcels")

A DynamicContainer built with no init starts at the level its ContainerConfig gives; init= sets another.

docs.title: Take and Add
docs.text:
A task takes with get and adds with put. For a container, each names the container and an amount: a number; an expression, such as payload.boxes for a field of the previous task's payload; or in the builder, a function of the task id and the previous task's payload. The amount is 1 when left out. For a store, each names the store: a put adds the task's finished payload as the item, and a get takes the oldest item and passes it to the task's function as item.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/stores_containers.yaml:take
pack_order:
  service: packing
  resource: packers
  # Takes the boxes the previous task's payload names, once it has a packer
  get: {container: stock, amount: payload.boxes}
docs/snippets/yaml/stores_containers.yaml:put
# Adds its finished payload to the store as an item
put: {store: parcels}
payload: {event_type: order_packed}
docs/snippets/pages/stores_containers.py:builder-take
# Takes the boxes the previous task's payload names, once it has a packer.
# The amount is a number, an expression, or a function of the task id and the
# previous task's payload, such as lambda task_id, payload: payload["boxes"].
@app.task(
    service_id="packing",
    resource_id="packers",
    get={"container": "stock", "amount": "payload.boxes"},
    put={"store": "parcels"},  # adds the finished payload as an item
)
def pack_order(task_id: int):
    return {"event_type": "order_packed"}


# Takes the oldest parcel, waiting while the store is empty; `item` is that parcel
@app.task(service_id="collecting", get={"store": "parcels"})
def collect(task_id: int, item):
    return {"event_type": "parcel_collected", "parcel": item["event_type"]}
docs/snippets/pages/stores_containers.py:low-level-take
def pack(env, order_id):
    yield stock.get(2)  # takes 2 boxes, waiting while fewer are left
    yield parcels.put({"order_id": order_id})  # waits while the store is full


def collect_parcel(env):
    parcel = yield parcels.get()  # waits while the store is empty
    print(f"collected order {parcel['order_id']}; {stock.level:g} boxes left")

get(amount), put(amount), put(item) and get() are SimPy events: yielding one waits until it succeeds, and a store's get() succeeds with the item.

A task with a resource gets its unit first and then takes its get, so it waits for stock while holding the unit. A task adds its put after its service time, then publishes the finished event. Tasks and Processes lists every step.

docs.title: Start With Items and Serve by Priority
docs.text:
A store can hold items when the run starts, as parcels left from yesterday: items lists them in the order a get returns them. A store with priority returns the item with the lowest priority first, as SimPy's PriorityStore does; its items are [priority, item] pairs, and a task's put gives each new item its priority, a number or an expression such as attr.priority. Items of equal priority come out in the order they went in. A store cannot start with more items than its current_cap; the blueprint or add_store is refused with the reason.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/parcel_store.yaml:store
stores:
  parcels:
    current_cap: 10
    max_cap: 10
    # A courier takes the lowest priority first, the oldest first among equals
    priority: true
    # Left from yesterday: [priority, item] pairs, held before the first put
    items:
      - [2, {order: standard-0}]
      - [1, {order: express-0}]
docs/snippets/yaml/parcel_store.yaml:put
pack:
  # Each parcel's priority, read when it is put in the store
  put: {store: parcels, priority: attr.priority}
  payload: {order: standard}
  id_field: number
docs/snippets/pages/parcel_store.py:builder-store
app = SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0.0)
# A courier takes the lowest priority first, the oldest first among equals.
# Left from yesterday: (priority, item) pairs, held before the first put.
app.add_store(
    "parcels",
    current_cap=10,
    max_cap=10,
    priority=True,
    items=[(2, {"order": "standard-0"}), (1, {"order": "express-0"})],
)

A task's put takes the priority the same way: put={"store": "parcels", "priority": "attr.priority"}.

docs/snippets/pages/parcel_store.py:low-level-store
parcels = DynamicStore(
    env,
    "Shop",
    "parcels",
    priority=True,
    # Each pair is held as a PriorityItem, ranked by priority and then by order
    items=[(2, {"order": "standard-0"}), (1, {"order": "express-0"})],
)


def courier_process(env):
    first = yield parcels.get()  # a PriorityItem; .item is the parcel
    print(f"collected {first.item['order']}")
    # A put of your own wraps the item the same way, so ties keep their order
    yield parcels.put(parcels.wrap({"order": "express-1"}, 1))

A low-level priority store holds simpy.PriorityItems. wrap(item, priority) makes one ranked by the priority and then by a rising number, which is how the builder and YAML keep equal priorities in order; a plain PriorityItem(priority, item) also works, with no order among equal priorities.

A get on a priority store takes no priority of its own and is refused with one: the item's priority decides the order. Priorities compares priority storage with a resource's priority queue.

docs.title: Pick an Item, or Give Up Waiting
docs.text:
A store get can take a filter, a condition that picks which item it takes, as SimPy's FilterStore does. item.<field> reads the item offered, beside the names any condition reads, such as attr.area for the entity's own attribute. The get takes the oldest item that matches and waits while none does; a waiting get that matches nothing does not stop a later one from taking an item that matches it. A priority store takes no filter, because SimPy has no store that both ranks and filters; the blueprint or run() refuses one with the task's name.

A task's patience covers its whole wait, for its wait, then its resource and then its get. When it runs out, the task publishes reneged and its get is cancelled, so it takes nothing later. In the low-level API, cancel() on a put or get event that has not succeeded takes it out of its queue, as in SimPy: a cancelled get takes nothing, and a cancelled put adds nothing. item_field adds the item a YAML task's get took to its payload, and a builder function receives it as item:

YAMLBuilderLow-level examples/yaml/filtered_inventory.yaml:collect
tasks:
  pack:
    service: packing
    resource: packers
    # The parcel goes on the shelf as the payload, with its area.
    put: {store: parcels}
    payload: {event_type: order_packed}
    attributes: [area]
  collect:
    # The oldest parcel for the courier's own area.
    get: {store: parcels, filter: item.area == attr.area}
    # A courier leaves without a parcel after 20 seconds.
    patience: 20 s
    # The parcel the courier took, in the finished event.
    item_field: parcel
    payload: {event_type: parcel_collected}
examples/builder/filtered_inventory_example.py:collect
@app.task(
    # The oldest parcel for the courier's own area
    get={"store": "parcels", "filter": "item.area == attr.area"},
    # A courier leaves without a parcel after 20 seconds
    patience=20,
)
def collect(task_id, context, item):
    """`item` is the parcel the courier took."""
    return {"event_type": "parcel_collected", "parcel": item}

A filter can also be a function of the item: "filter": lambda parcel: parcel["area"] == "north".

examples/low-level/filtered_inventory_example.py:collect
def collect(env, sampler, shop, key, area, task_id):
    """Takes the oldest parcel for its own area, or leaves after 20 seconds."""

    def publish(value):
        env.publish_event(key, value, task="collect", instance=task_id)

    flow = key.rsplit("-", 1)[0]
    env.stats.flow_started(flow)  # the courier enters the shop
    publish({"status": "queued"})
    env.stats.task_queued("collect", task_id)
    get = shop["parcels"].get(filter=lambda parcel: parcel["area"] == area)
    yield get | env.timeout(20)
    if not get.triggered:
        get.cancel()  # out of the queue, so it takes no parcel later
        publish({"status": "reneged"})
        env.stats.task_reneged("collect", task_id)
        env.stats.flow_ended(flow)
        return
    publish({"status": "started"})
    env.stats.task_started("collect", task_id)
    publish({"event_type": "parcel_collected", "parcel": get.value})
    env.stats.task_finished("collect", task_id)
    env.stats.flow_finished(flow)

item.<field> can also be read in the task's put and next, after its get. Filtered Inventory uses a filter and patience on a shelf of shirts.

docs.title: Registry Paths, Readings and Conditions
docs.text:
A container has three registry paths, <sim_id>.containers.<name>.current_cap, .max_cap and .level; a store has <sim_id>.stores.<name>.current_cap and .max_cap. With statistics at the minimal level or above, each publishes four readings, such as Shop.stats.containers.stock.level:

Reading Store Container capacity items it can hold largest amount level items held amount held getters_waiting tasks waiting to get an item tasks waiting to take an amount putters_waiting tasks waiting to put an item tasks waiting to add an amount

basic adds level_avg, the level averaged over time; Statistics describes it. These are the readings of the blueprint above at 30 and 40 seconds, before and after the stock count below:

[TEL] {'sim_ts': 30.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.stores.parcels.level', 'value': 3}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 30.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.stores.parcels.putters_waiting', 'value': 0}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 30.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.containers.stock.level', 'value': 0.0}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 30.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.containers.stock.getters_waiting', 'value': 2}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 40.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.stores.parcels.level', 'value': 5}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 40.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.stores.parcels.putters_waiting', 'value': 2}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 40.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.containers.stock.level', 'value': 38.0}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 40.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.containers.stock.getters_waiting', 'value': 0}

At 30 seconds the bin is empty and two orders wait for boxes; at 40 seconds the count has put 50 boxes in, those two have taken theirs, and the shelf of parcels is full, with two packed orders waiting for room.

A condition in a task's next reads a level as level.<name>, so an order can go to backorder when level.stock == 0, as Task Flow shows.

docs.title: Example: Stock, Parcels and Express Orders
docs.text:
The stock example puts it together: packing takes a box from a container and puts the parcel in a store, which starts with two parcels from yesterday, and a courier collects them. Express orders go first, at the packers and, as the parcels store is a priority store, at the courier. The stock runs out, so packing waits until a restock at 40 seconds sets the level to 30. It needs no Docker service and ends on its own.

def pack(env, sampler, shop, key, priority, task_id):
    """Queued, a packer by priority, a box from stock, packing, then a parcel."""
    path_id = "Shop.service.packing"

    def publish(value):
        env.publish_event(key, value, task="pack", instance=task_id)

    publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "queued"})
    env.stats.task_queued("pack", task_id)  # counted as in progress
    with shop["packers"].request(priority=priority) as req:
        yield req
        # Waits while the stock is empty

        # Waits while the store is full; wrap ranks the parcel by its priority
        yield shop["parcels"].put(shop["parcels"].wrap(payload, priority))
        publish(payload)
        env.stats.task_finished("pack", task_id)

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
A container keeps a level between 0 and its capacity, with a queue of getters and a queue of putters. A get succeeds as soon as the level covers its amount, and a put as soon as there is room for all of it; until then each waits in its queue, in the order it arrived:

A store keeps a list of items, up to its capacity. A put adds an item at the end, and a get takes the first, so items leave in the order they came; a get with a filter takes the first item its filter accepts:

SimPy and desflow. Underneath are SimPy's Container; a FilterStore for a store, which serves its gets as Store does while no waiting get has a filter; and a PriorityStore for a priority store, which hands out the lowest item first. A full put that waits for room and an empty get that waits for an item or an amount are checked against plain SimPy in all three APIs; SimPy Compatibility lists the checks. SimPy's capacities are fixed when they are created; desflow's follow the registry, keep the registry's level in step with every put and get, and report each change to the statistics. SimPy and desflow compares the two.

docs.title: Under Live Changes
docs.text:
• Capacity follows current_cap, clamped to between 0 and max_cap. A higher capacity wakes waiting putters. A capacity below what is held destroys nothing: puts wait until enough has been taken.
  • A container's level is set by an update to its level path, as a stock count or a restock from outside would. The new level is clamped to between 0 and current_cap, with a warning, and it wakes both queues: a higher level serves waiting getters, and a lower one can make room for putters.
  • current_cap is the capacity, not a level. A model that used a container's current_cap as a level, such as the wear of a roll, moves it to level.

The stock count in the blueprint above, in each way of writing:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/stores_containers.yaml:level
scenario:
  # A stock count at 30 seconds: the level path sets what the container holds
  - {at: 30, path: Shop.containers.stock.level, value: 50}
docs/snippets/pages/stores_containers.py:builder-level
def stock_count(context: SimulationContext):
    """A stock count at 30 seconds: the level path sets what the container holds."""
    yield context.env.timeout(30)
    context.env.registry.update("Shop.containers.stock.level", 50)


app.add_process(stock_count)
docs/snippets/pages/stores_containers.py:low-level-level
def stock_count_process(env):
    """A stock count: sets the level; waiting gets and puts are woken."""
    yield env.timeout(30)
    env.registry.update("Shop.containers.stock.level", 50)

docs.title: Stability and Limits
docs.text:
• A container that never refills blocks its getters for good, and a task that waits for stock while holding a resource blocks the resource too. Supply has to keep up with demand, as Stock shows.
  • Whole items. A store's capacity is a whole number, and it holds items, not amounts.
  • A filter checks every waiting get on each put. A store with many waiting gets and a filter that rarely matches does work in proportion to both, as SimPy's FilterStore does.
  • One store or container per get or put. A task has at most one get and one put.

docs.title: Task Flow: the Next Task by Condition or Probability
docs.text: An entity rarely leaves after completing just one task. An order is checked, perhaps wrapped as a gift, packed, sometimes packed again, and shipped. This page shows how a finished task chooses the next one, and what the entity carries from task to task.

docs.title: What It Is
docs.text:
A flow is the sequence of tasks one entity passes through. Each task names what follows it: always the same task, the first of several rules whose condition holds, or a task drawn at random by weight. A rule can send the entity back to a task it has passed, for rework. A task that names nothing ends the flow. The entity keeps its key and its attributes through the whole flow, and every task can read them.

A Flow of Tasks builds a pick, pack and ship flow step by step.

docs.title: Choose the Next Task
docs.text:
next takes one of these forms:

  • A task name, next: pack_order: always that task.
  • Rules, when with an optional default: each rule is a condition and a task. Rules are tried in order. The first matching rule wins, and default applies if none matches. With no default and no matching rule, the flow ends.
  • Weights, below.
  • In the builder, a function that takes the Upstream and returns a task name or None.
YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/task_flow.yaml:condition
check_order:
  payload: {total: 80}
  # Rules are tried in order; the first match wins. Otherwise, use the default.
  next:
    when:
      - {condition: "level.stock == 0", task: backorder}
      - {condition: "payload.total >= 100 or attr.gift == 1", task: wrap_gift}
    default: pack_order
docs/snippets/pages/task_flow.py:builder-condition
# Rules are tried in order; the first match wins. Otherwise, use the default.
@app.task(
    next={
        "when": [
            {"condition": "level.stock == 0", "task": "backorder"},
            {
                "condition": "payload.total >= 100 or attr.gift == 1",
                "task": "wrap_gift",
            },
        ],
        "default": "pack_order",
    }
)
def check_order(task_id: int):
    return {"total": 80}
docs/snippets/pages/task_flow.py:low-level-condition
# The same rules as next, as a Router; choose() returns the next task's name
route = Router(
    {
        "when": [{"condition": "attr.gift == 1", "task": "wrap_gift"}],
        "default": "pack_order",
    }
)
order = Entity("orders-1", "orders", {"gift": 0})  # key, arrival, attributes
finished = Upstream(0, order.key, order.attributes, {"total": 80})
assert route.choose(finished, env=None) == "pack_order"

A Router takes the same rules as next. When a task finishes, its process builds the Upstream, asks route.choose(upstream, env, levels=...) for the next task's name, and starts that task with the same entity. env lets a condition read registry[...] and t, and levels, a mapping of store and container names to the objects, lets it read level.<name>.

The condition is evaluated when the task finishes, after its set. payload. reads the payload of the task that just finished, attr. the entity's attributes, level. a store's or container's level, and registry["..."] a live parameter. How It Works lists everything a condition can use.

docs.title: Weights
docs.text:
weights maps task names to numbers, and the next task is drawn in proportion to them. The draw comes from a random stream of the routing task's own, route.<task>, so a seeded run repeats it and it changes no other draw:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/task_flow.yaml:weights
pack_order:
  service: packing
  resource: packers
  get: {container: stock, amount: 1}
  payload: {event_type: order_packed}
  # A task drawn in proportion to its weight: one in ten is packed again
  next:
    weights: {ship_order: 9, pack_order: 1}
docs/snippets/pages/task_flow.py:builder-weights
# A task drawn in proportion to its weight: one in ten is packed again
@app.task(
    service_id="packing",
    resource_id="packers",
    get={"container": "stock", "amount": 1},
    next={"weights": {"ship_order": 9, "pack_order": 1}},
)
def pack_order(task_id: int):
    return {"event_type": "order_packed"}
docs/snippets/pages/task_flow.py:low-level-weights
# Weights draw from a generator: the routing task's own stream, as the builder's do
rework = Router({"weights": {"ship_order": 9, "pack_order": 1}})
rework.rng = Sampler(seed=42).generator("route.pack_order")
choices = [rework.choose(finished) for _ in range(1000)]

docs.title: Attributes
docs.text:
An arrival gives each new entity its starting attributes, and a task's set changes them when the task finishes. Each entity gets its own copy. Attributes are not published: a condition reads them as attr.<name>, and a payload includes them only when it asks.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/task_flow.yaml:attributes
arrivals:
  # Each order starts with these attributes, read as attr.gift
  orders: {dist: exponential, rate: 0.5, spawn: check_order, attributes: {gift: 0}}
  gifts: {dist: exponential, rate: 0.1, spawn: check_order, attributes: {gift: 1}}
docs/snippets/yaml/task_flow.yaml:set
# Applied to the order's attributes when the task finishes
set: {backordered: 1}

A task's attributes list adds the named attributes to a mapping payload, as ship_order does in the full blueprint.

docs/snippets/pages/task_flow.py:builder-attributes
# Each order starts with these attributes, read as attr.gift
app.add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=0.5, attributes={"gift": 0})
app.add_arrival("gifts", dist="exponential", rate=0.1, attributes={"gift": 1})
docs/snippets/pages/task_flow.py:builder-set
# `set` is applied to the order's attributes when the task finishes
@app.task(service_id="supplying", set={"backordered": 1}, next="check_order")
def backorder(task_id: int):
    return {"event_type": "order_backordered"}

An Entity(key, arrival, attributes) carries them; the process updates entity.attributes itself after a task, as the low-level tab of A Flow of Tasks shows.

docs.title: Entity Key
docs.text:
Each arrival starts a new entity, keyed by the arrival's name and a counter from 1: orders-1, orders-2. Every event of every task in its flow carries that key as its record key, so a sink can follow one order through the whole flow, and Kafka keeps its events in order on one partition. The builder can replace the key with a function of the counter:

YAMLBuilderLow-level

A blueprint uses the default key.

docs/snippets/pages/task_flow.py:builder-key
# Keys ret-00001, ret-00002 instead of returns-1, from the counter, which starts at 1
app.add_arrival("returns", dist="exponential", rate=0.05, key=lambda n: f"ret-{n:05d}")

The process that creates each Entity gives it its key.

These are the finished events of gifts-5 in the blueprint above: checked while the shelf was empty, backordered, checked again, wrapped, packed and shipped, all under one key:

[EVT] {'sim_ts': 19.216, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'gifts-5', 'task': 'check_order', 'instance': 13, 'value': {'total': 80}}
[EVT] {'sim_ts': 49.216, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'gifts-5', 'task': 'backorder', 'instance': 1, 'value': {'event_type': 'order_backordered'}}
[EVT] {'sim_ts': 49.216, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'gifts-5', 'task': 'check_order', 'instance': 34, 'value': {'total': 80}}
[EVT] {'sim_ts': 52.216, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'gifts-5', 'task': 'wrap_gift', 'instance': 7, 'value': {'event_type': 'gift_wrapped'}}
[EVT] {'sim_ts': 54.362, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'gifts-5', 'task': 'pack_order', 'instance': 29, 'value': {'event_type': 'order_packed'}}
[EVT] {'sim_ts': 54.362, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'gifts-5', 'task': 'ship_order', 'instance': 27, 'value': {'event_type': 'order_shipped', 'gift': 1, 'backordered': 1}}

docs.title: Upstream
docs.text:
A task started by next receives what the task before it handed on, the Upstream: the finished task's instance id, the entity's key and attributes, and its payload. A builder function gets it by declaring a parameter called upstream, and the entity by declaring entity; a function that declares neither works as before. The first task of a flow gets upstream=None.

docs/snippets/pages/task_flow.py:builder-upstream
# A function declaring `upstream` receives what the previous task handed on,
# and `entity` the order itself; a payload includes attributes only when it asks
@app.task()
def ship_order(task_id: int, upstream, entity):
    return {
        "event_type": "order_shipped",
        "packed_by": upstream.task_id,  # the instance of pack_order before it
        "gift": entity.attributes.get("gift"),
        "backordered": entity.attributes.get("backordered"),
    }


# A rule can also be a function of the Upstream, returning a task name or None
@app.task(next=lambda upstream: "check_order" if upstream.payload["ok"] else None)
def inspect_return(task_id: int):
    return {"ok": False}

docs.title: Example: A Flow of Tasks
docs.text:
The flow example: orders are picked, gift orders are wrapped, one parcel in ten is packed again, and every order is shipped. Wrapping and shipping are timed steps. It needs no Docker service and ends on its own.

YAMLBuilderLow-level

Quick Start

desflow examples get downloads the example at the release you install, into a folder of its own. Pick uv or pip:

uvpip 
# 1. Install
uv tool install desflow

# 2. Download the example
desflow examples get flow --api yaml
cd flow/yaml

# 3. Run it
desflow run flow.yaml

# 1. Install
pip install desflow

# 2. Download the example
desflow examples get flow --api yaml
cd flow/yaml

# 3. Run it
desflow run flow.yaml
examples/yaml/flow.yaml:routes
tasks:
  pick:
    service: picking
    resource: pickers
    payload: {event_type: order_picked}
    # The first rule that holds wins; default catches the rest.
    next:
      when:
        - {condition: "attr.gift == 1", task: wrap}
      default: pack
  wrap:
    # A timed step: a service and no resource, so no queued event and no wait.
    service: wrapping
    payload: {event_type: gift_wrapped}
    # Applied to the entity's attributes when the task finishes.
    set: {wrapped: 1}
    next: pack
  pack:
    service: packing
    resource: packers
    payload: {event_type: order_packed}
    # Drawn from this task's own random sequence: one parcel in ten is packed again.
    next:
      weights: {ship: 9, pack: 1}

The whole file is examples/yaml/flow.yaml.

Quick Start

desflow examples get downloads the example at the release you install, into a folder of its own. Pick uv or pip:

uvpip 
# 1. Install
uv tool install desflow

# 2. Download the example
desflow examples get flow --api builder
cd flow/builder

# 3. Run it
uv run --no-project --with desflow flow_example.py

# 1. Install
pip install desflow

# 2. Download the example
desflow examples get flow --api builder
cd flow/builder

# 3. Run it
python flow_example.py
examples/builder/flow_example.py:routes
@app.task(
    service_id="picking",
    resource_id="pickers",
    # The first rule that holds wins; default catches the rest
    next={"when": [{"condition": "attr.gift == 1", "task": "wrap"}], "default": "pack"},
)
def pick(task_id, context):
    """Picks the order's items."""
    return {"event_type": "order_picked"}


# A timed step: a service and no resource, so no queued event and no wait.
# `set` is applied to the entity's attributes when the task finishes.
@app.task(service_id="wrapping", set={"wrapped": 1}, next="pack")
def wrap(task_id, context):
    """Wraps a gift."""
    return {"event_type": "gift_wrapped"}


# Drawn from this task's own random sequence: one parcel in ten is packed again
@app.task(
    service_id="packing",
    resource_id="packers",
    next={"weights": {"ship": 9, "pack": 1}},
)
def pack(task_id, context):
    """Packs the order."""
    return {"event_type": "order_packed"}

        {"when": [{"condition": "attr.gift == 1", "task": "wrap"}], "default": "pack"}
    ),

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
Conditions. A condition is a Python expression, parsed with Python's ast module and checked against a list of what is allowed before it is ever evaluated; nothing goes through eval. It may use:

  • numbers, True and False, and the arithmetic +, -, *, /, // and %;
  • the comparisons <, <=, >, >=, == and !=, and strings compared with == or !=;
  • and, or, not, and the conditional form a if c else b;
  • names with their source as a prefix: payload.<field>, attr.<name>, level.<name>, item.<field> (the item the task's store get took, Stores and Containers), wait.<branch>.done, .ok and .value (the task's wait) and signal.<name>.count, .ok and .value (Tasks and Processes), and registry["<path>"];
  • t, the simulation time in seconds.

A name carries its source so that adding a payload field cannot change what an attribute of the same name means, and so registry paths, which contain dots, can be written whole. Anything else is refused with a message that names it:

docs/snippets/pages/task_flow.py:refused
for text in ("payload.total ** 2", "x > 1", "open('orders.csv')"):
    try:
        Expression(text)
    except ValueError as error:
        print(error)

'payload.total ** 2' uses the operator Pow, which an expression cannot
'x > 1' uses the name 'x' (write payload.<field>, attr.<name>, level.<name>, item.<field>, wait.<branch>.<part>, signal.<name>.<part>, registry["<path>"] or t), which an expression cannot
'open('orders.csv')' uses a Call, which an expression cannot

A blueprint is checked when it loads: every condition parses, every task a rule names exists, every level.<name> names a store or container, and every registry["..."] is a path of the model, each with its YAML line. The builder makes the same checks when run() starts. A name that is missing when a condition is evaluated, such as a payload field, raises an error naming the expression.

Weights. The weights are turned into cumulative shares once. Each choice draws one uniform number from the routing task's stream and picks the task whose share it falls in.

Starting the Next Task. When a task finishes, it applies set, builds the Upstream, asks its rules for the next task and starts it as a new SimPy process, with the same entity and the next instance id from the task's counter. An arrival that spawns the task uses the same counter, so no two runs of a task share an id. In SimPy terms, one process starting the next is the whole mechanism; SimPy and desflow describes processes.

docs.title: Stability and Limits
docs.text:
• Flow balance. The rate into each task follows from the rates into the tasks before it and the routing shares. With weights 9 to 1 back to packing, each order is packed 1 ÷ 0.9 = 1.11 times on average, so the packers see 11% more work than there are orders.
  • Rework raises utilisation. Work the load out with the rework included, as Queues and Capacity does, or a rework loop can push a resource past full use.
  • Refused expressions. **, function calls, indexing other than registry["..."], list and dictionary literals, and bare names other than t are refused.
  • One entity, one flow. A task leads to at most one next task; splitting one order into several, or joining several into one, comes after 1.0.
  • decide is kept free. The task key decide is kept for decisions sent from outside for one entity, planned after 1.0; today it is refused like any unknown key.

docs.title: Tasks and Processes: SimulationContext
docs.text: A task is what one entity does: an order being packed, a return being logged. A process is anything else that runs over time: packers going on a break every hour, a speed that drifts, a shift plan. This page shows how to write each, what run() does with them, and what a task does step by step.

docs.title: What It Is
docs.text: Both are SimPy generators: functions that yield to wait. The builder and YAML write the common ones for you, and the low-level API writes them by hand. A task waits for what it needs, does its work for a sampled time, publishes an event at each step, and may lead to the next task. A process can do anything a generator can: wait, change values in the registry, publish records or start tasks.

docs.title: A Task
docs.text:
A task with a service and a resource asks for a unit of the resource, holds it for a time drawn from the service, and releases it. A task with neither takes no time and holds nothing: it publishes its payload at once, which suits an entity that only records that it happened, such as a return logged.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/tasks.yaml:task
tasks:
  pack_order:
    service: packing  # how long the work takes
    resource: packers  # what it holds while it works
    payload: {event_type: order_packed}  # the finished event's value
    next: print_label  # the task that follows; Task Flow has the other forms
  return_logged:
    # No service and no resource: publishes its payload at once
    payload: {event_type: return_logged}

payload is a fixed mapping. A payload that changes per entity is a Python function, called as function(task_id, context):

docs/snippets/yaml/tasks.yaml:payload-function
# also under tasks: a payload computed by a Python function
pack_with_delivery:
  service: packing
  resource: packers
  # Called as choose_delivery(task_id, context) when the order gets a packer
  payload: !python shop_logic.choose_delivery
docs/snippets/pages/tasks.py:builder-task
@app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="packers", next="print_label")
def pack_order(task_id: int):
    # Runs when the order gets a packer, before the packing time.
    # The returned dict is the finished event's value.
    return {"event_type": "order_packed"}


@app.task()  # no service and no resource: publishes at once
def return_logged(task_id: int):
    return {"event_type": "return_logged"}

The function is called with the task id and whatever the caller passes. It also receives entity, upstream and item by keyword when it declares a parameter of that name: the entity, what the previous task handed on, and what a store get took. A function that declares none of them works as before.

docs/snippets/pages/tasks.py:low-level-task
def pack_order_process(env, sampler, packers, key, task_id, label_ids):
    """What @app.task does, by hand."""
    path_id = "Shop.service.packing"

    def publish(value):
        env.publish_event(key, value, task="pack_order", instance=task_id)

    publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "queued"})
    with packers.request() as request:
        yield request
        publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "started"})
        payload = {"event_type": "order_packed"}
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(env.registry.get_config(path_id)))
        publish(payload)
    # next: print_label, a new instance for the same order
    env.process(print_label_process(env, sampler, key, next(label_ids)))

This is ordinary SimPy: packers.request() waits for a unit, env.timeout waits the service time, and leaving the with block releases the unit. env.publish_event at each step is what makes it produce records.

A task can also take from or add to a store or container (get, put), rank its requests (priority), and name the task that follows it (next); Stores and Containers, Resources and Task Flow describe each.

docs.title: A Timed Step
docs.text:
A task with a service and no resource is a timed step: work that takes time but needs nothing that can be busy, such as printing a label or waiting for a supplier. It publishes started at once, with no queued event, waits the sampled time, and publishes its finished event. Its wait is 0. It is SimPy's env.timeout: the tests check that it ends at the same simulation time as a plain SimPy timeout in all three APIs (SimPy Compatibility).

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/tasks.yaml:timed-step
print_label:
  # A service and no resource: a timed step that starts at once
  service: labelling
  payload: {event_type: label_printed}
docs/snippets/pages/tasks.py:builder-timed-step
@app.task(service_id="labelling")  # a service and no resource: starts at once
def print_label(task_id: int):
    return {"event_type": "label_printed"}
docs/snippets/pages/tasks.py:low-level-timed-step
def print_label_process(env, sampler, key, task_id):
    """A timed step: started at once, with no queued event."""
    path_id = "Shop.service.labelling"

    def publish(value):
        env.publish_event(key, value, task="print_label", instance=task_id)

    publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "started"})
    yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(env.registry.get_config(path_id)))
    publish({"event_type": "label_printed"})

docs.title: Arrivals Start Tasks
docs.text:
An arrival starts one task per arrival. The loop draws a gap from the arrival's distribution, waits for that duration, starts a task for the new entity, and repeats; the task runs on its own while the loop waits for the next arrival.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/tasks.yaml:arrival
arrivals:
  # Each arrival spawns one pack_order, and one return_logged
  orders: {dist: exponential, rate: 0.2, spawn: pack_order}
  returns: {dist: exponential, rate: 0.1, spawn: return_logged}
docs/snippets/pages/tasks.py:builder-arrival
@app.arrival_loop("orders")
def orders(context: SimulationContext):
    task_id = 0
    while True:
        # Draws the next gap, waits for it, and returns the new entity, keyed orders-1, ...
        order = yield context.wait_for_arrival("orders")
        context.spawn(pack_order(task_id, entity=order))  # the loop goes on at once
        task_id += 1

context.wait_for_arrival returns the new Entity, whose key is the arrival name and a counter: orders-1, orders-2. Pass it to the task with entity=. A task called without one starts an entity of its own, keyed by the task's name and a counter, such as pack_order-1. The task_id becomes the record's instance. When next or a second arrival also starts the task, take the id from context.next_instance("pack_order") instead: it is the task's one counter, which next uses too, so no two runs of the task share an id.

docs/snippets/pages/tasks.py:low-level-arrival
def orders_process(env, sampler, packers):
    """What @app.arrival_loop does, by hand."""
    gap = env.registry.get_config("Shop.arrival.orders")
    label_ids = itertools.count()
    task_id = 0
    while True:
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(gap))
        key = f"orders-{task_id + 1}"
        env.process(pack_order_process(env, sampler, packers, key, task_id, label_ids))
        task_id += 1

In the low-level API every loop is started once, before the run:

docs/snippets/pages/tasks.py:low-level-start
env.process(orders_process(env, sampler, packers))  # start each loop once
env.process(breaks_process(env, "packers", every=50, duration=5))

docs.title: A Process
docs.text:
A process runs alongside the tasks. This one sends the packers on a 5-second break every 50 seconds:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/tasks.yaml:process
processes:
  # Called as breaks(context, resource="packers", every=50, duration=5)
  - function: !python shop_logic.breaks
    kwargs: {resource: packers, every: 50, duration: 5}
docs/snippets/pages/tasks.py:builder-process
def breaks(context: SimulationContext, resource: str, every: float, duration: float):
    """Takes every packer off for a break of `duration` seconds every `every` seconds."""
    path = f"{context.sim_id}.resources.{resource}.current_cap"
    registry = context.env.registry
    while True:
        yield context.env.timeout(every)
        normal = registry.get(path).value
        registry.update(path, 0)
        yield context.env.timeout(duration)
        registry.update(path, normal)


app.add_process(breaks, resource="packers", every=50, duration=5)
docs/snippets/pages/tasks.py:low-level-process
def breaks_process(env, resource: str, every: float, duration: float):
    """What add_process starts, by hand: a plain SimPy generator."""
    path = f"Shop.resources.{resource}.current_cap"
    while True:
        yield env.timeout(every)
        normal = env.registry.get(path).value
        env.registry.update(path, 0)
        yield env.timeout(duration)
        env.registry.update(path, normal)

Setting current_cap to 0 stops new work but not the work in progress: Resources explains what happens to busy units when a capacity drops.

docs.title: Wait, Signals and Child Flows
docs.text:
A task can wait for something before it queues for its resource: its wait. A wait has one branch, or any or all of several named branches, as SimPy's AnyOf and AllOf wait for the first or for every event:

Branch Waits for Its value {signal: name} the next firing of a signal declared under signals (builder add_signal) the firing's value, the payload of the task that fired it {task: name} a child flow: that task, started for the same entity with its own instance id, and the tasks its next leads to, until the flow ends the last task's finished payload {timeout: 40 s} a time none {condition: level.stock >= 5} a condition to hold, checked when the wait starts and again after every store or container change, registry update, signal firing and finished task True

A single branch is named after its signal or task, or timeout or condition. After the wait, wait.<branch>.done says whether the branch happened before the wait ended, .ok whether it succeeded, and .value (or .value.<field>) is its value; next, fail and amounts read them, and a builder function that declares wait receives them as a mapping. A task fires a signal with signal: name when it finishes, with its payload as the value, and signal.<name>.count, .ok and .value read the signal in any condition. The process-interaction example waits for a child flow, then for the first of a courier's signal and a time limit:

YAMLBuilderLow-level examples/yaml/process_interaction.yaml:check
check:
  # Starts the child flow inspect and waits for it to end.
  wait: {task: inspect}
  payload: {event_type: order_checked}
  next: dispatch
inspect:
  service: inspecting
  payload: {event_type: inspected}
  # A gift fails inspection; on_fail sends it to wrap, and the flow goes on.
  fail: attr.gift == 1
  fail_reason: gift needs wrapping
  on_fail: wrap
wrap:
  service: wrapping
  payload: {event_type: wrapped}
examples/yaml/process_interaction.yaml:dispatch
dispatch:
  # The courier's departure, or 40 seconds, whichever comes first.
  wait:
    any:
      courier: {signal: courier_left}
      limit: {timeout: 40 s}
  payload: {event_type: dispatched}
  next:
    when: [{condition: wait.courier.done, task: by_courier}]
    default: by_post
examples/yaml/process_interaction.yaml:courier
courier:
  payload: {event_type: courier_left}
  # Fires courier_left with this payload; every order waiting for it resumes.
  signal: courier_left
examples/builder/process_interaction_example.py:check
# Starts the child flow inspect and waits for it to end
@app.task(wait={"task": "inspect"}, next="dispatch")
def check(task_id, context):
    return {"event_type": "order_checked"}


# A gift fails inspection; on_fail sends it to wrap, and the flow goes on
@app.task(
    service_id="inspecting",
    fail="attr.gift == 1",
    fail_reason="gift needs wrapping",
    on_fail="wrap",
)
def inspect(task_id, context):
    return {"event_type": "inspected"}


@app.task(service_id="wrapping")
def wrap(task_id, context):
    return {"event_type": "wrapped"}
examples/builder/process_interaction_example.py:dispatch
# The courier's departure, or 40 seconds, whichever comes first
@app.task(
    wait={"any": {"courier": {"signal": "courier_left"}, "limit": {"timeout": 40}}},
    next={
        "when": [{"condition": "wait.courier.done", "task": "by_courier"}],
        "default": "by_post",
    },
)
def dispatch(task_id, context):
    return {"event_type": "dispatched"}
examples/builder/process_interaction_example.py:courier
# Fires courier_left with this payload; every order waiting for it resumes
@app.task(signal="courier_left")
def courier(task_id, context):
    return {"event_type": "courier_left"}

context.signal(name) returns the Signal a process can fire, fail or wait for, and context.call(task, entity=...) starts a child flow from a process and returns its SimPy process, which a process can yield. context.spawn returns the process it starts too, so is_alive, triggered, ok and value inspect it, as in SimPy.

examples/low-level/process_interaction_example.py:check
def check(shop, key, arrival):
    """Starts the child process inspect and waits for it to end."""
    env, stats, task_id = shop.env, shop.env.stats, shop.next_id("check")
    shop.publish(key, "check", task_id, {"status": "queued"})
    stats.task_queued("check", task_id)
    yield env.any_of([env.process(inspect(shop, key, arrival))])
    shop.publish(key, "check", task_id, {"status": "started"})
    stats.task_started("check", task_id)
    shop.publish(key, "check", task_id, {"event_type": "order_checked"})
    stats.task_finished("check", task_id)
    env.process(dispatch(shop, key, arrival))


def inspect(shop, key, arrival):
    """A gift fails inspection and is wrapped instead; returns the last payload."""
    env, stats, task_id = shop.env, shop.env.stats, shop.next_id("inspect")
    path_id = "Shop.service.inspecting"
    shop.publish(key, "inspect", task_id, {"path_id": path_id, "status": "started"})
    stats.task_started("inspect", task_id)
    yield env.timeout(shop.service("inspecting")[1])
    if GIFT[arrival] == 1:
        failed = {
            "path_id": path_id,
            "status": "failed",
            "reason": "gift needs wrapping",
        }
        shop.publish(key, "inspect", task_id, failed)
        stats.task_failed("inspect", task_id)
        return (yield env.process(wrap(shop, key)))
    payload = {"event_type": "inspected"}
    shop.publish(key, "inspect", task_id, payload)
    stats.task_finished("inspect", task_id)
    return payload


def wrap(shop, key):
    env, stats, task_id = shop.env, shop.env.stats, shop.next_id("wrap")
    path_id = "Shop.service.wrapping"
    shop.publish(key, "wrap", task_id, {"path_id": path_id, "status": "started"})
    stats.task_started("wrap", task_id)
    yield env.timeout(shop.service("wrapping")[1])
    payload = {"event_type": "wrapped"}
    shop.publish(key, "wrap", task_id, payload)
    stats.task_finished("wrap", task_id)
    return payload
examples/low-level/process_interaction_example.py:dispatch
def dispatch(shop, key, arrival):
    """The courier's departure, or 40 seconds, whichever comes first."""
    env, stats, task_id = shop.env, shop.env.stats, shop.next_id("dispatch")
    shop.publish(key, "dispatch", task_id, {"status": "queued"})
    stats.task_queued("dispatch", task_id)
    courier = shop.courier_left.wait()
    done = yield env.any_of([courier, env.timeout(40)])
    shop.publish(key, "dispatch", task_id, {"status": "started"})
    stats.task_started("dispatch", task_id)
    shop.publish(key, "dispatch", task_id, {"event_type": "dispatched"})
    stats.task_finished("dispatch", task_id)
    task = "by_courier" if courier in done else "by_post"
    env.process(send(shop, key, arrival, task))
examples/low-level/process_interaction_example.py:courier
def courier(shop, key):
    """Fires courier_left; every order waiting for it resumes."""
    task_id = shop.next_id("courier")
    shop.env.stats.flow_started("couriers")
    payload = {"event_type": "courier_left"}
    shop.publish(key, "courier", task_id, payload)
    shop.env.stats.task_finished("courier", task_id)
    shop.courier_left.fire(payload)
    shop.env.stats.flow_finished("couriers")
    yield shop.env.timeout(0)

The low-level API is SimPy: a child is env.process(...), its value is what it returns, and env.any_of and env.all_of wait for the first or for every event. Signal(env, name) is the named event the builder and YAML use; env.watch_changes(check) calls check after every change a condition can read.

The task publishes queued when its wait starts, so the wait counts in its wait statistics, and its patience covers the wait as well as its resource and its get. When an any wait ends, its losing signal, timeout and condition branches are dropped, and its losing child flows keep running, as SimPy leaves processes running; Wait for One or All shows ties and failures. A wait holds no resource, so waiting for all of several things grants nothing at once.

docs.title: Failures
docs.text:
A task fails when its fail condition holds after its service, when the wait it needs fails, or when its function raises: a builder task's function, or a YAML task's !python payload function. fail reads the task's own payload as payload.<field>, as next does. A failed task publishes failed with a reason, the condition's text or its fail_reason, instead of its finished payload; it fails its signal, so every waiter of the signal fails too; and it goes to its on_fail task. Without on_fail the entity's flow ends, and a child flow fails the task waiting for it, with the same reason. Each failure is counted as tasks.<task>.failed, and a flow that ends in one as flows.<arrival>.failed, at basic and above. The inspect task of the example above fails a gift and sends it to be wrapped.

In the low-level API a failure is SimPy's: an exception raised in a process reaches the process that yields it, and one nobody handles stops the run. The builder and YAML end only the entity's flow, because a data generator should not stop on one failed order.

docs.title: Example: Process Interaction
docs.text:
The process-interaction example puts these together: a child flow, a failure that on_fail handles, and orders that wait for a courier's signal or a time limit. It needs no Docker service and ends on its own after 300 simulation seconds.

YAMLBuilderLow-level

docs.title: Records of a Task
docs.text:
Every event of a task carries three fields beside its value: key, the entity's key; task, the task's name; and instance, the number of this run of the task, counted from 0 for each task. The first order of the blueprint in A Task, packed and then labelled:

[EVT] {'sim_ts': 3.672, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'orders-1', 'task': 'pack_order', 'instance': 0, 'value': {'path_id': 'Shop.service.packing', 'status': 'queued'}}
[EVT] {'sim_ts': 3.672, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'orders-1', 'task': 'pack_order', 'instance': 0, 'value': {'path_id': 'Shop.service.packing', 'status': 'started'}}
[EVT] {'sim_ts': 5.369, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'orders-1', 'task': 'pack_order', 'instance': 0, 'value': {'event_type': 'order_packed'}}
[EVT] {'sim_ts': 5.369, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'orders-1', 'task': 'print_label', 'instance': 0, 'value': {'path_id': 'Shop.service.labelling', 'status': 'started'}}
[EVT] {'sim_ts': 7.369, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'orders-1', 'task': 'print_label', 'instance': 0, 'value': {'event_type': 'label_printed'}}

All five events share the key orders-1, so an order can be followed through every task it passes. The finished event's value is exactly the payload. Records and Telemetry describes every field.

docs.title: What run() Does
docs.text:
run() builds everything the context describes and runs it, in this order:

Until run() is called nothing exists but the description: context.env, context.spawn and context.get_resource raise RuntimeError before it. Teardown runs in a finally block, so the last statistics are published and every sink is flushed even when the run stops with an error or Ctrl+C.

docs.title: What @app.task Does
docs.text:
@app.task turns your function into a SimPy process that does these steps, publishing a record at three of them:

  1. If its balk condition holds, it publishes balked and stops.
  2. If it has a wait, a resource or a get, it publishes queued, starts its patience timer, which runs only while it waits, and waits for its wait.
  3. It asks for the resource, in the resource's queue order, then takes its get from a store or container, waiting while there is not enough.
  4. It publishes started, calls your function, and keeps what it returns as the payload. The payload is computed before the service time, so it can use the state of the simulation at that moment.
  5. It waits the service time, drawn from the live distribution.
  6. It adds its put to a store or container, waiting while there is no room, and checks its fail condition.
  7. It publishes the payload as the finished event, or failed, and releases the resource.
  8. It fires its signal (or fails it), sends its interrupt action to the tasks it names, applies set to the entity's attributes, and starts the next task its next chooses, or its on_fail task, as a new instance for the same entity.

A YAML task and its spawn make the same task and arrival loop that the builder code above makes. The code that runs these steps is TaskRun in desflow/core/task.py. In SimPy terms each task run is one process started with env.process, and each arrival loop is another; SimPy and desflow describes processes.

docs.title: Processes and the Low-level API
docs.text: add_process(func, **kwargs) starts func(context, **kwargs) when the run starts, and a YAML processes entry does the same with a !python function. Inside it, context.env is the DynamicRealtimeEnvironment, so a process can do anything a low-level script does: context.env.timeout, context.env.registry.update, context.env.publish_event. This is how low-level code joins a builder or YAML model.

docs.title: Stability and Limits
docs.text:
• Resources are acquired in one order. A task can hold several resources and hand one to the next task, but tasks that acquire two resources in opposite orders are refused: Resources.
  • An interrupt gives back everything. An interrupted task cancels its waits and releases every unit it holds before it follows its on_interrupt, so a resumed task queues again behind the requests already waiting: Interruptions.
  • A finished event is exactly the payload. It has no status or path_id unless the payload includes them.
  • A condition branch checks after every change. A model with many waits on conditions and many changes does work in proportion to both.
  • Runtime helpers need a running simulation. context.spawn, context.call, context.signal, context.get_resource, context.get_store, context.get_container and context.env raise RuntimeError before run(); call them inside a loop, task or process.

docs.title: Time and Pacing
docs.text: A run has two clocks, and a run can follow the wall clock, ignore it, or switch from one to the other. This page shows the clock settings, the warm-up, how long a run lasts, and which parts of the environment run on each thread.

docs.title: What It Is
docs.text:
Simulation time is the number of seconds SimPy has advanced, starting at initial_time, 0 by default; every record carries it as sim_ts. Logical time is the date and time a record carries as timestamp: logical_start_time plus the simulation time. factor sets how simulation time relates to the wall clock, and go_live_at switches that relation once during a run. One hour of simulation time is one hour of logical time, and takes as long on the wall clock as factor says:

The settings are the same on DynamicRealtimeEnvironment, on SimulationContext and in the simulation section of a blueprint.

docs.title: Logical Start Time
docs.text:
logical_start_time is the date and time that simulation time 0 maps to; without it, the run uses the moment the environment is created. A run with a backdated start writes history:

docs/snippets/pages/pacing.py:logical-start
app = SimulationContext(
    sim_id="Shop",
    factor=0.0,
    logical_start_time=datetime.now(timezone.utc) - timedelta(days=7),  # a week
)

A datetime without an offset is read in the run's time zone, described next. In a blueprint it takes now, a signed duration such as -7d, or an ISO datetime, as YAML Blueprints describes.

docs.title: Time Zone
docs.text:
timezone names the zone that record timestamps are written in, as an IANA name such as Australia/Melbourne. Every timestamp carries the offset of its moment, such as 2026-10-03T12:00:00.000+10:00, or +00:00 in UTC. By default the zone is that of logical_start_time when it has one, and UTC otherwise. A logical_start_time or go_live_at without an offset, now, and the default start are read in it:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/environment.yaml:timezone
# Under simulation: timestamps written in Melbourne time, with its offset; the
# start and now are read in it. UTC by default
timezone: ${SIM_TIMEZONE:-Australia/Melbourne}
docs/snippets/pages/pacing.py:timezone
# Timestamps in Melbourne time, with their offset: 2026-10-03T12:00:00.000+10:00
melbourne = SimulationContext(
    sim_id="Shop",
    factor=0.0,
    timezone="Australia/Melbourne",
    logical_start_time=datetime(2026, 10, 3, 12, 0),  # read in Melbourne time
)
docs/snippets/pages/pacing.py:low-level-timezone
zoned = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(
    factor=0.0,
    timezone="Australia/Melbourne",
    logical_start_time=datetime(2026, 10, 3, 12, 0),
)
print(zoned.start_datetime)  # 2026-10-03 12:00:00+10:00

The clock runs in UTC, so a daylight-saving change in the zone never adds or drops simulation time: in Melbourne, where the clocks went forward an hour on 4 October 2026, 24 hours of simulation from 12:00 on 3 October end at 13:00 on 4 October, 2026-10-04T13:00:00.000+11:00. A replayed timestamp without an offset is read in the zone too.

docs.title: Factor
docs.text:
The wall-clock duration of a stretch of the run is its simulation duration times factor:

docs/snippets/pages/pacing.py:factor
live = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=1.0)  # 1 simulated second takes 1 real second
twice_as_fast = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=0.5)  # takes half a real second
unpaced = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=0.0)  # takes no real time at all
  • factor: 1.0 follows the wall clock: a process that waits 5 simulation seconds waits 5 real seconds. It suits a live twin feeding a dashboard.
  • factor: 0 does not wait at all: the run goes as fast as the machine allows. It suits history, tests and experiments. At factor: 0, once no go_live_at is pending, each event is processed by SimPy's own Environment.step, without the real-time arithmetic, and strict is not checked, as there is no wall clock to fall behind; before a pending go-live the real-time step runs, as it does after.

docs.title: Go Live
docs.text:
factor applies until the logical clock reaches go_live_at, and from that instant the run is paced at one simulation second per real second. With a backdated logical_start_time and factor: 0, one run writes the history as fast as it can, then keeps going in real time:

docs/snippets/pages/pacing.py:go-live
go_live_at = datetime.now(timezone.utc)

env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(
    factor=0.0,  # until go_live_at
    logical_start_time=go_live_at - timedelta(days=7),
    go_live_at=go_live_at,  # from here, 1 simulated second per real second
)

A sink with when: history receives the records stamped before go_live_at, and one with when: live the rest, so the two halves can go to different places:

Parquet History, Kafka Live builds such a run.

docs.title: Lag
docs.text:
At a factor above 0 the run follows the wall clock, and system.simulation.lag_seconds says how many seconds it is behind, as telemetry. lag_interval sets how often, in simulation seconds or a duration. By default it is every simulation second at a factor above 0, and off at factor: 0, where the run is meant to be ahead of the wall clock; a run at factor: 0 that goes live starts it at the go-live instant. 0 turns it off:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/environment.yaml:lag
# Under simulation: how far the run is behind the wall clock, every 10 s; by
# default off at factor 0 and every second otherwise, and 0 turns it off
lag_interval: 10 s
docs/snippets/pages/pacing.py:lag
# system.simulation.lag_seconds every 10 simulation seconds; 0 turns it off
paced = SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=1.0, lag_interval="10 s")
docs/snippets/pages/pacing.py:low-level-lag
# The low-level API sets it with the sinks; the default "auto" is off at factor 0
# env.setup_egress(sinks, lag_monitor_interval=10)

docs.title: Warm-up
docs.text:
warmup leaves the start of a run out of what it reports. It is one time per run, in simulation seconds or a duration. No sink receives a record or telemetry stamped before it, and the built-in statistics are reset once at that moment, so they describe the rest of the run. A run without it sends everything, which is what a data generator usually wants.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/trusting_results.yaml:warmup
# Records and statistics start after the first 2 minutes; 0 keeps everything
warmup: ${WARMUP:-2 min}
docs/snippets/pages/pacing.py:warmup
# No sink receives a record stamped before 10 minutes, and the statistics restart then
measured = SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0.0, warmup="10 min")
# In the low-level API, the warm-up is set with the sinks:
# env.setup_egress(sinks, warmup=600)

The warm-up is an argument of the sinks, because it is the sinks that leave records out: env.setup_egress(sinks, warmup=600). A run with no sink has nothing to leave out, and its statistics are reset at the warm-up as well when it is set through the builder.

The warm-up drops early records; go_live_at drops nothing and only decides which sink gets each one. Trusting Results shows how to choose a warm-up length.

docs.title: Initial Time
docs.text:
initial_time is the reading of the simulation clock when the run starts, 0 when left out, in seconds or as a duration. A model of a shift that starts at 8 in the morning can start its clock at 8 hours, so every event time, every record's sim_ts and until read that clock; a record's timestamp is still logical_start_time plus sim_ts, to within the 1 millisecond by which a rounded sim_ts and a cut timestamp can differ:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/initial_time.yaml:initial-time
simulation:
  sim_id: Shop
  factor: 0
  # The clock starts at 8 h, so the first order at 8 h 10 min is at sim_ts 29400
  initial_time: 8 h
docs/snippets/pages/pacing.py:initial-time
# The clock starts at 8 hours: event times, sim_ts and until all read it
shift = SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0.0, initial_time="8 h")
docs/snippets/pages/pacing.py:low-level-initial-time
# The clock starts at 8 hours, in seconds, as in SimPy's Environment(initial_time=)
morning = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=0.0, initial_time=8 * 3600)

until is a clock reading too, so a run with initial_time: 8 h and until: 16 h lasts 8 hours. A scenario step's at and the warmup are lengths of time from the start of the run instead, so with initial_time: 8 h a step at 30 min applies at 8.5 hours, and a warm-up of 10 min ends at 8 hours 10 minutes. The state the run starts with is declared beside it: a resource's current_cap, a container's level, a store's items and an arrival's attributes hold from the initial time, before the first arrival, and the tests check each against plain SimPy (SimPy Compatibility).

docs.title: Run Length
docs.text:
until is in simulation seconds. run() and a blueprint's run.until also take a duration such as "10 min", "8 hours" or "1 week"; a month counts as 30 days and a year as 365.

docs/snippets/pages/pacing.py:run-length
app.add_resource("packers", current_cap=1, max_cap=1)
app.run(until="1 week")  # 604,800 simulation seconds; a number is seconds too

The run stops at until before any event due at exactly that time, as SimPy's run(until=...) does: an order due at the horizon never arrives, and a task due to finish there stays unfinished. Statistics published at teardown read the model at until.

Without until, SimPy runs until no events remain, and a run with an arrival never runs out of events. Neither does any run with a sink or an ingress connector, even when its own work is done, because the environment's own processes repeat for as long as the run lasts. Give such a run an until, a stop or a drain, or stop it with Ctrl+C.

docs.title: Stop Early
docs.text: stop ends the run before until when something happens: {signal: name}, the next firing of a signal, or {condition: ...}, the first moment a condition holds, checked after every change of a level, a capacity, a registry value or a signal, and after every finished task. The builder's run(stop=...) also takes a signal's name, or a function of the context, called once the run is built, that returns any SimPy event, such as lambda context: context.env.timeout(30). The run ends at whichever comes first, stop or until, and no other event at that moment runs after it; when both fall at the same moment, until ends the run, as SimPy's own until would. In the low-level API it is SimPy's env.run(until=event).

docs.title: Drain
docs.text:
A fixed horizon cuts the run at until with orders still in the shop. A drain stops the arrivals at until and keeps running until every entity in the model has left: drain: true, or drain: {limit: 1 h} to stop at the latest that long after until; desflow run --drain sets it from the command line. The environment's own processes, such as the statistics timer, never hold a drain open. The end-conditions example closes the shop at 120 seconds, drains for at most a minute, and stops at once if the boxes run out:

YAMLBuilderLow-level examples/yaml/end_conditions.yaml:run
run:
  # No new orders after closing time.
  until: 120
  # Then pack the orders in the shop, for at most 60 seconds.
  drain: {limit: 60}
  # Stop at once when the last box is taken.
  stop: {condition: level.boxes == 0}
examples/builder/end_conditions_example.py:run
app.run(
    # No new orders after closing time
    until=120,
    # Then pack the orders in the shop, for at most 60 seconds
    drain={"limit": 60},
    # Stop at once when the last box is taken
    stop={"condition": "level.boxes == 0"},
)

context.stop_arrivals() stops the arrival loops by hand, as a drain does at until.

examples/low-level/end_conditions_example.py:run
def run_to_end(env, shop, source):
    """Runs to closing time, then drains for at most 60 s, or until no boxes are left."""
    out_of_boxes = env.event()

    def check():
        if shop["boxes"].level == 0 and not out_of_boxes.triggered:
            out_of_boxes.succeed()

    env.watch_changes(check)
    # Closing time, unless the boxes run out first, which ends the run at once
    env.run(until=env.timeout(120) | out_of_boxes)
    if out_of_boxes.triggered:
        return
    source.interrupt()  # no new orders after closing time
    packed = env.all_of([p for p in shop["orders"] if p.is_alive])
    env.run(until=packed | env.timeout(60) | out_of_boxes)

The low-level API writes a drain as SimPy does: interrupt the source process, then run until all the admitted processes end.

With statistics at basic or above, flows.<arrival>.started, finished and in_system say how many entities entered, left and are still in the model, and from minimal, tasks.<task>.in_progress how many instances of each task are queued or being served; End Conditions compares a fixed horizon with a drain.

docs.title: Step and Peek
docs.text:
start() builds everything run() builds and starts every process, with the clock still at its start. step() then processes one event, and peek() gives the time of the next one, infinity when none is left, as SimPy's env.step() and env.peek() do. The event can be one of desflow's own, such as the statistics timer or a resource's capacity watcher, as well as one of the model's; finish() runs a started run on to the end run() would reach, until, the stop or the end of the drain, then closes it, so run() is start() then finish(); close() ends the run where it is. A context from from_yaml steps the same way:

docs/snippets/pages/pacing.py:step
def every_ten(context):
    while True:
        yield context.env.timeout(10)


stepped = SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0.0).add_process(every_ten)
stepped.start()  # builds everything run() builds; the clock is still at 0
while stepped.peek() < 30:  # the time of the next event
    stepped.step()  # processes exactly one event
print(f"stopped before {stepped.peek()} at {stepped.env.now}")
stepped.close()  # the teardown run() does at its end

It prints stopped before 30 at 20. Stepping does not stop at until: compare peek() with the time you want to stop at.
